Kubernetes Events are a third source, and distinct from both: they are the cluster’s account of what happened to your objects, they expire (typically an hour), and they are where this chart’s failures show up first: Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503 when a dependency is down, FailedCreate … violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest" when a pod spec regresses under enforcement, Unhealthy and Killing during a rollout. Check kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp before the application log when a pod will not start: the reason is usually there, and it is usually not in the log, because the container never ran.

On a managed control plane

On EKS, GKE, AKS or an equivalent, several controls in this audit stop being yours: you cannot set API-server flags, reach etcd, or configure kubelet authentication. In exchange you inherit the provider’s defaults, which may be stronger or weaker than this sheet assumes, and which you should verify rather than assume.

ControlOn a managed cluster
Host hardening, node OS patchingprovider’s, though node images and upgrades are usually still yours to trigger
API-server flags, authorization modeprovider’s (RBAC is on by default everywhere mainstream)
etcd access + encryption at restprovider’s, but envelope encryption with your own KMS key is usually opt-in, and it is the control our Secrets need
Kubelet authenticationprovider’s
Control-plane audit loggingprovider’s to enable, often off or short-retention by default, and usually billed
User namespaces (hostUsers: false)depends on the node image’s runtime version, which is why the pod fails loudly rather than downgrading
Pod Security Admissionyours (namespace labels)
NetworkPolicyyours to write; enforcement depends on the CNI
Everything the chart setsunchanged: it is a workload

Check the CNI before relying on the shipped NetworkPolicy. This is the item that varies most and fails most silently: a NetworkPolicy on a cluster whose network plugin does not enforce it is an object the API accepts, stores and displays, with no effect and no warning. Provider defaults differ, versions change them, and some require enabling enforcement at cluster creation, which cannot be changed afterwards on some platforms. Do not read your provider’s documentation and conclude; test it:

kubectl create namespace ferroehr-probe
kubectl -n ferroehr-probe run probe --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never --command -- sleep 600
kubectl -n ferroehr-probe exec probe -- nc -w3 -z <ferroehr-pod-ip> 5432   # must fail
kubectl -n ferroehr-probe exec probe -- nc -w3 -z <ferroehr-pod-ip> 8080   # must succeed

If the first command succeeds, the policy is decoration and every claim in this section that rests on it is void for your cluster. This is also the reason the project’s own deployment probe harness declares NetworkPolicy enforcement as something it does not exercise: a green result on one cluster’s CNI would say nothing about yours.

Provider audit tooling exists: for EKS, hardeneks is the commonly cited one. We have not run it, so it is named as a starting point rather than a recommendation: treat its output as input to the same ownership question this section asks, not as a verdict.

From source

You can build the ferroehr binary yourself: for a platform without a published image, for local development, or to run the test suite. This chapter covers the prerequisites and the build. Most operators should prefer the published container images (Docker Compose, Kubernetes & Helm); build from source when you need to.

Prerequisites

  • The pinned Rust toolchain. The repository pins Rust 1.99.1 (edition 2024) via rust-toolchain.toml, so rustup installs and selects it automatically the first time you build in the checkout; you do not choose a version by hand.
  • Docker: required only for the integration tests, which spin up a real PostgreSQL 18 in a container.
  • xmllint: required only for the canonical-XML tests.

Building

From the repository root:

cargo build --workspace

To build just the server binary in release mode (what the container image ships):

cargo build --release --locked -p ferroehr-server

The binary crate is ferroehr-server; the executable it produces is named ferroehr, so the resulting binary is target/release/ferroehr. It links a pure-Rust TLS stack (no OpenSSL, no JVM, no runtime dependencies) so it drops into a minimal base image or runs directly on the host.

Running the tests

cargo nextest run --workspace

Every database-backed test takes its database from a shared harness: one PostgreSQL 18 server, one migrated template database, and a fast clone per test. By default the harness starts (or re-adopts) a single reusable postgres:18 container, so Docker must be running; reclaim it afterwards with docker rm -f ferroehr-testkit-pg18. To use a PostgreSQL 18 server you already run instead, point the suite at it and Docker is not needed at all:

export FERROEHR_TEST_PG_URL='postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/postgres'
cargo nextest run --workspace

The role in that DSN must be allowed to CREATE DATABASE.

Running the binary

The binary is configured entirely through FERROEHR_* environment variables (see the configuration reference). At minimum it needs a database URL:

export FERROEHR__DATABASE__URL='postgres://ferroehr:ferroehr@localhost:5432/ferroehr'
target/release/ferroehr

It runs its schema migrations at boot and then serves on the configured bind address (default 0.0.0.0:8080). That boot-time migration is a setting, not a fixture: db.migrate = "verify" makes the server issue no DDL at all, for a deployment whose database role has none of those rights (see Operations).

Two global flags and three subcommand groups round the CLI out:

  • --config <path> points at a configuration file, overriding FERROEHR_CONFIG (with neither, the server reads no file);
  • --set <key>=<value> is a repeatable dotted-path override with the highest precedence of all (--set db.max_connections=40);
  • ferroehr config check validates the effective configuration and prints it redacted, exiting 0 when valid and 78 otherwise, the fastest way to test a deployment’s configuration before starting it;
  • ferroehr db migrate applies the embedded migrations and exits, the out-of-band schema step, run under a ferroehr_migrator DSN;
  • ferroehr db verify checks, without issuing any DDL, that the database carries exactly this build’s migrations, exiting 0 when it does;
  • ferroehr healthcheck (used by the container healthcheck and Kubernetes exec probes) asks GET /health/readiness on the configured server.listen port over the loopback and exits 0 on 200, 1 otherwise.

Note

Building from source gives you the same binary the images use: the container Dockerfile pins its Rust version from the same rust-toolchain.toml, and CI cross-checks the two so they cannot drift.

Build features

The server builds with two additive cargo features, both on by default: fhir (the FHIR terminology providers, and the FHIR AuditEvent the audit store, the audit feed and the ITI-81 retrieval carry), and multimedia (DV_MULTIMEDIA externalization to S3-compatible object storage). Their implementations live in a separate crate that the platform library pulls in only when the matching feature is on, so a build without them contains none of their code.

A slim build compiles them out entirely:

cargo build --release --locked -p ferroehr-server --no-default-features

A slim binary refuses loudly at boot if the configuration enables an integration it was built without: multimedia.enabled, audit.store.enabled, audit.fhir_feed.enabled, or a configured external FHIR terminology provider. The syslog ATNA feed and the in-process terminology bundle remain available in slim builds.

Warning

The local audit store is on in the shipped defaults, so a slim build refuses to start on an untouched configuration. To run one, disable it explicitly (FERROEHR__AUDIT__STORE__ENABLED=false) or configure the syslog feed as the audit sink; silently dropping the audit trail is not a boot mode.

Configuration reference

FerroEHR is configured by one file, ferroehr.toml, whose sections cover the entire server, with FERROEHR_* environment variables (and repeatable --set flags) as per-key overrides on top. This page is the entry point: the quickstart, how configuration loads and how environment names map onto the file, the one key that selects the openEHR specification generation set, and a map of which page documents which section.

  • Quickstart
  • How configuration loads
    • The environment-variable mapping
    • File discovery
    • Strict validation
    • Durations, sizes and periods
    • Keys a release before v5.7.0 read
  • deployment.spec_profile
    • Why it is one key and not two
    • Seeing which profile is active
    • What changes on the wire
    • Changing the profile on an existing deployment
  • deployment.profile
  • Where each section is documented

Quickstart

Copy the shipped template, edit it, and run:

# Every key under its description, each at its default, generated from the
# configuration types.
curl -fsSLo ferroehr.toml \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FerroHEALTH/FerroEHR/main/app/ferroehr/assets/ferroehr.default.toml

# Edit it — at minimum set database.url and an auth mechanism.
$EDITOR ferroehr.toml

# Validate without touching the database, then run.
ferroehr config check --config ferroehr.toml
ferroehr --config ferroehr.toml

A server started with no file and no environment still boots, with one exception you will hit immediately: authentication is on by default and a server with no mechanism configured refuses to start. See Zero-config boot and the production checklist.

How configuration loads

Configuration is assembled once at boot from four layers, lowest precedence to highest:

  1. Built-in defaults: the values in the tables on the section pages.
  2. The config file: ferroehr.toml (see file discovery).
  3. FERROEHR_* environment variables: override individual keys.
  4. --set key=value CLI flags (repeatable), which win over everything.

Some conventional names sit below their FERROEHR_ forms within layer 3:

  • DATABASE_URL → database.url, and RUST_LOG → telemetry.filter.
  • PORT → a 0.0.0.0:<PORT> value for server.listen (the port container platforms such as Vercel, Cloud Run and Heroku inject and route traffic to).
  • The libpq environment set (PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE, PGPORT, PGSSLMODE), which managed-Postgres integrations such as Neon inject: when PGHOST is set and no URL form is, the server assembles the DSN from them. An explicit DATABASE_URL beats the assembled form, and FERROEHR__DATABASE__URL beats both.

Nothing else has a non-FERROEHR_ name.

The environment-variable mapping

Every key has one mechanical environment spelling: FERROEHR + the TOML path, upper-cased, with a double underscore (__) between every segment, including after the FERROEHR prefix. A single underscore only ever appears inside a key word.

TOMLEnvironment variable
[database] max_connections = 20FERROEHR__DATABASE__MAX_CONNECTIONS=20
[authz.rbac] admin_role = "…"FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ADMIN_ROLE=…
[management.endpoints] env = "off"FERROEHR__MANAGEMENT__ENDPOINTS__ENV=off
[terminology.endpoint] url = "…"FERROEHR__TERMINOLOGY__ENDPOINT__URL=…

Scalars are typed automatically (bool / int / float, else string). List-typed keys take comma-separated values (FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ROLE_ISSUERS=https://a,https://b). Map-keyed tables are reachable too: the map key is just another segment (FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__POLICY__COMPOSITION__NAME). An array of tables is set by element index: FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCE=ferroehr sets audience of the first [[auth.issuer]] table key by key over the file’s, and the next index past the end adds a table. An index with a leading zero, one that skips an element, or one under a key that holds no array of tables refuses the start.

Note

Enum values are lowercase / snake_case tokens, exactly as the tables show. Secret-typed keys are redacted everywhere the configuration is rendered (the /management/env snapshot, GET /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/config, ferroehr config check, ferroehr report, logs), and a secret-URL key shows its host and path with the embedded credentials masked. Each secret, and each database URL, has a *_file sibling that reads the value from a file, for Kubernetes and Docker secret mounts. Setting a key and its *_file sibling at once is a boot error.

File discovery

The server reads the file --config <path> names, or else the file FERROEHR_CONFIG=<path> names; later layers still override its values. A named file is fatal if absent, unreadable or unparseable. With neither set, the server reads no file and searches no directory: the environment and the defaults make the whole configuration.

Strict validation

Configuration is validated at boot (and by ferroehr config check), and the server refuses to start on any error:

  • Unknown keys are rejected: in the file, naming the key and the closest valid one, and in every FERROEHR__… override, so a misspelled security key can never be silently ignored. Only the uniform FERROEHR__<SECTION>__<KEY> form sets a key. Any other FERROEHR_ variable, such as the single-underscore FERROEHR_DB_URL, sets nothing and is left alone, because the viewer’s FERROEHR_VIEWER_ variables share the prefix.
  • Type errors are boot errors, naming the key and what was expected.
  • Semantic errors are aggregated: one pass reports every problem at once, so a broken configuration is fixed in a single iteration.

Durations, sizes and periods

Every duration is one string with its unit and no space: "30s", "10min", "12h", "7d", or milliseconds with ms. The unit symbols are the UCUM codes (ms, s, min, h, d), the unit system FHIR Quantity and openEHR DV_QUANTITY use, so "10m" is refused (m is the metre) and a bare number is refused, never read as seconds or milliseconds. Every size is one string with an IEC 80000-13 binary unit: "512B", "256KiB", "64MiB", or GiB; a decimal unit such as MB is refused. A retention is an ISO 8601 calendar period of whole years or days, "P5Y" or "P1830D"; unset keeps forever. The environment carries the same strings: FERROEHR__RECORD__QUERY__TIMEOUT=45s. [server] and [auth] are family sections that keep their own key shapes until the family releases move them.

Keys a release before v5.7.0 read

v5.7.0 moved the configuration tree to one table per concern. Every key an earlier release read is refused at load with the key that replaced it, all of them in one pass, so ferroehr config check --config <old file> prints the whole move list for an old file:

db was replaced by [database]: db.acquire_timeout_secs is database.acquire_timeout ...
rest was replaced by [api]: rest.swagger_ui is api.openapi_ui ...
audit.store.retention_days was replaced by audit.store.retention, a calendar period ...

No key is read under two names. These refusals ship in v5.7.0 only; the next release removes them, and an old key is then an unknown key. The full map is in the v5.7.0 changelog.

deployment.spec_profile

# The openEHR specification generation set the server runs.
[deployment]
spec_profile = "development"   # or "stable"

openEHR publishes released specification versions and keeps developing the next ones. FerroEHR generates both, and this key decides which set the running server serves.

ValueRMBASEChoose it when
development (default)1.2.01.3.0You want the generations this build is developed against. This is the default for every deployment that does not set the key.
stable1.1.01.2.0Your governance requires running on released openEHR specifications only.

Environment form: FERROEHR__DEPLOYMENT__SPEC_PROFILE=stable.

Why it is one key and not two

The components’ generations are modelled against each other, not independently: RM 1.1.0’s own machine-readable model declares that it includes BASE 1.2.0. Letting you pick RM 1.1.0 with BASE 1.3.0 would offer a combination openEHR never published, so the profile is a single coupled choice and incoherent sets are unrepresentable.

Seeing which profile is active

The profile is reported in two places, so it is never a guess:

  • the boot banner, on every start, alongside the RM version it serves;
  • GET /management/info, which names the active profile with the RM and BASE generations it selects, next to the build provenance.

What changes on the wire

The profile is an acceptance boundary, and it is exact in both directions.

Under stable, a query that addresses specification surface the released generations do not define is refused with a typed error naming the active profile: an AQL FROM class or a path attribute RM 1.1.0 does not declare is rejected at planning time rather than answered as though it existed.

Released surface the development line later dropped stays accepted under stable, which is the half most implementations get wrong. A demographic party carrying the RM 1.1.0 PARTY.reverse_relationships attribute is read and accepted under stable; development refuses it as an undeclared key, because RM 1.2.0 removed it. The attribute is derived data the server recomputes from relationships, so the copy you send is validated and then dropped rather than stored.

Reading a stored object is bounded the same way. Every commit records whether the released generations can express the body it accepted, and under stable a stored version they cannot is refused with 409 Conflict naming the active profile, the version, and the remedy; never served under a generation set that does not define it, and never rewritten to fit one. Under development the same object reads normally. This is FerroEHR’s own extension: no openEHR specification governs runtime version selection, so the status follows HTTP itself (RFC 9110 §15.5.10, a conflict with the current state of the target resource, whose resolution the response describes).

Queries take the same refusal wherever they serve a version body. AQL is gated in two places, and they answer different questions. At planning time the query text is checked: a FROM class or path attribute the released generations do not declare is rejected. At result assembly the projection is checked: a whole-object projection (SELECT c FROM EHR e CONTAINS COMPOSITION c) returns stored version bodies, so if any row of the page comes from a version the released generations cannot express, the whole query answers 409 Conflict naming that version. The row is never quietly dropped from the result set instead: a RESULT_SET is columns and rows of values with nowhere to explain a missing row, so silently eliding one would be an answer you could not tell from “no such data”.

A leaf projection over the very same rows (SELECT c/name/value FROM EHR e CONTAINS COMPOSITION c) still answers 200. It serves data values rather than version bodies, over paths the planning gate has already bounded to the released generation’s declared surface. That is the honest boundary: the profile is an acceptance boundary on what is served as an openEHR object, not a content filter over the values inside one.

Under development none of this applies and it costs nothing: the assembly gate returns before it touches the database.

The exact additive delta between the two generation sets is pinned in the build, so a future openEHR re-vendoring cannot silently widen or narrow what a profile accepts.

Changing the profile on an existing deployment

Treat the profile as a deployment commitment. Both directions are defined, but they are not symmetric:

DirectionSupported?Why
stable → developmentAlways safeopenEHR minor releases are additive by the Foundation’s own release strategy, so every object stored under the released generations is valid under the development ones.
development → stableOnly for data that never used a development-only constructThere is no down-conversion. An object that did use one becomes unreadable (409, not a silently degraded body) until you switch back.

If you need to stay on released specifications, choose stable on day one rather than migrating into it later. Silently rewriting stored clinical content to fit an older generation would be data loss disguised as a setting, so no tool does it.

Objects committed before this stamp existed, and objects written by the verbatim-replay paths (EHR-Extract import, archive load), carry no recorded answer; they are assessed at read instead, which costs one extra parse per read of such an object and only under stable. Nothing is written back: a read stays a read.

Note

No openEHR specification governs runtime version selection; this key is FerroEHR’s own design. What the specifications do govern is the compatibility direction it relies on: minor releases within a major line are additive supersets.

deployment.profile

# The declared posture: what this deployment may hold.
[deployment]
profile = "sandbox"   # or "production"
accepts = []          # production only: gaps run without, by name

Every separation FerroEHR can make is a configuration key an operator can leave unset, and a deployment that has made none of them looks, from its own logs and its own API, like one that has made all of them. This key gives the server a declared posture and makes the two impossible to confuse.

ValueAssertsOn boot
sandbox (the binary’s default; the Helm chart has none and refuses to render until you choose)Nothing; the deployment must not hold real personal dataSays which separations are missing: a red notice on the banner, one warn line per gap with the structured field posture = "deployment", and the same list on GET /management/status under deployment; the public GET /ferroehr/rest/status carries the profile only
productionEvery separation below holds, or is accepted by name in deployment.acceptsRefuses to start otherwise, naming each open gap, what it found and what to change

The separations, each a real property the server checks rather than a box ticked by being present:

Gap tokenWhat production requires
shared_credential[database.party] url (or [database.clinical] url) set, so the two domains connect on their own database roles
shared_clusterThe three pools reach three different PostgreSQL clusters, read from pg_control_system().system_identifier on each pool, never from the DSN text. The audit pool counts: Swiss law keeps the access log on a system separate from the one processing the data
open_subject_namespace[privacy] subject_namespaces declared, so an EHR_STATUS subject is an opaque pseudonym
audit_off[audit] enabled with a durable sink (the local store, syslog or the FHIR feed)
audit_fails_open[audit] fail_mode = "closed", so an operation whose access record cannot be taken is refused instead of succeeding unlogged
no_category_mapA category map applies while auditing is on: the one FerroEHR ships (the default) or [audit.categories] templates and archetypes of your own, so every access record names the categories of the data it reached (EHDS Annex II 3.2(c)). The gap opens only with [audit.categories] shipped_map = false and nothing declared
open_ehr_access_default[authz.rbac] ehr_access_default = "restricted", so an EHR carrying no ACCESS_CONTROL_SETTINGS is reachable only by an admin. The shipped default is open. The setting is enforced with [authz.rbac] enabled on or off
migrate_on_runtime_credential[database] migrate_url set, or migrations = "verify", so no credential that serves requests can alter the schema. Evaluated per domain database: a domain relocated to a database of its own is prepared on [database.<domain>] migrate_url when that is set, and on that domain’s runtime DSN, which opens the gap, when it is not
auth_off[auth] enabled = true, so no request is served unauthenticated (CRA Annex I Part I(2)(d))
rbac_off[authz.rbac] enabled = true whenever authentication is on, so a caller reaches only the operations its roles allow (CRA Annex I Part I(2)(d)). Not reported while auth_off is
plaintext_listener[server.tls] set, or [server] listen on a loopback address, so data does not cross the network in clear (CRA Annex I Part I(2)(e)). A deployment behind a TLS-terminating ingress accepts plaintext_listener by name, which records that the ingress carries the encryption. The gap also opens when management.listen is set on an enabled management surface: that listener never speaks TLS, so unset it (the surface then shares the main listener) or accept the gap by name where it is unreachable off the host
plaintext_audit_feedAn https:// URL for an enabled audit FHIR feed ([audit.fhir_feed] url), so the access records, which name the patient and the professional, do not cross the network in clear (CRA Annex I Part I(2)(e)). A deployment whose repository is reached on a segment it trusts accepts plaintext_audit_feed by name
plaintext_object_storeAn https:// record.multimedia.url on an enabled multimedia store, so the externalised clinical blobs travel over an https:// endpoint (CRA Annex I Part I(2)(e)). A deployment whose object store is reached on a segment it trusts accepts plaintext_object_store by name

An accepted gap is stated on every boot and on /management/status; it can be run, not hidden. Environment form: FERROEHR__DEPLOYMENT__PROFILE=production, FERROEHR__DEPLOYMENT__ACCEPTS=shared_cluster. There is no research value: the key controls rigour, not purpose, and a secondary-use platform under an EHDS data permit runs on real patient data at production rigour whatever it is for.

This is FerroEHR’s own posture, not a legal requirement. GDPR Art. 4(5) asks that the additional information needed to re-identify a person be “kept separately and … subject to technical and organisational measures”, not that it sit on a separate server; one cluster with separated schemas and roles is a defensible reading. Two clusters are materially stronger, because a superuser, an instance-wide point-in-time recovery and a single compromise are bridges no grant can close, and that is a choice a deployment should make deliberately rather than inherit from a quickstart. See Compliance.

Server, database & telemetry

The listener ([server]), the REST surface ([api]), the PostgreSQL connection ([database]), the observability section ([telemetry]), and the usage report ([usage_report]). Precedence, the environment-name grammar, and file discovery are on the Configuration reference index.

  • [server]
    • [server.caller_rate]: per-caller request rates
    • [server.tls]: native TLS and mutual-TLS client authentication
  • [api]
    • base_path: shortening the REST base path
    • Behind a path-prefixed reverse proxy
    • system_id: the data-authoring identity
    • [api.options]
  • [database]
  • [database.<domain>]
  • [telemetry]
  • [usage_report]

[server]

The HTTP listener: the section every FerroHEALTH product shares (ferrohealth-server), so the keys and their behaviour are the same in each. It carries the stack every request passes through: the server’s request id, the request timeout, the body limit, the concurrency bound, compression, the request log, the health routes and the bounded drain on SIGTERM.

[server]
listen = "0.0.0.0:8080"
base_path = ""
request_timeout = "30s"
header_read_timeout = "30s"
idle_timeout = "2min"
body_limit = "64MiB"
drain_delay = "0s"
shutdown_timeout = "10s"
# max_concurrent_requests = 256
retry_after = "1s"
trusted_proxies = []
forwarded_header = "forwarded"
compression = true
compression_min_size = "1KiB"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
listensocket address0.0.0.0:8080The IP address and port the listener binds: every interface at the port the container image exposes. A host name is refused at startup. PORT alone gives 0.0.0.0:<PORT>, and FERROEHR__SERVER__LISTEN wins over both. Set 127.0.0.1:8080 to keep a bare binary on the loopback.
base_pathstringemptyThe path every route is served under, the health routes included. Empty serves them at the process root. The openEHR API path is api.base_path.
request_timeoutduration"30s"A request still running after this long is answered 408 with the openEHR error body.
header_read_timeoutduration"30s"How long a client may take to send its request head, counted from accept for a connection’s first request and from the first byte of each later request on a kept-alive connection; a client that has not sent it by then, one that sent nothing after connecting included, is disconnected. Bounds the slow-header and the silent connection, which no other limit reaches. "0s" is refused.
idle_timeoutduration"2min"How long a kept-alive HTTP/1.1 connection may wait for its next request; past it the server closes the connection with a clean end of stream. Keep it longer than the idle timeout of your clients (Go’s http.DefaultTransport keeps an idle connection 90 s) and of any load balancer, ingress controller or proxy in front, so they close an idle connection first and never send a request into one the server is closing. "0s" is refused.
body_limitsize"64MiB"The largest request body any route reads, refused 413 above it. The bulk routes (operational-template upload, /message/import) take up to this; api.body_limit narrows the rest of the clinical surface below it. The largest operational template in the vendored CKM corpus is several megabytes, well below this ceiling.
drain_delayduration"0s"On SIGTERM or SIGINT, readiness answers 503 this long while the listener still accepts, so an orchestrator stops routing first.
shutdown_timeoutduration"10s"Then the listener closes and the requests in flight get this long to finish; a connection still open after it is dropped.
max_concurrent_requestsintunsetThe requests served at once. Past it a request is answered 503 with Retry-After and the openEHR error body, never queued, so offered load beyond capacity cannot exhaust memory. The health routes are never refused. Unset, there is no bound.
retry_afterduration"1s"The Retry-After of a 503 or 429 the listener writes, in whole seconds (RFC 9110 §10.2.3).
trusted_proxieslist[]The reverse proxies, as addresses or CIDR blocks, whose forwarded client address is believed. Empty, every request is named by its peer address.
forwarded_headerenum{forwarded,x-forwarded-for}forwardedThe header a trusted proxy names the client in (Forwarded is RFC 7239).
compressionbooltrueCompress a response with gzip or Brotli when the client accepts one.
compression_min_sizesize"1KiB"The smallest response body that is compressed.

A refusal the listener writes itself (408, 413, 429, 503) and a handler that panics (500) answer the standard openEHR { error, message } body. 413 and 429 are not in the ITS-REST status table; ITS-REST admits them as additional, non-conflicting codes, and they are what RFC 9110 §15.5.14 and RFC 6585 §4 define for these refusals. A panic’s message reaches neither the body nor the log.

Every request gets a request id the server mints, which the request log and the access record carry and the response returns in X-Request-Id. A client’s own X-Request-Id is returned to it unchanged and never recorded.

[server.caller_rate]: per-caller request rates

[server.caller_rate]
requests_per_second = 1024
burst = 2048
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
requests_per_secondint(required in the table)Sustained requests per second one authenticated subject may send on the clinical API.
burstint(required in the table)How many requests one subject may send at once before the rate applies.

Unset, no caller is limited. The chart and the Compose quickstart set the values above.

This is not max_concurrent_requests, and you can tell them apart from the status alone. max_concurrent_requests protects capacity: too many requests in flight at once, from anyone, and the excess is refused 503 + Retry-After. The caller rate protects fairness: one caller asking too often over time, refused 429 + Retry-After. A 503 means the server is full; a 429 means you are asking too fast.

The limit is keyed on the authenticated subject, the only fair key for a clinical API: a hospital behind one NAT is a single address. It sits inside authentication, so the health routes, the status document and the discovery document are never refused by it.

Tip

Benchmarking this server? Lift the caller rate first, or you will measure it instead of the server. The project’s own measurement lanes compose an overlay that does exactly that, and both instruments refuse to write a record if the server answered any 429.

[server.tls]: native TLS and mutual-TLS client authentication

Native TLS termination on the main listener, unset by default; deployments commonly terminate TLS at an ingress. client_auth = "required" is the IHE ATNA ITI-19 mutually-authenticated-node posture (see the Audit trail chapter). The separate-port management listener always stays plain HTTP, so under deployment.profile = "production" setting management.listen opens the plaintext_listener gap.

[server.tls]
certificate_file = "/etc/ferroehr/server.pem"
key_file = "/etc/ferroehr/server.key"
client_auth = "none"
min_version = "1.3"
# reload_interval = "1min"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
certificate_filepath(required in the table)Server certificate chain (PEM), the leaf first. A missing, unreadable or certificate-less file stops startup.
key_filepath(required in the table)Server private key (PEM), read as a secret file. A key that does not belong to the leaf stops startup.
client_authenum{none,optional,required}noneClient-certificate policy. optional verifies a certificate when one is presented and still accepts connections without; required rejects any client without a verified certificate at the handshake.
client_ca_filepathunsetThe explicit CA bundle client certificates must chain to, never the web PKI. Required when client_auth is optional or required, and refused at load when it is none, since a listener under none asks no client certificate.
min_versionenum{“1.3”,“1.2”}"1.3"The lowest TLS version this listener negotiates. "1.0" and "1.1" are refused when the configuration is read (RFC 8996).
reload_intervaldurationunsetHow often the certificate, key and client CA are read again while the server runs. The files are always read again on SIGHUP. A changed pair is served, and a changed client CA verifies, from the next handshake on without a restart; a read that fails is logged and the running configuration stays.
healthcheck_identity_filepathunsetThe client certificate chain and key, in one PEM, that ferroehr healthcheck presents to a listener requiring one.

Before 5.5.0, client_ca_file alone meant that every client presents a certificate. From 5.5.0, client_auth decides it and defaults to none, so a configuration carried over from an earlier release set client_ca_file and no client_auth, and 5.5.0 served it without asking a client certificate. Such a configuration is now refused at load. Set client_auth = "required" beside client_ca_file to keep mutual TLS (GHSA-52mf-qg39-4q4j).

ferroehr healthcheck speaks TLS to a TLS listener over the loopback and accepts exactly the leaf certificate in certificate_file.

Note

min_version defaults to 1.3 only, as RFC 9325 §3.1.1 has it supported. Setting "1.2" enables 1.2 alongside 1.3, with the four forward-secret suites RFC 9325 §4.2 recommends; pick it only for a client that cannot do 1.3, such as an older integration engine or a pinned Java runtime.

Note

An EC certificate must name its curve. RFC 5480 §2.1.1 forbids explicit curve parameters, TLS clients refuse such a certificate, and the server refuses the pair at startup. LibreSSL (the openssl that ships with macOS) writes explicit parameters from genpkey and req -newkey ec unless you add -pkeyopt ec_param_enc:named_curve; openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey writes a named curve.

[api]

The openEHR REST surface the listener serves.

[api]
base_path = "/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1"
openapi_ui = "private"
system_id = "ferroehr.local"
# body_limit = "16MiB"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
base_pathstring/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1ITS-REST base path all API routes hang off. Shortening it is supported; see below. The served OpenAPI document describes whatever paths this setting produces, never the defaults.
openapi_uienum{off,admin_only,private,public}privateWho may read the Swagger UI and the OpenAPI documents under the REST root: off does not mount them, admin_only needs the admin role, private needs any authenticated principal (unauthenticated is 401 with the server’s WWW-Authenticate challenge, so a browser prompts for the Basic credential), public needs nothing. The documents list the whole enabled operation surface, admin and message groups included, so public discloses it to anyone who can reach the port; the hosted sandbox sets it deliberately. With authentication off the guard admits everyone, as the management endpoints do.
corstableabsent[api.cors], the CORS protocol answers (Fetch Standard §3.2.3): allow_origins, allow_methods, allow_headers, expose_headers, allow_credentials and max_age (a duration), each named for the header it sets. Absent, no CORS header is sent. allow_origins = ["*"] admits any origin, which the server warns about at boot and which refuses allow_credentials. Production lists its origins.
body_limitsizeunsetThe largest body the ordinary clinical surface accepts, below server.body_limit, which the bulk routes keep. Unset, every route takes the listener’s limit. A value at or above the listener’s is refused at startup. The largest example composition in the vendored corpus is 526 KB; raise it if your compositions embed large DV_MULTIMEDIA data.
adminboolfalseServe the ADMIN API group (physical delete); off, every admin route answers 405.
terminologyboolfalseMount the terminology extension API; the server it asks is [terminology].
system_idstringferroehr.localThis deployment’s own openEHR system identifier; see below. Set a stable, deployment-unique name in production (FERROEHR__API__SYSTEM_ID).

base_path: shortening the REST base path

ITS-REST leaves the API base to the deployment and fixes only the version segment at its end, so you may shorten base_path. The shape is checked at boot, and a value that breaks a rule stops the server with an error naming the key and every rule it broke:

  • The first segment is ferroehr. /ferroehrx/v1 and /x/ferroehr/v1 are refused. This segment is not configurable away.
  • The last segment is v1, the openEHR API version this server implements. The shortest accepted value is therefore /ferroehr/v1.
  • No trailing slash, no empty segment (//), and every segment uses only the unreserved URL characters A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~.

The status and documentation routes hang off the REST root, which the server derives from base_path by dropping the segments that name the openEHR API: the trailing v1, plus an openehr segment directly before it when you spell one.

base_pathREST rootStatus document
/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1 (default)/ferroehr/rest/ferroehr/rest/status
/ferroehr/openehr/v1/ferroehr/ferroehr/status
/ferroehr/v1/ferroehr/ferroehr/status
/ferroehr/cdr/v1/ferroehr/cdr/ferroehr/cdr/status

The Swagger UI ({rest root}/swagger-ui), the OpenAPI documents ({rest root}/api-docs/…) and the SMART discovery document ({rest root}/.well-known/smart-configuration) move with it. The health family is served under server.base_path, which is empty by default, so it stays at the process root: /health, /health/liveness, /health/readiness.

Set it from the environment with:

FERROEHR__API__BASE_PATH=/ferroehr/v1

Note

The ferroehr healthcheck subcommand, which the published container images run as their Docker health check, asks GET /health/readiness on the server.listen port over the loopback, so api.base_path does not move it.

Behind a path-prefixed reverse proxy

A proxy that mounts the CDR under a prefix stacks that prefix on top of base_path. A proxy serving the server at /cdr with the default base path gives clients URLs like:

https://cdr.example.org/cdr/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1/definition/template/adl1.4

Two ways to shorten that. Strip the prefix at the proxy, so the server sees the path it serves (nginx proxy_pass http://cdr:8080/; with the trailing slash, Caddy handle_path, Traefik StripPrefix). Or shorten the base path:

FERROEHR__API__BASE_PATH=/ferroehr/v1

which gives https://cdr.example.org/cdr/ferroehr/v1/definition/template/adl1.4.

Whichever you choose, tell every client. The server builds its Location headers, its served OpenAPI paths and its SMART discovery document from its own api.base_path, and it cannot see a prefix the proxy adds. The FerroEHR Viewer has its own mirror key, cdr.base_path, which must match.

system_id: the data-authoring identity

system_id is the identifier this CDR stamps into the data it authors. It appears on the wire in three places:

  • EHR.system_id, recorded when an EHR is created. The openEHR RM (EHR Information Model, EHR Identifier Allocation) says the EHR.system_id “should be set to the value that would normally be used for locally created EHRs”: a value the deployment chooses, not a product constant.
  • AUDIT_DETAILS.system_id on every commit for which the client did not supply one through the openehr-audit-details header. The openEHR REST API requires that “when system_id is not provided by the client, the server MUST set it to its own configured system identifier”.
  • OBJECT_VERSION_ID.creating_system_id: the middle segment of every version identifier the server mints (<object_id>::<creating_system_id>::<version>).

Practical notes:

  • The value must be a legal openEHR UID: a UUID, an ISO OID, or an internet id (a reverse-domain / DNS-style name) per the openEHR BASE identification grammar. The server judges it with the same validating constructor its reader uses and refuses to boot on an illegal value, because it becomes the creating_system_id segment of every version identifier the server mints and an illegal value would produce ids the server’s own reader rejects. A DNS-style name like cdr.hospital.example is valid; an empty value, or one containing the :: field separator, is not.
  • Choose it before going live and keep it stable. The value is stored with each EHR and each version; changing it later affects only newly authored data: existing EHR ids, audit rows and version identifiers are never rewritten, and previously issued OBJECT_VERSION_IDs stay valid.
  • Make it unique per system, so data exchanged between openEHR systems keeps unambiguous provenance. A node of a federation must hold a system_id no other member uses (Federation Tier N42a); the default ferroehr.local is the same on every node that leaves it unset. See FerroEHR as a federation node.
  • system_id is not [api.options]. system_id says which system authored the data; [api.options] is the display identity of the OPTIONS System-Options manifest. Rebranding changes the manifest and nothing in stored data; changing system_id changes what new data says about its origin and leaves the manifest alone.

[api.options]

The System-Options manifest identity (OPTIONS on the API base path, e.g. OPTIONS /ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1, the System API’s one location). This is the deployment’s display identity only; the identifier stamped into authored data is system_id.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
solutionstringFerroEHRProduct name.
solution_versionstringthe build’s versionProduct version.
vendorstringCadasto B.V.Providing organisation: by default the manufacturer of the release, the name ferroehr --version and GET /management/info give.
restapi_specs_versionstringthe ITS-REST release this build implements (1.1.0)The openEHR REST API edition advertised.

The defaults are derived from the build rather than typed into the handler. Override them only to rebrand. The manifest’s conformance_profile is no identity field and has no key here: the build derives it from the committed conformance record (see Using the API).

[database]

PostgreSQL connection.

[database]
url = "postgres://ferroehr:ferroehr@localhost:5432/ferroehr"
migrations = "apply"
max_connections = 20
min_connections = 2
acquire_timeout = "30s"
statement_timeout = "1min"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
urlsecret URLpostgres://ferroehr:ferroehr@localhost:5432/ferroehrConnection DSN. The default suits a local from-source run against a localhost PostgreSQL, and the server logs a prominent warning at boot while it is in use; production MUST set it. Credentials are redacted from every rendering. DATABASE_URL is a recognized lower-priority alias.
url_filepathunsetRead the DSN from a file instead of the key above, for a mounted secret. Preferred over the environment form in Kubernetes: an environment value is readable through /proc/<pid>/environ and inherited by every child process. At most one of the pair, where the built-in development default does not count as “set”.
migrate_urlsecret URLunsetDSN that PREPARES the schema, used for that one boot step and then closed. Preparation spans every schema of a database at once, which no domain-scoped runtime credential can do, so a deployment separating the runtime roles names the credential that can here. It prepares every domain whose DSN reaches the SAME DATABASE — which is the whole of the separated-credential posture, where each domain has a login role of its own on one database; a domain whose DSN reaches a different database is prepared on that database’s database.<domain>.migrate_url (on the domain’s own DSN when that is unset). Which it is, is read from the server (pg_control_system() plus current_database()), never from the DSN text. Unset, it falls back to url. See Operations → Which credential prepares the schema.
migrate_url_filepathunsetRead migrate_url from a file instead, for a mounted secret. At most one of the pair.
migrateenum{apply,verify}applyWhether the server applies its embedded migrations at boot. apply is what makes an empty configuration boot against an empty database. verify issues no DDL at all: it checks that the database already carries exactly this build’s migrations and refuses to start otherwise, so the serving DSN can authenticate as a role with no DDL rights. That check still READS every _sqlx_migrations table of each database, which no least-privilege role can do, so pair it with migrate_url above and with ferroehr db migrate run out of band; see Operations.
max_connectionsint20Pool ceiling. Write-heavy deployments benefit from raising it.
min_connectionsint2Idle connections kept open, avoiding cold-reopen churn under variable load.
acquire_timeoutduration"30s"How long to wait for a free connection before failing.
statement_timeoutduration"1min"statement_timeout applied to every pooled connection; "0s" leaves the server default.

statement_timeout is the backstop for every statement. An AQL query (ad hoc or stored) and the composition-count statistics stop sooner when their caller goes away: a client that disconnects, or the AQL engine’s own record.query.timeout, closes the statement’s connection, its pool slot frees at once, and every pooled session sets PostgreSQL’s client_connection_check_interval to one second, so the backend stops the statement within about a second. Other statements run to their end or to this timeout, so keep it above record.query.timeout: the AQL engine’s typed refusal then fires first and this only catches what the engine does not govern.

[database.<domain>]

One DSN per storage domain. Every domain always lives in its own schema (clinical, party, audit) and every pool carries only its own on its search_path, so no statement can reach another domain’s relations without naming a schema it is not granted. Setting a url here adds the CREDENTIAL separation, and — if the DSN names another host — lets the domain live in a database or cluster of its own.

[database.party]
url_file = "/run/secrets/db-party-dsn"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
database.clinical.urlsecret URLunsetDSN the clinical domain connects on (role ferroehr_clinical). Unset, it uses database.url.
database.party.urlsecret URLunsetDSN the party (demographic) domain connects on (role ferroehr_party). Unset, it uses database.url.
database.audit.urlsecret URLunsetDSN the audit repository is written through. Unset, it uses database.url.
database.<domain>.url_filepathunsetRead that domain’s DSN from a file instead, for a mounted secret. At most one of the pair.

Why a schema is not always enough: a base backup, WAL archiving and physical replication carry every schema of a database together (PostgreSQL 18, Backup and Restore), so a separation that must survive those is a separation of databases. The Swiss EPDV Art. 10 Abs. 1 lit. b asks for storage “von anderen Datenbeständen getrennt” and the DSV Art. 4 Abs. 5 for the log to be kept “getrennt vom System, in welchem die Personendaten bearbeitet werden”; openEHR reads the same way for the identity cross-reference, which “could be located on different machines” (BASE architecture_overview/master07-security.adoc §Anonymity). No openEHR spec governs pools or database roles — this is our own design.

What the server checks at boot:

  • a runtime role that can read another domain’s relations is refused, always;
  • two domains configured on different DSNs that turn out to authenticate as the same database role are refused — a separation that exists only in the configuration is worse than none, because it reads as one that holds;
  • a missing domain role is a warning under deployment.profile = "sandbox" and a refusal under production, where there are no grants to separate anything with.

Each database is prepared on its own migration credential. [database] migrate_url names one database; a domain whose DSN reaches another database is prepared there, and verified there under migrations = "verify", on the credential named in [database.<domain>]:

[database.party]
url_file = "/run/secrets/db-party-dsn"                   # postgres://ferroehr_party:…@party-db/…
migrate_url_file = "/run/secrets/db-party-migrate-dsn"   # postgres://ferroehr_migrator:…@party-db/…
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
database.<domain>.migrate_urlsecret URLunsetDSN that prepares the database the domain lives in, when that is not the database database.migrate_url reaches. Used for that one step and closed again. Unset, such a database is prepared on the domain’s own url, which a DML-only runtime role cannot do: it is refused on the first bookkeeping table it cannot read.
database.<domain>.migrate_url_filepathunsetRead it from a file instead, for a mounted secret. At most one of the pair.

The server refuses to start when a domain’s url and its storage.migrate URL reach different databases. [storage.linkage] and [storage.migrate.linkage] are refused as unknown keys: the linkage domain is gone (Operations → Upgrading past the linkage domain).

[telemetry]

The console, the request log and the OpenTelemetry export: the section every FerroHEALTH product shares (ferrohealth-telemetry). With no [telemetry.otlp] table nothing is exported.

[telemetry]
format = "auto"
filter = "info,hyper=warn,tower=warn,h2=warn"
logged_query_parameters = []
# environment = "production"

# [telemetry.otlp]
# endpoint = "http://collector:4317"
# traces = true
# metrics = true
# sample_ratio = 1.0
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
formatenum{auto,json,pretty}autoStdout rendering. auto picks json when stdout is not a TTY and the human format when it is. NO_COLOR turns colour off.
filterstringinfo,hyper=warn,tower=warn,h2=warnConsole filter directives, refused at boot when they do not parse; also the value /management/loggers resets to. RUST_LOG is a lower-priority fallback. The filter decides what the console writes and never thins a trace.
logged_query_parameterslist of strings[]The query parameters whose values the request log may carry, each cut to 64 characters. Empty, the request log carries no query value.
environmentstringunsetThe deployment.environment.name resource attribute of every span and metric.
otlp.endpointsecret URL(required in the table)OTLP/gRPC collector endpoint; https:// speaks TLS. Credentials in it are masked in every rendering.
otlp.tracesbooltrueExport FerroEHR’s spans.
otlp.metricsbooltruePush the metrics over OTLP beside the Prometheus pull surface. One meter provider feeds both.
otlp.sample_ratiofloat1.0The share of traces sampled (0.1 is a common production start). A client’s traceparent is never read: every request starts a trace of the server’s own.
otlp.trust_roots_filepathunsetPEM trust roots the collector’s certificate may chain to, beside the platform’s. Refused at boot beside an endpoint that is not https://, and when the file holds no PEM certificate.
otlp.client_identity_filepathunsetPEM client certificate chain and key, for mutual TLS with the collector. Refused at boot beside an endpoint that is not https://, and when the file lacks a PEM certificate or a PEM private key.

The service.name of every span and metric is ferroehr, and service.version is the release and its commit.

The request log writes one line per request: the method, the matched route template, the status, the latency and the server’s request id, never a body, the raw path or a header value. It records the http.server.request.duration histogram, scraped as http_server_request_duration_seconds with the http_request_method, http_route, http_response_status_code and url_scheme labels, and the http.server.active_requests counter of the requests in flight, scraped as http_server_active_requests with the http_request_method and url_scheme labels.

Tip

The ASCII boot banner follows the rendering that is actually installed, not the configured word: it prints for pretty, and for auto only when stdout is a terminal. Under json, and under auto off a terminal (a container, a pipe into a log collector) stdout is parseable JSON from the first byte.

Note

Instrument names carry no Prometheus suffix; the exporter derives one. A counter named auth_failures is scraped as auth_failures_total, and units add _seconds/_bytes. Over OTLP the unsuffixed name is what a collector receives.

The scrape endpoint itself is not opened here; it is management.endpoints.prometheus, which is off until you name a level.

[usage_report]

The daily installation report to FerroPULSE, the collector Cadasto B.V. runs. It is on by default, and every boot logs one line saying whether it is on. What a report carries, when it is sent, the network it needs and the privacy notice are on the Usage report page.

[usage_report]
enabled = true
endpoint = "https://report.ferropulse.eu/v1/report"
deployment = "unknown"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
enabledbooltrueSend the report. false sends nothing and writes nothing to the database for it. In a CI run (GITHUB_ACTIONS or CI set to true or 1) the report is off whatever this says. Environment: FERROEHR__USAGE_REPORT__ENABLED.
endpointURLhttps://report.ferropulse.eu/v1/reportWhere reports go. Must be an absolute https URL without credentials; plain http is accepted for a loopback host only. Anything else is refused when the configuration is read. Environment: FERROEHR__USAGE_REPORT__ENDPOINT.
deploymentenum{helm,compose,binary,unknown}unknownHow the instance was deployed, as the report states it. The Helm chart sets it to helm. Environment: FERROEHR__USAGE_REPORT__DEPLOYMENT.
state_dirpathunsetRefused. The section is the one every FerroHEALTH product shares, where this key names the directory of the instance id; FerroEHR keeps the instance id and the counts in the clinical database, so every replica reports as one installation.

Under the Helm chart, set the switch with usageReport.enabled. The chart writes enabled and deployment = "helm" into the rendered file itself and refuses to render if either is also set under config.usage_report; endpoint passes through config.usage_report unchanged.

Authentication & access

Who may call the server, what they may do once identified, and the surfaces that are gated rather than always-on: [auth], [authz], [api] admin, [auth.smart], [management], and [record.signing]. Precedence, the environment-name grammar, and file discovery are on the Configuration reference index.

  • [auth]

    • [[auth.party]], [[auth.federation]], [[auth.attributes]], [auth.dpop] and [auth.idp.entra]

  • [authz]
    • [authz.assurance]: the assurance level patient data requires
    • [authz.party_binding]
      • The party mapping
      • Changing the mapping
      • How a login is looked up
      • Just-in-time creation
    • [authz.import] and [[authz.system_client]]

    • [authz.rbac]
    • [authz.abac]
  • [api] admin
  • [auth.scim]
    • Users
    • Groups
    • Provision from Microsoft Entra ID
  • [privacy.access_delay]

    • Choose an Ed25519 signing key
  • [record.versioning]

[auth]

Authentication: bearer tokens of one or more trusted issuers, Basic credentials, or both. [auth] is the section every FerroHEALTH product shares, checked by the ferrohealth-smart crate (0.9). FerroEHR is a resource server: it checks tokens and never issues them. Every person a request comes from is bound to a demographic PERSON (see [authz.party_binding]).

[auth]
enabled = true

[[auth.issuer]]
issuer = "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/staff"
kind = "persons"
profile = "keycloak"
audience = ["ferroehr"]
first_party_clients = ["ferroehr-viewer"]

[[auth.party]]
issuer = "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/staff"
identifier_issuer = "urn:example:staff-login"
identifier_type = "uuid"

[[auth.basic.users]]
user = "clinician"
password_hash = "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$…$…"   # never a plaintext password
scopes = ["user/composition-*.cruds", "user/template-*.cruds", "user/aql-*.cruds"]

The section keys:

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
enabledbooltrueMaster switch. false = all requests pass unauthenticated (development only). With true and no mechanism configured the server refuses to start; see below.
issuer[[auth.issuer]] tablesnoneThe trusted issuers, one table each; see below. A flat issuer = "…" string is a type error at boot.
tlstableplatform roots[auth.tls], the family’s outbound TLS table: trust_roots_file, a PEM bundle of certificate authorities trusted in addition to the platform roots for an issuer behind a private PKI (every issuer’s metadata and key set are read trusting it), client_identity_file (one PEM holding a client certificate chain and its key) and min_version ("1.3" by default). An introspection grant’s calls use the grant’s own tls table. A file that cannot be read, holds no certificate, or does not parse refuses the start.
realmstring"" ⇒ ferroehrThe realm every WWW-Authenticate challenge names.
scopeless_subjectslist of { issuer, sub }[]The subjects whose token, when it carries no resource scope of either the SMART on openEHR or the SMART on FHIR grammar, meets every SMART on openEHR requirement. Only a system (app-only) caller of that issuer is admitted by an entry. A token that carries resource scopes gets only its scopes, and the allowlist reaches neither the ADMIN API nor the DEMOGRAPHIC API, which need the product scope. A string entry refuses the start.
capabilitieslist of string[]SMART capabilities the discovery document adds: one SMART App Launch or the SMART on openEHR draft lists, or a full URI.
scopes_supportedlist of string[]The scopes the discovery document lists. Empty, it lists the scopes the route table honours.
product_scopestring"" ⇒ __ferroehr.platformFerroEHR’s own scope. It admits the ADMIN API and, beside the bearer clients in [auth.smart] demographic_clients, the DEMOGRAPHIC API, the two surfaces no SMART on openEHR resource family covers. A full URI or a string starting with __ (SMART App Launch 2.2.0, Scopes and Launch Context, §Extensibility).

The keys audience, algorithms, token_profile, clock_skew_seconds, jwks_max_age_seconds, jwks_refresh_interval_seconds, jwks_file, timeout_ms, mode, introspection, role_claims, acting_for_claim, client_tokens and ca_file, which v5.6 read in [auth], are refused in v5.7.0 naming what replaces each: the first ones live on each [[auth.issuer]] table, the caller classification replaces acting_for_claim and client_tokens, and [auth.tls] replaces ca_file. From v5.8.0 they are unknown keys.

[[auth.issuer]]: the trusted issuers

Each issuer’s metadata is read at boot, at the RFC 8414 §3 location first and the OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §4 location after a 404, and with it the key set at its jwks_uri, so an authorization server that cannot be reached refuses the start. Every setting of an issuer lives on its own table. No two issuers of one node share an audience, so one audience is one issuer and one token form; the node’s audience must also differ from every other node’s, an operator rule boot cannot see.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
issuerstringrequiredThe issuer identifier: an https URL with no query, no fragment and no user name or password; plain http on a loopback host only.
kindpersons, patients, machines or federationrequiredWhose tokens it signs. persons signs the deployment’s own people (and the app-only tokens of its machines), patients tokens naming only the record subject, machines client credentials tokens only, and federation another party’s professionals or organisation. One issuer is one kind, so patients and professionals sign in at separate issuers, a realm or tenant each.
profilerfc9068, entra, keycloak, okta or nlrfc9068The preset of what the issuer’s tokens look like, each value labelled with its source in the crate. Every profile key below may be set on the table over it.
audiencelist of stringrequiredAccepted aud values; a token naming none of them is refused (RFC 9068 §4, RFC 8725 §3.9).
algorithmslist of string["RS256","RS384","PS256","PS384","ES256","ES384"]Accepted signature algorithms. Asymmetric only: an HS* algorithm is a boot error, and none is no algorithm at all (RFC 8725 §3.1, §3.2).
clock_skewduration"60s"Leeway on exp, nbf and iat. At most "5min".
jwks_max_ageduration"10min"A key set older than this is read again.
jwks_refresh_intervalduration"1min"A token naming an unknown kid reads the key set again at most once per interval.
jwks_filepath""A JWK Set of public keys handed over out of band, read instead of the issuer’s metadata. A symmetric key (kty: "oct") or a private-key member (d, p, q, dp, dq, qi, oth, k) is a boot error. An issuer read from a file has no metadata, so it serves the SMART discovery document only with [auth.smart] issuer_metadata_file set.
timeoutduration"10s"One call to the authorization server.
modejwt or introspectionjwtHow the issuer’s tokens are checked: as JWTs against its key set, or posted to its RFC 7662 endpoint (see Opaque tokens).
role_claimslist of string["roles","groups","entitlements"]Token claim paths the caller’s roles are read from; dotted paths walk nested claims, and a role is matched without regard to case. scope is not a role source. A federation issuer reads no role. Whether a role grants admin_role and the other privileged roles is [authz.rbac] role_issuers.
sender_constraintnone or requirednonerequired admits only a token bound to a DPoP key (RFC 9449) or to the client certificate of a mutual-TLS connection (RFC 8705 §3). A token carrying cnf is held to it under either value.
assurancetableunsetThe assurance level the issuer’s tokens carry, in the shape of [authz.assurance].
person_keystringsub (preset)The claim a person is bound by. email, phone_number, preferred_username and name are never accepted as a key (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.7).
first_party_clientslist of string[]The deployment’s own clients. A persons token is admitted only through a client listed here or in delegates.
delegateslist of { client } or { sub, issuer }[]Third-party clients or RFC 8693 actors that act for a person; their tokens are recorded as the client acting for the person the token names.
act_represents_patientboolunsetOn a patients issuer, read a token whose sub is the patient and whose top-level act (RFC 8693 §4.1) names someone else as that person acting for the patient. FerroEHR binds no party to such a representative, so it refuses the token with 403 (refused-patient-representative). Without the key, ferrohealth-smart refuses a patients token that carries act with 401.
token_types, required_claims, scope_claim, app_only_scope_claimpresetThe token shape that replaces token_profile: the accepted typ values, the claims every token carries, and where its scopes are read. For an issuer that minted under token_profile = "jwt", set token_types = ["JWT"] and the required_claims its tokens carry.
client_claims, app_only, guest, impersonation_marker, expect, user_claims, person_equality, unstable_claims, max_actor_chain, representation, tenant_claim, adapter, onward_*presetThe other profile keys of ferrohealth-smart: which claim names the client, what marks an app-only token or a guest, what refuses an impersonation, the claims a token must carry exactly, how a representative names whom it acts for, the claim naming the tenant, the vendor adapter (idp-entra) and the onward grants.

[[auth.party]], [[auth.federation]], [[auth.attributes]], [auth.dpop] and [auth.idp.entra]

TableDescription
[[auth.party]]One per persons issuer, keyed by issuer: where its logins are looked up. identifier_issuer and identifier_type (guid and uuid compare in lower case) name the identifiers the issuer profile’s person_key is matched against; group_claim with group_identifier_issuer reads the groups a token asserts; guests looks a guest up. Boot refuses a persons issuer without one, a table that sets claim (the profile’s person_key is the key), two tables sharing an issuer or an identifier_issuer, and a table whose identifier_type is the type of no [[authz.party_binding.person.template]] key: SCIM and just-in-time creation write the key under that type and the lookup compares the type exactly, so no login of the issuer would bind.
[[auth.federation]]One per federation issuer: how its tokens’ claims map to the fields of another party’s professional or organisation (mapping = "iua", "ehdsi" or per field), the countries, issuing authorities and provider prefixes that bound them, and contact_point for a MyHealth@EU contact point. fields maps a field to its claim ({ claim = "..." }) or authorization_details member, among them consent.reference, the consent decision reference of a consent-conditioned read, and correlation_id, the requester’s id a chained organisation request carries.
[[auth.attributes]]At most one per persons issuer, keyed by issuer: where its tokens state the professional’s attributes (mapping = "iua", the IHE IUA claims under extensions.ihe_iua, or per field in fields), and authorization_details_purposes, whether the purpose_of_use of each RFC 9396 authorization_details entry is a purpose of use too. Its purposes of use and roles go into each access record, and a [audit] purpose_header naming a purpose the token does not state refuses the request with 403.
[auth.dpop]The DPoP proof check of a sender-constrained issuer: external_url (required, the base URL clients address; a proof’s htu is it plus the request path), max_age ("60s"), clock_skew ("10s") and algorithms. Each accepted proof is recorded in the database every replica shares until its window ends, so a proof is accepted once across all of them (RFC 9449 §11.1), and a database that cannot record it refuses the request with 503.
[auth.idp.entra]The Microsoft Graph access of the idp-entra adapter, which an issuer turns on with adapter = "idp-entra" to read the groups of an Entra ID groups overage: base_url (https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0), timeout ("2s"), max_response_size (a size), security_enabled_only and the client credentials of [auth.idp.entra.credentials]. An issuer naming the adapter without this table refuses the start.

Warning

auth.enabled = true with no mechanism is a boot error. Such a server could only refuse every request while advertising an authentication scheme it does not implement, which RFC 9110 §11.6.1 forbids: a 401 challenge must name a scheme applicable to the target resource. Configure an issuer, configure [[auth.basic.users]], or set auth.enabled = false for a development server.

The key-set fetches verify the identity provider’s certificate against the platform trust store and follow no redirects. An identity provider whose certificate comes from a private CA is trusted once that CA is in the image’s system store or in a directory or file named by SSL_CERT_DIR or SSL_CERT_FILE. A key set that cannot be read when a token needs it answers 503, never 401: the server cannot decide, and a 401 would tell a caller with a valid token that its credential was refused.

A validated token must also carry a non-blank sub claim: the authenticated subject is stamped into the audit trail, so a token without one is refused with 401 rather than recorded under a placeholder identity. A bearer token outside the RFC 6750 §2.1 b64token alphabet is refused the same way, with 401 and error="invalid_token".

Opaque tokens by introspection

An authorization server that issues opaque access tokens is served with mode = "introspection" on its [[auth.issuer]] table, whose [auth.issuer.introspection] table holds the keys below. Each bearer token is posted to the issuer’s introspection endpoint (RFC 7662 §2.1), and the active response stands in for the JWT claims: sub, scope, the roles of role_claims, aud against audience and iss against the issuer. An inactive token is a 401. An endpoint that cannot answer is a 503, because the server cannot decide. An active response is reused until its exp, at most cache_max_age.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
endpointURLunsetThe introspection endpoint; unset reads the introspection_endpoint of the issuer’s metadata. https, or http on a loopback host.
cache_max_ageduration"60s"The longest an active response is used; "0s" caches nothing.
cache_capacityint10000The most responses held at once.
clienttableunsetThe client authentication of the call (RFC 7662 §2.1), with the keys of an outbound grant: client_id and client_secret, private_key_jwt or mutual TLS (see the grant keys).
bearertableunsetA client credentials grant whose token authorizes the call instead (SMART App Launch 2.2.0, Token Introspection). Exactly one of client and bearer.
 
[[auth.issuer]]
issuer = "https://idp.example.org/realms/ferroehr"
kind = "persons"
audience = ["ferroehr"]
mode = "introspection"

[auth.issuer.introspection.client]
client_id = "ferroehr-rs"
client_secret_file = "/run/secrets/introspection-client"

The Basic-auth user store

[[auth.basic.users]] is an array of tables. A Basic user is always a person: it maps to the PERSON carrying its binding key through [[authz.party_binding.basic_user]], and a Basic user with no mapping refuses the start, naming the user. A machine authenticates with the client credentials grant (RFC 6749 §4.4), and a system/ scope on a Basic user refuses the start.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
userstringrequiredThe user-id. Empty, or with a colon or a control character, is a boot error (RFC 7617 §2).
password_hashsecretrequiredArgon2id PHC hash ($argon2id$v=19$…), never a plaintext password. Boot-validated against the OWASP floor; see below.
password_hash_filepathunsetRead the hash from a file instead, for a mounted secret. A hash is an offline cracking target, so prefer this wherever the configuration file itself is not treated as sensitive. Exactly one of the pair is required.
scopeslist of string[]The SMART on openEHR scopes the user holds, checked on every route exactly like a token’s scope claim. A user with none is refused everywhere a requirement applies.
roleslist of string[]The user’s RBAC roles, upper-cased on authentication. A user with none holds no role and is refused wherever [authz.rbac] asks for one.

[auth.basic] itself takes one key beside the users:

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
cache_ttlduration"5min"How long a credential that verified is kept, so a repeat request skips the Argon2id derivation; "0s" turns the cache off and checks every request. The entry is named by a keyed hash of user-id:password under a key drawn at boot, never the password, and only a credential that verified is kept, so a wrong password always pays the derivation. The cache holds at most 4096 credentials and empties at a restart. The TTL bounds how long a removed user keeps working, which matters only until the restart that applies the new user list. Argon2id is slow by design, so with the cache off its cost bounds how many Basic requests a core can answer.

Warning

Every password_hash must meet the OWASP Argon2id floor: m>=19456 (19 MiB), t>=2, p>=1, algorithm argon2id. Anything weaker (or a non-argon2id PHC string, or an unparsable one) is a boot error naming the user. This is checked at startup because the verifier takes its cost parameters from the stored hash, so a deliberately cheap hash would otherwise verify happily and silently weaken every password in the store. The floor is the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet §Argon2id minimum.

An unknown user-id is checked against a decoy hash of the same cost, so the time a refusal takes does not say whether the user exists.

[authz]

Role-based (RBAC) and attribute-based (ABAC) authorization, and the patient-data assurance gate. The full evaluation order and design rationale are in Security.

[authz.assurance]: the assurance level patient data requires

Off by default. What it refuses and the 401 challenge it sends are described in Security.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
claimstringacrThe token claim carrying the authentication context class; a dotted path reaches into a JSON object.
levelstable of string → low | substantial | highemptyMaps each value your identity provider puts in claim to an eIDAS level of assurance. A value the table does not name carries no level. File-only: the keys are usually URIs.
minimumlow | substantial | highunsetThe level a patient-data request must carry. Unset refuses nothing.
 
[authz.assurance]
minimum = "substantial"

[authz.assurance.levels]
"http://eidas.europa.eu/LoA/substantial" = "substantial"
"http://eidas.europa.eu/LoA/high" = "high"

Boot refuses a minimum with an empty levels table or with no value mapped at or above it (every patient-data request would be refused), a blank claim beside a declared table, and a levels value that is blank or carries whitespace, a quote or a backslash, because the refusal names the accepted values in one quoted, space-separated acr_values parameter (RFC 9470 §3).

A Basic credential carries no level, so with minimum set every Basic user, mapped to a person or not, is refused on patient data. While minimum is unset and a Basic user is mapped in [[authz.party_binding.basic_user]], boot logs a warn naming those users.

The access record carries the acting mode and the professional the caller classification names; see Audit trail. [authz.professional] is refused at boot: the issuer’s kind and profile classify the caller, and a client acting for a person is one the issuer lists in delegates.

[authz.party_binding]

How a person is attributed. There is no switch: binding is how FerroEHR attributes a person, and enabled is refused at boot.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
provider{ issuer, id }, or [[authz.party_binding.provider]] tablesrequired once [auth] admits a credentialThe healthcare provider this deployment acts for, as an identifier issuer and id (in the Netherlands the URA). Every access record of a bound or provisional person and every version a person commits name it (EHDS Art. 13(4), Annex II 3.2(a)). A deployment that serves several providers declares one table per value of its issuers’ tenant_claim (tenant, issuer, id) instead; the two forms cannot be combined, and a bound issuer that names no tenant_claim is refused beside the table form.
namespacestringdemographicThe PARTY_REF.namespace a bound party is written under, the value of the ITS-REST overview example (committer.external_ref.namespace="demographic"), held to the OBJECT_REF.namespace pattern [a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_.:/&?=+-]*.
basic_user[[authz.party_binding.basic_user]] tables[]One per Basic user: user, key_issuer (the identifier_issuer of an [[auth.party]] table) and key, the binding key the user’s PERSON carries. A Basic user with no table, a table naming no Basic user and a key_issuer no table names refuse the start.
issuer[[authz.party_binding.issuer]] tables[]One per persons issuer that creates a provisional PERSON at a first login; see Just-in-time creation.
provisional_report_afterduration"30d"The age past which ferroehr party-binding check reports a provisional PERSON.
 
[authz.party_binding]
provider = { issuer = "urn:oid:2.16.528.1.1007.3.3", id = "12345678" }

[[authz.party_binding.basic_user]]
user = "clinician"
key_issuer = "urn:example:staff-login"
key = "3f2b0c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001"

The party mapping

SCIM provisioning, just-in-time creation and the login binding read and write the same demographic parties under one mapping. It names the templates each party is valid against, the identifier selectors of the binding key, userName and externalId, and where each SCIM attribute and OpenID Connect claim goes. Names go in PARTY.identities and identifiers in PARTY.details (RM demographic §Names and Addresses, §Party Identification), and boot refuses a name mapped into details or an identifier mapped into identities. No openEHR specification governs this mapping: it is FerroEHR’s own design, and its targets are RM demographic paths.

SectionKeysDescription
[[authz.party_binding.person.template]]template_id, key, user_name, external_id, defaultOne per template a professional’s PERSON may use, so a migrated template can stay beside a new one. key, user_name and external_id are selectors, each { path, type }: the path of the ELEMENT holding the DV_IDENTIFIER and its type. Every identifier can sit at one path (the repeated element of an identifier cluster), so two selectors at one path are told apart by type, and the key by its issuer, the identifier_issuer of an [[auth.party]] table. Exactly one table sets default = true: SCIM and just-in-time creation create new persons with it.
[[authz.party_binding.person.attribute]]scim, oidc, jit, name, pathOne per mapped value: a SCIM attribute path (the RFC 7644 valuePath form, emails[type eq "work"].value, and the FerroEHR extension urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:ferrohealth:2.0:User:loginIdentifier that feeds the binding key), an OpenID Connect claim, whether just-in-time creation writes it (jit, default false), whether it is the name the committer reads (name, at most one), and path, one path per template id. id, schemas, meta, active, userName and externalId are SCIM’s own and are never mapped.
[authz.party_binding.professional_role]template_idThe template of the professional ROLE, rooted at ROLE. A PERSON is a professional while it lists a ROLE of this template that names it as performer, is complete or incomplete, and whose time_validity holds today.
[authz.party_binding.group]template_id, external_id, display_nameThe template of a SCIM Group’s GROUP, its externalId selector and the path of its displayName.
[authz.party_binding.membership]archetype_idThe PARTY_RELATIONSHIP archetype of a group membership, as each membership’s archetype_node_id carries it (the interface form of an ADL 2 id, openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-PARTY_RELATIONSHIP.membership.v1). SCIM serves /Groups when the group table names a display_name and this table is set.
[authz.party_binding.representation]archetype_id, relationship_codesThe PARTY_RELATIONSHIP archetype a representative acts through, from the representative’s PERSON to the subject’s, and the code of the openEHR subject_relationship group each of its relationship types maps to.

A worked example over the openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-CLUSTER.person_identifier.v2 cluster, with the Microsoft Entra object id as the binding key:

[[authz.party_binding.person.template]]
template_id = "FerroEHR professional"
default = true
