full_verify_intervalduration"7d"The time between two scheduled full passes over the hash chain, which also recompute the records before the checkpoint; "0s" leaves the full pass to SELECT * FROM audit.verify_audit_chain() on demand. A run that found damage is always followed by a full pass.

The local store is the durability anchor of the whole subsystem: with it on, the FHIR feed drains from it, so a down repository loses nothing.

The floors and ceilings are written in calendar years. In every EU Member State the floor is three years (EHDS Art. 9(2)), and a longer national floor wins: five years in the Netherlands. Switzerland keeps its one-year floor. A retention value is compared against them exactly. A retention value is held to the most days the years can span for a floor (1096 for three years, 1830 for the Dutch five, 366 for one) and to the fewest for a ceiling (1095 for the German three). A declared § 309 controller in Germany therefore has no retention value that passes both the EHDS floor and the § 309 ceiling, and sets retention = 3:

[audit.store]
retention = 3
sgb_v_309_controller = true

[audit.categories]

The map every access record is classified through by EHDS category (Annex II 3.2(c); see the EHDS logging elements). The classification is done by ehds-logging, the EHDS logging component the FerroHEALTH products share (FerroAUDIT); this section is the deployment’s map. A template id, or failing that a root archetype id, maps to a list of categories, or to the word none for data of no category. An access the map in force cannot classify is recorded unclassified with its ids, never refused.

The shipped map. While the section declares no template and no archetype, the map FerroEHR ships applies (app/ferroehr/assets/audit-categories.default.toml). It names the published CKM templates and COMPOSITION archetypes whose purpose places their data in one priority category:

KeyCategory
template International Patient Summary, archetype openEHR-EHR-COMPOSITION.health_summary.v1Patient-Summaries
template ePrescription (FHIR), archetype openEHR-EHR-COMPOSITION.prescription.v0Electronic-Prescriptions
template Generic lab test result example simpleLaboratory-Reports
template CCTA reportMedical-Imaging
archetype openEHR-EHR-COMPOSITION.transfer_summary.v1Discharge-Reports

It leaves out the generic report.v1 and report-result.v1 containers, which carry laboratory, imaging and other reports alike, so an access through them is recorded unclassified instead of guessed. CKM publishes no composition for an electronic dispensation. A deployment that declares any template or archetype replaces the shipped map whole, so copy its entries into your own map to keep them. A national category declared alone keeps the shipped map. shipped_map = false with nothing declared leaves no map: every access is then recorded unclassified, and deployment.profile = "production" refuses to start on the no_category_map gap unless deployment.accepts names it.

[audit.categories]
national = ["urn:oid:2.16.840.1.113883.2.4.3.11.60.1|beeld"]

[audit.categories.templates]
"International Patient Summary" = ["Patient-Summaries"]
"Laboratory Report" = ["Laboratory-Reports"]

[audit.categories.archetypes]
"openEHR-EHR-COMPOSITION.report-result.v1" = ["Laboratory-Reports"]
"openEHR-EHR-COMPOSITION.encounter.v1" = "none"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
shipped_mapbooltrueApply the map FerroEHR ships while no template and no archetype is declared.
nationallist of <system>|<code>emptyThe national categories (EHDS Art. 14(1) third subparagraph) the map may name.
templatestable of template id → list of category, or "none"emptyConsulted first, by the template id the object was committed against.
archetypestable of archetype id → list of category, or "none"emptyConsulted for an object whose template the map does not name, by its root archetype id. A key that is not an archetype id refuses boot.

A priority category of EHDS Art. 14(1) is named by its code in HL7 Europe’s EEHRxFDocumentPriorityCategoryCS: Patient-Summaries, Electronic-Prescriptions, Electronic-Dispensations, Medical-Imaging, Laboratory-Reports and Discharge-Reports, or as <system>|<code>. A national category is named by the <system>|<code> it is declared with. Keys compare case-insensitively. An unknown code, an empty list, a word other than none, or two keys that differ only in case refuses boot with a message naming the entry. A record stores each category as its <system>|<code> token.

The map’s SHA-256 digest is on the boot line, on GET /management/info under audit.category_map, and on every access record. At boot the map is also mirrored into the retention register, so a retention period can be keyed on a category through the admin marks API.

[[authz.origin]]: the origins a deployment recognises

Every version records where its data came from at commit: each FEEDER_AUDIT originating-system id its body carries, and the access log reports them (EHDS Annex II 3.2(e)). Annex II 3.4 also asks for retention periods and access rights that take the origin into account. The ids a sending system writes are free text, so this register declares the origins your deployment recognises, which a retention period and an ABAC rule may then name. A top-level table, not part of [audit].

[[authz.origin]]
id = "lab.example"
clients = ["lab-gateway"]
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
registeredlist of tablesemptyThe recognised origins.
registered[].idstring(required)The id the origin’s data carry: the FEEDER_AUDIT system_id its feed writes, compared exactly, and the origin a direct commit by one of its clients is stamped with.
registered[].clientslist of stringemptyThe clients whose direct commits come from this origin: a Basic user name, or an access token’s client_id, failing that its azp.

A body that carries no FEEDER_AUDIT, committed by a listed client, is stamped with that client’s origin; a direct commit by any other caller keeps this server’s [api] system_id, as before. A blank id or one with whitespace, an id registered twice, a blank client, or a client listed under two origins refuses boot.

[audit.syslog]: the classic DICOM/syslog feed (ITI-20)

The DICOM PS3.15 audit message, framed as RFC 5424 syslog and sent over RFC 5425 TLS 1.2 or later by ihe-atna (FerroAUDIT). TLS is the one transport: an audit message names a patient (ITI TF-2 §3.20.4.1.2.1.1).

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
urlstringtls://localhost:6514The repository, tls://host:port; RFC 5425 §4.1 names port 6514. The table’s presence ships records; absent, nothing is sent.
tls.trust_roots_filepathunsetPEM bundle of trust roots for the repository, beside the platform’s.
tls.client_identity_filepathunsetThe client certificate chain and its private key in one PEM, for mutual TLS.
tls.client_identitysecretunsetThe same PEM inline, in place of client_identity_file.
tls.min_versionstring"1.3"The oldest TLS version the client speaks; set "1.2" for a repository that offers no TLS 1.3.
spool_dirpathunsetThe directory of the spool every frame is stored in before it is sent. It must give no access to the group or to other users. Unset, the spool is held in memory, and a restart loses the frames not yet delivered.
spool_max_eventsint100000The most frames the spool holds; a frame past it is refused and counted in atna_audit_dropped.
spool_max_sizesize"256MiB"The most the spool holds in size.
retry.max_backoffduration"1min"The longest wait between two delivery attempts after a failure.

[audit.syslog.tls] is the outbound TLS table every FerroHEALTH product takes, as [pixm.endpoint.tls] is. Concatenate the certificate chain and the private key into the one PEM client_identity_file names.

The drain stores each frame in ihe-atna’s spool, and the crate’s forwarder delivers it: one connection held open, a failed send retried with an exponential backoff and jitter, and the connection closed with a TLS close_notify on shutdown, so nothing is lost to a reset (ITI TF-2 §3.20.4.1.1, RFC 5425 §4.4). The local audit store keeps only the FHIR document, never the syslog frame, so the spool, not the store, is syslog’s outbox. delivered_syslog_at is no longer written.

[audit.fhir_feed]: the RESTful-ATNA feed (ITI-20 ATX:FHIR Feed)

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
endpointendpoint tablerequiredThe repository: url, its FHIR base (records go to {url}/AuditEvent; credentials embedded in it are masked in every rendering), timeout for one POST, the retry of a delivery (retry.max_backoff defaults to "1min" here), the TLS and the credential. The table’s presence turns the feed on.
poll_intervalduration"2s"How long the forwarder waits for a new record before it reads the store again.

ihe-atna’s forwarder delivers the feed. With the local store on, it delivers from the store, oldest record first: a record not yet delivered has no delivered_fhir_feed_at, so a repository outage loses nothing, and the record is stamped once the repository accepts it. A record the repository refuses (a 4xx other than 401, 408 or 429) is set aside until the next start. It is reported on GET /management/health as audit_delivery, and the records behind it keep flowing. With the store off, the feed delivers from an in-memory spool. The forwarder retries until the repository answers.

Authenticating the feed

The feed authenticates with the credential of [audit.fhir_feed.endpoint]: HTTP Basic, or the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant [audit.fhir_feed.endpoint.credentials.oauth] (the IHE IUA authorized-client model), with the grant’s keys. Under the grant FerroEHR sends the token as a bearer token, renews it before it expires, and when the repository refuses the held token with 401 fetches a new one and sends the record once more. Credentials in url beside a credential stop startup.

With the local store on, the feed delivers from the store and loses nothing across a repository outage. With the store off it delivers from an in-memory spool, so a restart loses what the spool holds.

Privacy & data minimisation

[privacy] is what the clinical side refuses to hold. Precedence, the environment-name grammar, and file discovery are on the Configuration reference index.

  • What this section is for
  • [privacy]
    • The subject reference
    • Identified parties
  • [privacy.identifier_scan]
    • The shipped rules
    • Why every rule is active by default
    • False positives, and what narrows them
    • Identifiers that declare their own type
    • Local patterns
  • [privacy.cohort]
    • The allow-list
  • Interaction with the audit trail
  • Protecting national identifiers in the demographic domain

What this section is for

FerroEHR keeps clinical content, demographic parties and the map between them in three separate database schemas reached by separate roles. That separation is only worth something if the clinical side does not carry the subject’s identity anyway, in the subject reference, in a party proxy, or in free text. This section is the three rules that keep it out.

No openEHR specification governs any of them. The Reference Model leaves EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref open and only advises against identifying content on a party proxy (PARTY_IDENTIFIED: “Should not be used to include patient identifying information”). GDPR Art. 4(5) and Art. 25(2) are what make it a duty; this section is where a deployment states its side of it.

All three rules run on the write path, before anything is stored. A refusal is 422 Unprocessable Entity with one errors[] entry per finding (sent when the request carries Prefer: return=representation), each naming the RM path and the rule that matched. A refusal never echoes the offending value — it would otherwise travel into the response body, the access log and the traces, which is the leak the rule exists to prevent.

[privacy]
subject_namespaces = []
allow_identified_parties_in_ehr = false

[privacy.identifier_scan]
mode = "strict"
rules = ["ch-ahvn13", "ch-epd-pid", "de-kvnr", "fi-hetu", "gb-nhs-number", "nl-bsn", "no-fodselsnummer", "se-personnummer"]
patterns = []

[privacy]

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
subject_namespaceslist of strings[]The pseudonymisation domains this deployment issues subject pseudonyms in.
allow_identified_parties_in_ehrboolfalseAccept a PARTY_RELATED whose relationship is self carrying name or identifiers in clinical content. Off already accepts every other party proxy; see the matrix below.

The subject reference

EHR_STATUS.subject is a PARTY_SELF whose optional external_ref points at a demographic service. Once subject_namespaces names at least one namespace, that reference must name one of them and carry a UUID as its id.value:

[privacy]
subject_namespaces = ["urn:ferroehr:pseudonym"]

FERROEHR__PRIVACY__SUBJECT_NAMESPACES=urn:ferroehr:pseudonym,mpi.example

What a deployment gets by default, and what declaring a namespace adds:

subject_namespaces empty (default)declared
EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref written by a clientaccepted with any namespace and any identifier, as the openEHR REST API admitsmust name a declared namespace and carry a UUID; anything else is a 422
The databaseno shape helda trigger on ehr refuses a non-UUID subject reference whichever session writes it
MintingFerroEHR mints noneFerroEHR mints none: the IHE patient identity source does

FerroEHR mints no pseudonym. Under the IHE patient identity source ([pixm]), the source answers the pseudonym the clinical domain holds for a patient, and the identity source mints it on the first ask; that domain’s assigning authority is a declared namespace. Every value that arrives from elsewhere, a client writing EHR_STATUS directly, an EHR-Extract, an archive load, meets the same rule, which is why declaring the namespace is the deployment’s act.

Empty is the default, and it leaves the rule out of force. A pseudonym namespace is a deployment fact — which service mints the tokens — and there is no name a server could invent for an operator. Declaring one is the same act as turning the rule on. An EHR with no subject reference at all is unaffected either way: that is the default EHR_STATUS the openEHR REST API describes, and it carries nothing to minimise.

Both spellings of a UUID’s case are accepted; the braced, URN and unhyphenated forms are not, because the promoted subject column is compared as text and four spellings of one pseudonym would be four subjects.

The rule has a second line of defence in the database. On every boot the server stamps whether namespaces are declared, and a trigger on the ehr table then refuses a subject reference that is not a UUID whichever code path or session writes it (ehr_subject_pseudonym_guard). Declaring namespaces over an existing store does not rewrite stored rows: the boot log names how many EHRs carry a subject reference that is not a pseudonym, and those need re-pseudonymising.

Identified parties

A party proxy inside clinical content — the composer, participations, the health care facility and the feeder-audit party slots — is governed by which class it is:

nameidentifiers
PARTY_IDENTIFIEDacceptedaccepted
PARTY_RELATED, relationship a third party (mother, guardian, donor, …)acceptedaccepted
PARTY_RELATED, relationship selfrefusedrefused

The two classes mean different things, so one rule for both was the wrong shape. PARTY_IDENTIFIED is the Reference Model’s own provider proxy: “Proxy data for an identified party other than the subject of the record”, “Typically for health care providers, e.g. name and provider number of an institution”. A composer name or a performing clinician’s name is that, not patient identity, and refusing it invented a prohibition the specification does not contain. ctx/composer_name in the simplified formats produces exactly this shape, and so does the example composition this server generates for a template.

identifiers follows the same line. The class is “Used to describe parties where only identifiers may be known … e.g. name and provider number of an institution”, so a clinician’s registration number on the composer is the class’s own paradigm case, and the simplified formats build exactly that from ctx/participation_identifiers. What the separation between the two database schemas exists to prevent is the subject’s national identifier on the clinical side, and that is caught in two places: a self party’s identifiers slot is refused by this rule, and a national-identifier value is refused by the identifier scanner below in free text and in every DV_IDENTIFIER.id the scanner reads by its type (identifiers that declare their own type).

PARTY_RELATED is the “Proxy type for identifying a party and its relationship to the subject of the record”, and that relationship “is coded as self” where the party is the patient. A name on a self party is the subject’s own identity and is refused. A name on any other relationship, the mother who consented, the guardian, the donor, is a third party the Reference Model models on purpose, and the openEHR REST API obliges a server to accept a composition that carries it, so it is accepted. A relationship the server cannot read counts as self: the rule refuses what it cannot prove harmless, and the Reference Model validator names the missing attribute on its own.

A refused proxy stays expressible: PARTY_IDENTIFIED’s own validity rule is satisfied by external_ref alone, so it points into the demographic domain instead of restating the identity.

The commit’s own AUDIT_DETAILS.committer is not clinical content and is never touched by this rule.

A deployment that needs a name or formal identifiers on a self party sets:

[privacy]
allow_identified_parties_in_ehr = true

which is announced at boot with a warning naming what it permits.

[privacy.identifier_scan]

Every string leaf of every clinical write is checked against the active identifier rules: the EHR, EHR_STATUS, COMPOSITION and directory writes, the CONTRIBUTION path, EHR-Extract import and the admin archive load. The two replay paths store a record verbatim, so for them a finding refuses the whole import or load rather than rewriting the content; demographic parties are the domain that holds identity and are not scanned.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
modestrict or warnstrictstrict refuses the write; warn accepts it and records a warning naming the RM path and the rule.
ruleslist of rule keysevery rule the build shipsThe national personal-identifier rules to scan for. An unknown key is a boot error listing the shipped keys.
patternslist of regular expressions[]Extra patterns for the kinds no build can ship a rule for.

The shipped rules

Each rule transcribes the checksum its own issuing register publishes. A kind whose current algorithm could not be established from its own register is not shipped, because a rule that guesses is worse than an absent one: it tells an operator their data was scanned.

KeyJurisdictionIdentifierPublished by
ch-ahvn13CHAHV-Nummer (AHVN13)AHVV Art. 133 for the structure; the check digit from the BSV Wegleitung VA/IK 318.106.02 d, Anhang 7; matches the plain run and the 756.3047.5009.62 display form
ch-epd-pidCHPatientenidentifikationsnummer (EPD-PID)EPDV-EDI Anhang 1, vendored at docs/law/ch/epdv-edi/: the fixed prefix 76133761 and a mod-10 check digit
de-kvnrDEKrankenversichertennummer (the unchangeable part)GKV-Spitzenverband, Richtlinie nach § 290 SGB V, 3.4.1, with Anlage 1; the letter-to-digit convention (A=01 … Z=26) is stated in prose only in the same Richtlinie’s Anlage 2 and fixed for A and C by the KVNR’s own worked examples
fi-hetuFIhenkilötunnusValtioneuvoston asetus väestötietojärjestelmästä 128/2010, 2 §: the date of birth, the century sign, the individual number and the mod-31 check character
gb-nhs-numberGBNHS NumberNHS Data Model and Dictionary
nl-bsnNLburgerservicenummerRijksdienst voor Identiteitsgegevens, Logisch Ontwerp BSN
no-fodselsnummerNOfødselsnummerSkatteetaten
se-personnummerSEpersonnummerSkatteverket

Two are deliberately absent. The Danish CPR-nummer has been issued without its modulus-11 control since 2007, and those numbers are fully valid, so a checksum rule would pass most recent ones through while reporting Denmark as covered. The Belgian rijksregisternummer’s modulo-97 check is widely reproduced but no definition published by the Rijksregister itself could be retrieved.

Why every rule is active by default

Clinical data crosses borders: a Dutch hospital receives referrals carrying a Norwegian fødselsnummer. An operator who has not configured the scanner is exactly the operator who has not yet worked out which identifiers their content carries, so the default covers all of them.

The two costs are not symmetric. A false positive is a loud 422 naming the RM path and the rule, which an operator answers by narrowing rules or moving to warn. A false negative is a national identifier stored on the clinical side indefinitely.

A deployment that knows its jurisdictions narrows the list:

[privacy.identifier_scan]
rules = ["nl-bsn", "no-fodselsnummer"]

FERROEHR__PRIVACY__IDENTIFIER_SCAN__RULES=nl-bsn,no-fodselsnummer

A Dutch deployment that receives no British content, for example, has no use for gb-nhs-number, whose check accepts one ten-digit run in eleven.

The boot log states which rules are active, so a jurisdiction that is not covered is visible rather than assumed.

False positives, and what narrows them

Every checksum accepts some fraction of random digit runs, and clinical content is full of numbers. Three things narrow it:

  • A digit run must be delimited — bounded by something other than a letter, a digit or an underscore. Without that, every hex digest and long numeric identifier produces hits at the checksum’s own rate. It also means a UUID can never match any rule: its groups are 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12 characters, so no delimited run of 9, 10 or 11 digits occurs in one, and the opaque subject pseudonym the boundary mandates passes unconditionally.
  • CODE_PHRASE.code_string is skipped. A terminology code system’s identifiers are digit runs by construction, so this one slot is where the collision is systematic rather than incidental. Measured over this repository’s vendored corpora: of the 30 distinct nine-digit values that satisfy the Dutch elfproef, 27 are SNOMED CT concept identifiers, all of them in a code slot. The carve-out names an RM slot, not a country.
  • Each rule narrows itself with whatever structure it has. Two independent control digits (no-fodselsnummer, 1 in 120), an embedded date (se-personnummer, 1 in 139 with the Luhn check), a non-numeric token shape (fi-hetu, 1 in 31 among tokens of that shape). nl-bsn at 1 in 11 is the loosest shipped rule, which is why the code-slot carve-out matters most to it. Every figure here is measured, over 100 000 random tokens of each rule’s own shape, by a test that fails if a rule drifts from the rate it publishes.

A deployment measuring its own content runs warn first, reads the recorded findings, then moves to strict.

Identifiers that declare their own type

A DV_IDENTIFIER carries an optional type, which the Reference Model describes as the “identifier type, such as prescription, or Social Security Number”, and its examples run from a social security number to an “order id”. The scanner reads it before it scans the id. When the type is absent or names neither kind, the scanner reads the name of the ELEMENT that holds the identifier instead, by the same words. Every ELEMENT is a LOCATABLE, whose name the Reference Model calls “the original label by which this entry was known to end users”, and an archetyped element carries its node name there:

DV_IDENTIFIERIn clinical contentIn FEEDER_AUDIT.originating_system_item_ids or feeder_system_item_ids
type names a person identifierscannedscanned
type names an item (an order, specimen, accession, sample, lot)not scannednot scanned
no type, or one naming neither, and the element name names a personscannedscanned
no type, or one naming neither, and the element name names an itemnot scannednot scanned
no type, or one naming neither, and no element name naming eitherscannednot scanned

A type that names a kind takes precedence over the element name, so an identifier typed NHS Number is scanned under any element name.

The type is free text, so it is read by its words, in any case and in snake_case, camelCase or spaced form. Words such as patient, person, subject, national, social, insurance, NHS, BSN and the name of every shipped rule name a person; order, placer, filler, accession, specimen, sample, requisition, prescription, lot, batch, serial, barcode and container name an item. A person word wins: patient order number is scanned. The feeder audit’s item-id lists are, in the Reference Model’s words, “Identifiers used for the item in the originating system, e.g. filler and placer ids”, so an identifier there is scanned only when its type says it identifies a person.

A laboratory filler order number typed filler_order_number is therefore stored even when its ten digits pass the NHS Number check by chance, which one ten-digit run in eleven does. So is an untyped order number in the Requester order identifier or Receiver order identifier element of openEHR-EHR-OBSERVATION.laboratory_test_result.v1, while an untyped value in an element named NHS number or Patient identifier is scanned. The archetype’s Laboratory internal identifier names neither kind, so a value there is scanned unless its type names an item. The same number written into free text is still claimed by every rule in rules; a deployment with no NHS Numbers in its content leaves gb-nhs-number out of that list.

Local patterns

Medical-record numbers, payer references and postcode forms have no single issuing register to transcribe, so a deployment declares them itself as Rust regular expressions:

[privacy.identifier_scan]
patterns = [
  "\\bMRN-[0-9]{6}\\b",
  "(^|[^0-9A-Za-z])[1-9][0-9]{3} ?[A-Z]{2}[^0-9A-Za-z]{1,3}[0-9]{1,4}([^0-9A-Za-z]|$)",
]

The second refuses a Dutch postcode paired with a house number — the pair is what identifies a household; a postcode alone does not. A pattern that does not compile is a boot error naming it.

[privacy.cohort]

Cross-domain cohort queries: select a population in the demographic domain, resolve it to the EHRs whose EHR_STATUS subject names it, and run AQL over exactly those EHRs. A FerroEHR extension — no openEHR spec governs it. The wire contract and a worked example are in Querying with AQL.

Off until a predicate is bound. Which demographic leaf may be selected on is a deployment fact about the archetypes in use, never something the server can infer, so [privacy.cohort.predicates] is empty by default and POST /query/cohort answers 404 until it is not. subjects = true turns the surface on without a predicate, for cohorts that name their subjects by identifier. That is the one form an IHE patient identity source serves ([pixm] subject_index = "pixm"): it holds no party-to-EHR map, so a predicate is refused there.

[privacy.cohort]
small_cell_threshold = 5
max_cohort_size = 100000

[privacy.cohort.predicates]
city = { archetype = "openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-ADDRESS.address.v1", node = "at0012", kind = "text" }
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
small_cell_thresholdint5The distinct-EHR floor a result set must reach to be served. Below it the rows are withheld and the response is marked suppressed; 0 disables suppression.
max_cohort_sizeint100000The largest cohort a predicate may select. A wider one is refused 422 rather than truncated: a silently shortened cohort is a wrong denominator.
predicatestableemptyThe allow-list, keyed by the name a caller uses. Empty, with subjects off, leaves the surface off.
subjectsboolfalseLet a request name its subjects by identifier, in any identifier domain, each resolved through the [pixm] provider: under the IHE provider by a forward PIXm translation into the server’s clinical domain, never back.

The allow-list

Exactly five keys are bindable — city, postcode_area, sex, age_band and organisation — and an unknown key is a boot error. Each binding carries three fields:

FieldDescription
archetypeThe archetype HRID of the leaf ELEMENT’s nearest archetyped ancestor, e.g. openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-PERSON.person.v1. Must be a demographic HRID; anything else is a boot error.
nodeThe ELEMENT’s archetype_node_id at-code, e.g. at0012.
kindHow a caller’s value is matched: text (exact, against value/value), text_prefix (prefix, LIKE-escaped), coded (exact, against value/defining_code/code_string), or birth_date (an inclusive age band in whole years, 40-49).

age_band must be bound birth_date, and no other key may be — both halves are boot errors, because a mismatch would bind a predicate that matches nothing while reporting an empty cohort.

The archetype must be one the node model reaches. A party is decomposed into its own rows for the party root, for each PARTY_IDENTITY, CONTACT, ADDRESS and CAPABILITY nested in it, and for every archetyped ITEM_TREE or CLUSTER under any of their details. An ADDRESS under a CONTACT is therefore bindable like anything else.

Interaction with the audit trail

The ATNA Patient-Number participant is filled from the promoted subject column, so constraining the subject reference to an opaque pseudonym is also what keeps the audit trail and its forwarding sinks free of the identity. The contribution outbox carries no subject at all. Both are covered by a CI test that fails when any subject identifier other than the opaque UUID appears in an outbox payload, an ATNA message or a trace record.

Protecting national identifiers in the demographic domain

The rules above keep national identifiers off the clinical side. The demographic side is where a party’s identifiers legitimately live, and [privacy.identifier_protection] decides how they are held there.

With the table present, an identifier of a configured scheme never sits in the versioned body. The value moves to party.national_identifier, sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived per domain, and the body keeps a reference in its place. Beside the ciphertext sits an HMAC-SHA-256 digest of the value, which is what makes “which party holds this identifier” answerable without decrypting anything — and, because it is keyed, what stops the database, a backup or a read replica from reversing a nine-digit space.

#? [privacy.identifier_protection]
#? schemes = ["nl-bsn"]
#? key_file = "/run/secrets/ferroehr-identifier-key"
KeyTypeDefaultDescription
enabledboolfalseWhether protection is in force. Off leaves identifiers stored as written.
schemeslist of string["nl-bsn"]The DV_IDENTIFIER.type values to protect. Each must exist in the party.identifier_scheme registry; with protection on, the server refuses to boot when one does not.
keysecretunsetThe root key, 64 hex characters. Prefer key_file.
key_filepathunsetA file holding the root key, read at boot.

Turning it on with no key, with an empty schemes list, or with a scheme the registry does not hold, is a boot error. A server that believes it seals national identifiers and does not is worse than one that never claimed to.

Four properties worth knowing before you enable it:

  • The stored, signed and served body are the same form. Sealing runs before the body is decomposed and signed, exactly like the multimedia offload, so a signature still verifies against the bytes the server holds. What a reader receives carries the reference; the value is available through the admin read below. A create or update response serves the stored form as well, so the value you submitted does not come back in it.
  • Each party version keeps its own sealed rows. A later version retires the rows of the one before it without rewriting them, so an older version still expands to the value it committed. Only live rows take part in the one-party-per-value rule.
  • Nothing resolves an identifier to a party. The server offers no lookup from an identifier value to the party that holds it. The keyed digest keeps a value live for at most one party at a time.
  • Reading a value back is audited and needs its own role. GET /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/party/identifiers serves a party version with its values put back, for a caller holding both the admin role and authz.rbac.identifier_reader_role, and records each scheme it expands (reading a party’s protected identifiers).
  • The key is load-bearing and rotation is a re-encryption. The runbook is in Operations.

Only the demographic writer role reaches the sealed value. The read-only twin sees that a party holds a protected identifier and which party it is, and is refused the ciphertext and the digest by column-level grant; the clinical roles are refused the table outright.

CLI & production checklist

The binary’s command-line surface, what a zero-configuration boot actually gives you, the minimum a production deployment sets, and which material belongs in a mounted file rather than an environment variable. Precedence, the environment-name grammar, and file discovery are on the Configuration reference index.

  • The command line
    • Exit status
    • ferroehr config …
    • ferroehr db …
    • ferroehr definitions load
    • ferroehr party-binding refill
    • ferroehr party-binding check
    • ferroehr party-binding adopt
    • ferroehr healthcheck
    • ferroehr usage-report --print
    • ferroehr report
  • Zero-config boot and the production checklist
  • What belongs in a mounted file (versus the environment)
  • Variables outside the server’s namespace

The command line

Two flags are global: they apply to the server and to every subcommand:

FlagDescription
--config <path>The configuration file to load, overriding FERROEHR_CONFIG. Fatal if missing or unreadable.
--set <key>=<value>A dotted-path override, repeatable, highest precedence of all layers (e.g. --set database.max_connections=40).

With no subcommand, or with serve, the binary boots the server. ferroehr --version prints the version and the manufacturer of the release:

ferroehr <version>
Manufactured by Cadasto B.V., Comeniusstraat 2d, 1817 MS Alkmaar, The Netherlands, info@cadasto.com
https://www.cadasto.com/contact/

Exit status

Every command, the server included, exits with one of these statuses, the failure written to stderr with its whole cause:

StatusMeaning
0The command did what it was asked.
1The command failed for any other reason: a database it cannot reach, a probe that reads unhealthy, a server that cannot serve.
2clap could not parse the command line.
78The binary refuses its configuration (EX_CONFIG of sysexits(3)): an unknown or invalid key, a semantic rule the configuration breaks, an [auth] table with no mechanism, or a SCIM mapping it cannot serve.

An orchestrator can tell a configuration to fix from a failure to retry by the status alone.

ferroehr config …

ferroehr config check [--config P]  # validate file + environment + --set

The starting point for a real ferroehr.toml is app/ferroehr/assets/ferroehr.default.toml, every key under its description and set to its default, generated from the configuration types. Every configuration key shows it whole.

config check runs the same validation the server runs at boot (the strict unknown-key sweep, the type pass, the aggregated semantic rules, and the “authentication enabled needs a mechanism” rule) and touches no database, so it is safe in CI and before a rollout. It exits 0 when the configuration is valid and 78 otherwise; on success it prints the effective configuration as TOML with every secret redacted, and notes on stderr when database.url is still the built-in development default.

ferroehr db …

ferroehr db migrate   # apply the embedded migrations and exit
ferroehr db verify    # verify, issuing no DDL, that the schema matches this build

These exist so a least-privilege deployment can separate the two database identities: run db migrate once under a DSN that holds DDL rights (a Kubernetes Job, an init container, a CI/CD stage), then boot the server with database.migrations = "verify" under a DSN with no DDL rights at all. verify still reads all five _sqlx_migrations bookkeeping tables, which no least-privilege role can do, so point [database] migrate_url at the credential that prepares the schema. See Operations.

ferroehr definitions load

ferroehr definitions load person.adls role.adls   # store each file, then exit

Stores each file in the definition store, in the order given, before serve starts. An .opt file is an OPT 1.4 template and an .adls file an ADL 2 archetype or template, whose parents and slot fillers come before it in the list. Each file is validated and versioned exactly as the REST upload (POST /definition/template/adl1.4 or /adl2) would, and the command stops at the first refusal, naming the file. A file whose id is already stored with the same text is left alone, so the step runs at every start; one stored under the same id with other text is refused, because a stored definition never changes and a changed one takes a new version in its id.

A deployment that maps its professionals to demographic parties runs it first, so the party mapping finds its templates when the server boots: as a one-shot compose service, a Helm init container or a setup step. The repository’s deploy/definitions/professional/ holds the PERSON and ROLE pair the development lanes and the quickstart load, adapted from openEHR CKM archetypes; a production deployment loads the templates its own modelling chose.

ferroehr party-binding refill

ferroehr party-binding refill   # rebuild the party binding side table under the configured mapping

Rebuilds the binding side table from the party versions under the configured party mapping and stores the mapping’s digest. Run it with every replica stopped after a mapping change: it refuses while a replica holds a live lease, and refuses a store in which two parties carry one selector value, naming both.

ferroehr party-binding check

ferroehr party-binding check [--admin <PARTY_ID>]... [--admin-key <ISSUER> <KEY>]...
                             [--migration <COMMITTER_NAME>]...
                             [--expected <FILE> [--expected-issuer <ISSUER>]]

The pre-flight of a migration to party binding. It reads the party versions under the configured party mapping and writes nothing: the side-table categories are read from a refill inside a transaction that is rolled back, so it runs before any boot fill and beside a running server. It connects with the configured database credentials and runs no migration.

The report is a JSON document on stdout:

  • issuers: per identifier_issuer, the PERSONs that carry a binding key;
  • duplicates: every binding key, userName or externalId two PERSONs carry, which a fill refuses;
  • inactive and abandoned: the key-bearing PERSONs whose head is 800|inactive| or 801|abandoned|;
  • side_table.provisional: the provisional PERSONs that just-in-time creation created more than [authz.party_binding] provisional_report_after days ago (default 30) and that SCIM or an administrator has not completed, by container id and creation time, oldest first, with no name or other personal data;
  • side_table.unadopted: the key-bearing PERSONs that perform no professional ROLE, which adopt has not reached;
  • side_table.basic_users: every [[authz.party_binding.basic_user]] with the PERSON it binds today, or none;
  • provenance: for each key, the committer of the version that introduced it and who that committer is under the provenance rule;
  • expected: with --expected, every login of the file (one per line) that no live PERSON carries.

A key passes the provenance rule when the version that introduced it was committed by a [[auth.scim.client]] (its client identifier under its token issuer), by an administrator, by a declared migration, or by just-in-time creation at a first login of an [[authz.party_binding.issuer]] with jit = true (a 249|creation| version carrying its description, committed by the new PERSON itself). A stored version records no role its committer held, so you name the administrators: by the id of their PERSON with --admin, or by the identifier_issuer and value of a key their PERSON carries with --admin-key. --migration declares a migration by the committer name its versions carry. The report repeats what you named.

The command exits non-zero, after printing the report, on a duplicate, a mapped Basic user or expected login with no PERSON, or a key whose committer fails the provenance rule.

ferroehr party-binding adopt

ferroehr party-binding adopt (--admin <PARTY_ID> | --admin-key <ISSUER> <KEY>)...
                             [--migration <COMMITTER_NAME>]... <PARTY_ID>...

Gives each listed PERSON a professional ROLE, so a prepared PERSON of an existing deployment binds: a ROLE of the mapping’s [authz.party_binding.professional_role] template with the PERSON as performer, and a new PERSON version listing it in roles. Every adoption of one run is one demographic CONTRIBUTION, committed by the first administrator you name (a PARTY_IDENTIFIED committer whose external_ref is that administrator’s PERSON), and each adopted PERSON gets one access record through the configured [audit] trail. Adopt the existing persons before the first SCIM provisioning run: without the ROLE, a userName eq filter finds no User and the identity provider creates a duplicate.

The command applies the provenance rule of check with the same --admin, --admin-key and --migration operator input, and refuses the whole run, naming them, while any listed PERSON’s key was introduced by another committer. It also refuses a party that is no live key-bearing PERSON of a mapped template, an inactive or abandoned one, and a store in which two PERSONs carry one selector value. A PERSON that already performs the ROLE is reported under already and left alone. The report is a JSON document on stdout with the CONTRIBUTION and each new ROLE.

ferroehr healthcheck

Asks the running server’s GET /health/readiness and exits 0 on 200, 1 otherwise, with the reason on stderr: the container HEALTHCHECK and the Kubernetes exec-probe fallback. A draining server answers 503, so it reads unhealthy. The subcommand loads the same configuration as the server (file, environment, --set) and asks the server.listen port under server.base_path, on the loopback when the server listens on every interface. With [server.tls] set it speaks TLS and accepts exactly the leaf in server.tls.certificate_file, presenting server.tls.healthcheck_identity_file to a listener that requires a client certificate. It waits three seconds for the answer.

ferroehr usage-report --print

ferroehr usage-report --print                  # the start report
ferroehr usage-report --print --event daily    # the daily report, with its metrics

Prints the exact JSON body of the usage report this instance would send now, on one line to stdout, and sends nothing. It loads the same configuration as the server and connects to the database to read the instance id and the shared metrics window, writing nothing. Notes go to stderr: a sample id when the database holds none yet, and a line saying so when the report is off. --print is required; printing is the only action.

ferroehr report

ferroehr report                              # writes ferroehr-report-<UTC time>.json here
ferroehr report --output /tmp/report.json    # writes to the path you name
ferroehr report --output -                   # writes the JSON to stdout

Writes one JSON document naming what this deployment runs. Attach it to a complaint, a non-conformity finding or a serious-incident report: it is the “which FerroEHR does this deployment run” answer those start from. It loads the same configuration as the server and must pass the same validation. It reads the databases and writes nothing to them.

PartWhat it holds
manifestevery part below with its status (included, partial or unavailable) and, for the last two, the reason
buildversion, commit, build date, rustc, the active deployment.spec_profile and the specification versions it selects, the PostgreSQL target, the audit posture, and the manufacturer
imagenamed in the manifest only: a running binary cannot read the digest of the image it was started from, so attach docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' <image> or the pod’s status.containerStatuses[].imageID
targetthe CPU architecture and operating system the binary was built for, and whether it is a debug build
featuresthe optional integrations compiled in (fhir, multimedia)
openehr_crateseach openehr-* crate the binary links, with its version
openehr_crates_originpublished in a release build, whose openehr_crates versions are the ones that release published to crates.io; source_tree in any other build, a pre-release included, whose versions are the source tree’s manifests
licencethe licence summary GET /management/status serves (state, use, licensee, last valid day, what the configured token contributed); never the token
deploymentthe deployment profile, the open gaps and the accepted ones, measured over the databases, or from the configuration alone when they do not answer
schemafor each database, the highest migration version applied and the highest this build embeds, per schema
configurationthe effective configuration as config check prints it

The crate versions on main are a floor below the line on crates.io: the release that publishes the crates picks the version and writes it into its checkout before it builds the server, so only a release build can name the published version. A pre-release publishes no crates, and a build from source names the version its manifests hold, which may be an older published version than the code it links. Read openehr_crates_origin before you look a version up on crates.io.

Nothing in it identifies a person: it reads no clinical, demographic or audit table. Every secret in the configuration shows ***, every URL shows *** in place of its user name and password, and a database error quoted as a reason has each configured database user name and password masked too. A database that does not answer within 15 seconds leaves the schema part out and names it unavailable with unreachable: … as the reason.

Zero-config boot and the production checklist

With no file and no environment, the effective configuration is: listener 0.0.0.0:8080 at the ITS-REST base path with Swagger UI, reading bodies up to 64 MiB; the database at the built-in development DSN with migrations applied at boot; RBAC on; signing on in digest mode with read-time verification strict; the audit trail on with only the local store; no caller rate limit; logs in auto format at info; and every integration off. The one outbound connection on by default is the usage report, which usage_report.enabled = false switches off.

One thing that configuration does not do is serve requests. auth.enabled defaults to true, and authentication enabled with no mechanism configured is a boot error rather than a running server that refuses everything: RFC 9110 §11.6.1 requires a 401 challenge to name a scheme applicable to the resource, and a server with no mechanism has none: it could only refuse every request while advertising a scheme it does not implement. The error names the three ways out: add [[auth.basic.users]], add an [auth] issuer, or set auth.enabled = false for development. So a bare docker run of the image with no configuration stops at startup with that message, while the downloadable Compose quickstart boots because it ships a user.

For production, set at least:

  • database.url: the real DSN, via FERROEHR__DATABASE__URL from a secret or a url_file-mounted value, never inline in a world-readable file. Leaving the development default in place is warned about loudly at every boot.
  • database.migrations = "verify" with the schema applied out of band, so the serving role needs no DDL rights, plus database.migrate_url naming the credential that reads every schema’s migration state at boot. The serving credential cannot.
  • deployment.profile = "production" once the deployment holds real personal data. The server then refuses to start while a separation is open and not accepted by name, instead of running as a sandbox that looks identical.
  • an authentication mechanism: a Basic user store and/or an [auth] issuer.
  • telemetry.format = "json" for cluster log collectors.
  • api.cors stays false; api.openapi_ui per posture.
  • api.system_id: this deployment’s own openEHR system identifier. Choose it before the first EHR is created: it is stored with every EHR, audit entry and version identifier, and changing it later never rewrites what is already committed.
  • management.* per posture. A dedicated management.listen is recommended so the introspection surface is never reachable on the clinical listener, and every endpoint stays off until you name a level for it.
  • TLS everywhere a transport supports it: server.tls (or a TLS-terminating ingress), HTTPS for the object store; the audit syslog feed always speaks TLS.
  • real secrets via the environment or a *_file sibling, never inline.

Before a deployment holding real patient data goes live, work through the go-live checklist: it turns each item above into something you run and read back, and adds the privacy and audit checks a controller is asked for.

What belongs in a mounted file (versus the environment)

The environment sets an array of tables only by element index (FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUER), so the issuers, the party tables and the Basic-auth user store read more clearly from a file.

Genuinely file-shaped material (the PGP signing key, Cedar policies, ATNA and terminology-server PEMs, a JWKS blob) is referenced by an in-TOML *_path / *_file key pointing at a mounted path. On Kubernetes the chart’s config.files map materialises each entry under /etc/ferroehr/, read-only, from a Secret.

Prefer a *_file sibling over the environment form for any secret in a container: an environment value is readable through /proc/<pid>/environ and is inherited by every child process the container spawns.

Everything else is a plain key you can set in the file or override with a FERROEHR_* variable.

For a worked development example (the server section, CORS, admin, management and the Basic-auth user store) read the configuration carried inline in the quickstart docker-compose.yml; see Docker Compose.

Variables outside the server’s namespace

The PostgreSQL init container’s variables are PG_INIT_USER, PG_INIT_PASSWORD and PG_INIT_DB; they configure the database container, not the server, and sit outside the server’s reserved FERROEHR_ namespace.

Inside that namespace, a handful of names are deliberately not configuration keys and pass the strict sweep untouched: FERROEHR_CONFIG (the config-file pointer), the build-stamp variables, and the Compose parameterization (image tags, host ports, CPU and memory limits). They keep a single _ by design, which is exactly what distinguishes them from configuration keys, and why a single-underscore misspelling of a real key is reported at boot with the uniform spelling it should have had.

Every configuration key

This page shows the shipped ferroehr.toml template, ferroehr.default.toml. It holds every key FerroEHR reads, each under its description and set to its default. tools/config-reference generates it from the configuration types, so it matches the server you run.

  • A live line is a key at its default. Change the value to set it.
  • A #? line is a key with no default, a secret, or a key of a table the defaults leave out. Remove the #? marker and the space after it, then fill in the value, to set it.
  • A # [table.<name>] header shows a table you name yourself, with its keys commented out.

Every key can also be set as an environment variable: FERROEHR, then the TOML path with __ between the segments, such as FERROEHR__DATABASE__MAX_CONNECTIONS. The guides under Configuration reference explain the sections.

# @generated by tools/config-reference from the configuration types. DO NOT EDIT.
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Cadasto B.V.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: BUSL-1.1
#
# ferroehr.toml: every key FerroEHR reads, each under its description and set to
# its default. Copy this file to ferroehr.toml and edit what you change. A line
# marked `#?` is a key with no default, a secret, or a table the defaults leave
# out: remove `#? ` and fill the placeholder to set it. A line marked `#` under a
# `# [table.<name>]` header shows a table you name yourself.
#
# A duration is a string with its unit ("500ms", "30s", "10min", "12h",
# "7d"), a size a string with an IEC binary unit ("64MiB"). Each key can
# also be set as FERROEHR__<TABLE>__<KEY>, such as
# FERROEHR__DATABASE__MAX_CONNECTIONS; `--set key=value` wins over it.

# The declared posture, the openEHR specification set and the licence token.
[deployment]
# The declared posture (`sandbox` | `production`; default `sandbox`).
# `production` refuses to start while a separation it asserts is missing and
# not accepted by name (#3226).
profile = "sandbox"
# The `DeploymentGap`s a `production` deployment runs without, each stated on
# every boot and on `/management/status`. Ignored under `sandbox`, which
# accepts everything.
accepts = []
# The openEHR specification generation set the server runs (`development` |
# `stable`; default `development`).
spec_profile = "development"
# The commercial licence token file the licensor issued. Optional in every
# respect: an unset, missing, malformed or expired token is logged once at boot
# and the server runs unlicensed, identically in every other way.
#? licence_file = ""

# The HTTP listener: the family's section (the listen address, the timeouts,
# the body limit, the overload bound, the drain, TLS, the trusted proxies, the
# caller rate and compression).
[server]
# The socket address the listener binds.
listen = "0.0.0.0:8080"
# The path every route is served under: empty, or starting with `/` and not
# ending with one.
base_path = ""
# How long one request may take before the server answers `408`.
request_timeout = "30s"
# How long a client may take to send its first byte once it connected, and each
# HTTP/1.1 request head from that head's first byte; a client still sending its
# head then is disconnected, which bounds a connection that never finishes one.
# Never zero.
header_read_timeout = "30s"
# How long a kept-alive HTTP/1.1 connection may wait for its next request
# before the server closes it. Keep it longer than the idle timeout of the
# clients and proxies in front, so they close an idle connection first. Never
# zero.
idle_timeout = "2min"
# The largest request body the server reads before answering `413`.
body_limit = "64MiB"
# How long readiness stays withdrawn before the listener closes, so an
# orchestrator stops sending requests first.
drain_delay = "0s"
# How long the requests in flight may take once the listener closed.
shutdown_timeout = "10s"
# How many requests the server serves at once; past it a request is answered
# `503`. Unset, there is no bound.
#? max_concurrent_requests = 0
# How long a refused request is told to wait (`Retry-After`), a whole number of
# seconds, since the header carries delay-seconds (RFC 9110 §10.2.3).
retry_after = "1s"
# The reverse proxies whose forwarded client address is believed, each an
# address or a CIDR block; empty, every request is named by its peer.
trusted_proxies = []
# The header a trusted proxy names the client in.
forwarded_header = "forwarded"
# Whether a response is compressed with gzip or Brotli when the client accepts
# one.
compression = true
# The smallest response body that is compressed.
compression_min_size = "1KiB"

# The listener's TLS; unset, the listener speaks plain HTTP behind a proxy that
# terminates TLS.
#? [server.tls]
# The certificate chain, the leaf first.
#? certificate_file = ""
# The private key of the leaf.
#? key_file = ""
# Whether the listener asks a client certificate.
#? client_auth = "none"
# The CA bundle a client certificate must chain to; required unless
# `client_auth` is `none`, and refused when it is.
#? client_ca_file = ""
# How often the files are read again, never zero; unset, only `SIGHUP` reads
# them again.
#? reload_interval = "500ms"
# The client certificate chain and key, in one PEM, the healthcheck presents to
# a listener that asks one.
#? healthcheck_identity_file = ""
# The oldest TLS version the listener speaks: `"1.3"` unless lowered to
# `"1.2"`.
#? min_version = "1.3"

# The requests one caller may send; unset, a caller is not limited.
#? [server.caller_rate]
# The requests per second a caller may send once its burst is spent.
#? requests_per_second = 0
# The requests a caller may send at once.
#? burst = 0

# The console, the request log and the OpenTelemetry export, the family's
# shared section.
[telemetry]
# The console rendering.
format = "auto"
# The `tracing` filter directive of the console.
filter = "info,hyper=warn,tower=warn,h2=warn"
# The query parameters whose values the request log may carry; empty, it
# carries none.
logged_query_parameters = []
# The deployment environment, `deployment.environment.name` on the resource,
# such as `production`.
#? environment = ""

# The OTLP collector, when spans and metrics are exported.
#? [telemetry.otlp]
# The collector's OTLP/gRPC endpoint; `https://` speaks TLS. It may carry a
# credential, so it renders masked.
#? endpoint = ""
# Whether the product's spans are exported.
#? traces = true
# Whether the metrics are pushed.
#? metrics = true
# The share of the server's traces that are sampled.
#? sample_ratio = 1.0

# The TLS to the collector: trust roots beside the platform's, the client
# identity for mutual TLS and the minimum version. The crate reads none of it:
# the product reads the table with `ferrohealth-server`'s `TlsClient` and hands
# the built configuration to `Telemetry::with_tls`. TLS material is refused
# beside an endpoint that is not `https://`.
#? [telemetry.otlp.tls]
# The client certificate chain and its private key, in one PEM.
#? client_identity = ""
# A file holding `client_identity`.
#? client_identity_file = ""
# A PEM bundle of trust roots beside the platform's.
#? trust_roots_file = ""
# The oldest TLS version the client speaks: `"1.3"` unless lowered to `"1.2"`,
# as for the listener.
#? min_version = "1.3"

# The installation report to `FerroPULSE` (on by default).
[usage_report]
# The off switch: `false` sends nothing.
enabled = true
# The collector.
endpoint = "https://report.ferropulse.eu/v1/report"
# The directory the instance id lives in; without one nothing is sent, since
# every restart would count as a new installation.
#? state_dir = ""
# How the product is deployed.
deployment = "unknown"

# Authentication: the `ferrohealth-smart` section, whose serialization writes
# every secret as `***`, `[auth.idp]`, `[auth.smart]` and `[auth.scim]`.
[auth]
# Whether inbound authentication is on; a product may refuse `false`.
enabled = true
# The realm the challenges name; empty for none, which a product replaces with
# its own default.
realm = ""
# The SMART capabilities the discovery document adds, each a capability SMART
# App Launch 2.2.0 or the SMART on openEHR draft defines, or a full URI.
capabilities = []
# The scopes the discovery document lists as `scopes_supported`: only scopes
# the product honours, because "the server SHALL support all scopes listed
# here".
scopes_supported = []
# The product's own scope, a full URI or a string starting with `__`; empty for
# none.
product_scope = ""

# The `[auth.issuer]` tables, each issuer with its own settings.
#? [[auth.issuer]]
# The issuer identifier. It renders with any userinfo masked, as `SecretUrl`
# renders itself.
#? issuer = ""
# Whose tokens the issuer signs; required, with no default.
#? kind = "persons"
# The preset the profile starts from.
#? profile = "rfc9068"
# The audiences, of which a token's `aud` must contain one.
#? audience = []
# The signature algorithms admitted.
#? algorithms = ["RS256", "RS384", "PS256", "PS384", "ES256", "ES384"]
# The clock skew, at most `300s`.
#? clock_skew = "1min"
# How long a held key set is used.
#? jwks_max_age = "10min"
# The shortest time between two reads of the key set.
#? jwks_refresh_interval = "1min"
# A key set file handed over out of band, in place of the issuer's `jwks_uri`;
# empty for none.
#? jwks_file = ""
# How long one call to the authorization server may take.
#? timeout = "10s"
# How the issuer's tokens are checked.
#? mode = "jwt"
# Whether the issuer's tokens must be bound to a `DPoP` key or a client
# certificate: `none` (the default) or `required` (`crate::sender`).
#? sender_constraint = "none"
# The claims the issuer's roles are read from, each a dotted path; by default
# `roles`, `groups` and `entitlements` (RFC 9068 §2.2.3.1), and none, never
# settable, on a `federation` issuer.
#? role_claims = []
# `ProfileKeys::person_key`.
#? person_key = ""
# `ProfileKeys::tenant_claim`.
#? tenant_claim = ""
# `ProfileKeys::client_claims`.
#? client_claims = []
# `ProfileKeys::impersonation_marker`.
#? impersonation_marker = ""
# `ProfileKeys::expect`.
#? expect = {}
# `ProfileKeys::user_claims`.
#? user_claims = []
# `ProfileKeys::person_equality`.
#? person_equality = []
# `ProfileKeys::unstable_claims`.
#? unstable_claims = []
# `ProfileKeys::first_party_clients`.
#? first_party_clients = []
# `ProfileKeys::max_actor_chain`.
#? max_actor_chain = 0
# `ProfileKeys::act_represents_patient`.
#? act_represents_patient = false
# `ProfileKeys::token_types`.
#? token_types = []
# `ProfileKeys::required_claims`.
#? required_claims = []
# `ProfileKeys::adapter`.
#? adapter = ""
# `ProfileKeys::max_onward_lifetime`.
#? max_onward_lifetime = "500ms"
# `ProfileKeys::onward_grant`.
#? onward_grant = "token_exchange"
# `ProfileKeys::onward_indicator`.
#? onward_indicator = "resource"
# `ProfileKeys::onward_parameters`.
#? onward_parameters = {}
# `ProfileKeys::onward_client_id`.
#? onward_client_id = false
# `ProfileKeys::onward_subject_audience`.
#? onward_subject_audience = false
# `ProfileKeys::onward_preview`.
#? onward_preview = []

# The introspection check, under `mode = "introspection"`.
#? [auth.issuer.introspection]

# renders with its userinfo and its query masked.

#? cache_max_age = "1min"

# The client identifier.

# How the client authenticates.

# The client secret, rendered redacted.
#? client_secret = ""
# The file holding the client secret.
#? client_secret_file = ""

# The `audience` request parameter; empty for none.

#? dpop_key_file = ""
# Whether the tokens are bound to the client certificate (RFC 8705 §3).
#? certificate_bound = false
# The security profile: `oauth2` (the default) or `fapi2`.
#? security_profile = "oauth2"
# The hosts a FAPI 2.0 mutual-TLS alias may be on (RFC 8705 §5).
#? mtls_alias_hosts = []

#? previous_private_key_file = ""
# How long the previous key stays published; `0s` for as long as it is set.

# The PEM file of the next assertion key, published and never signing.
#? next_private_key_file = ""
# The RFC 9396 `authorization_details` JSON text; empty for none.

# The PEM file holding the private key of the client assertion under

#? assertion_audience = "token_endpoint"
# The PEM file of the `DPoP` key the tokens are bound to (RFC 9449).

#? security_profile = "oauth2"
# The hosts a FAPI 2.0 mutual-TLS alias may be on (RFC 8705 §5).
#? mtls_alias_hosts = []
# The PEM file of the previous assertion key, published, never signing.
#? previous_private_key_file = ""
# How long the previous key stays published; `0s` for as long as it is set.
#? previous_key_overlap = "0s"
# The PEM file of the next assertion key, published and never signing.
#? next_private_key_file = ""

#? authorization_details = ""

# The TLS of the token endpoint connection: trust roots beside the platform's,

#? [auth.issuer.introspection.bearer.tls]

# The sources of each field, over the mapping's.

# The `[auth.party]` tables, one per `persons` issuer whose logins are bound to

#? identifier_issuer = ""
# The type of those identifiers, which declares the key's canonical form:
# `guid` or `uuid` is compared in lower case, any other type exactly.
#? identifier_type = ""
# The claim naming the groups the token asserts, an array of strings; empty to
# read no group.
#? group_claim = ""
# The issuer of the group identifiers the group claim names; set with
# `group_claim`.
#? group_identifier_issuer = ""
# Whether a guest of the issuer is looked up; a guest is not by default.
#? guests = false

# The `[auth.idp]` table: the vendor adapters a profile may name, each read in
# a build that compiles it in.
[auth.idp]

# The Microsoft Graph access of the `idp-entra` adapter (`[auth.idp.entra]`),
# which resolves an Entra ID groups overage.
#? [auth.idp.entra]
# The Microsoft Graph root every URL is built from, `https` without a query or
# a fragment.
#? base_url = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0"
# The adapter's budget for one call, the token fetch and the Graph round trip
# together; never zero.
#? timeout = "2s"
# The largest Graph answer read; never zero.
#? max_response_size = "1MiB"
# The `securityEnabledOnly` parameter of `getMemberObjects`: `false` reads
# every group, administrative unit and directory role, `true` only the security
# groups.
#? security_enabled_only = false

# The client credentials grant the Graph token is obtained with, under the
# Graph permission the deployment grants.
#? [auth.idp.entra.credentials]
# The issuer whose metadata names the token endpoint; exclusive with
# `token_endpoint`. It renders with any userinfo masked, as `SecretUrl` renders
# itself.
#? issuer = ""
# The token endpoint itself; exclusive with `issuer`. It renders with its
# userinfo and its query masked.
#? token_endpoint = ""
# The client identifier.
#? client_id = ""
# How the client authenticates.
#? client_auth = "client_secret_basic"
# The client secret, rendered redacted.
#? client_secret = ""
# The file holding the client secret.
#? client_secret_file = ""
# The PEM file holding the private key of the client assertion under
# `private_key_jwt`, and of the actor assertion of an onward exchange
# (`credentials.onward.actor_assertion`) whatever the client authentication.
#? private_key_file = ""
# The `kid` the assertion names; the RFC 7638 thumbprint when empty.
#? kid = ""
# The algorithm the assertion is signed with; when unset, by key type, an EC
# key by its curve (P-256 ES256, P-384 ES384).
#? assertion_alg = ""
# The `scope` request parameter; empty for none.
#? scope = ""
# The RFC 8707 resource indicator; empty for none.
#? resource = ""
# The `audience` request parameter; empty for none.
#? audience = ""
# How long before the token expires a new one is fetched.
#? refresh_margin = "30s"
# How long one call to the authorization server may take.
#? timeout = "10s"
# The `aud` of a `private_key_jwt` assertion: `token_endpoint` (the default) or
# `issuer`, which needs `issuer` set.
#? assertion_audience = "token_endpoint"
# The PEM file of the `DPoP` key the tokens are bound to (RFC 9449).
#? dpop_key_file = ""
# Whether the tokens are bound to the client certificate (RFC 8705 §3).
#? certificate_bound = false
# The security profile: `oauth2` (the default) or `fapi2`.
#? security_profile = "oauth2"
# The hosts a FAPI 2.0 mutual-TLS alias may be on (RFC 8705 §5).
#? mtls_alias_hosts = []
# The PEM file of the previous assertion key, published, never signing.
#? previous_private_key_file = ""
# How long the previous key stays published; `0s` for as long as it is set.
#? previous_key_overlap = "0s"
# The PEM file of the next assertion key, published and never signing.
#? next_private_key_file = ""
# The RFC 9396 `authorization_details` JSON text; empty for none.
#? authorization_details = ""

# The TLS of the token endpoint connection: trust roots beside the platform's,
# the client identity presented over mutual TLS (RFC 8705 §2) and the minimum
# version. The crate reads none of it: a table that names material resolves
# through the product's `TlsBuilder`.
#? [auth.idp.entra.credentials.tls]
# The client certificate chain and its private key, in one PEM.
#? client_identity = ""
# A file holding `client_identity`.
#? client_identity_file = ""
# A PEM bundle of trust roots beside the platform's.
#? trust_roots_file = ""
# The oldest TLS version the client speaks: `"1.3"` unless lowered to `"1.2"`,
# as for the listener.
#? min_version = "1.3"

# The SMART App Launch resource-server posture.
[auth.smart]
# Serve the `/.well-known/smart-configuration` discovery document (SMART App
# Launch 2.x §Conformance; default `false`). The document is built from one
# `[auth]` issuer's metadata: the issuer `Self::issuer_metadata_file` names,
# else the first whose metadata is read from it, else the first.
discovery = false
# The RFC 8414 §2 authorization-server metadata of the `[auth]` issuer it
# names, whose key set is a `jwks_file` and carries none: a JSON document read
# at boot. SMART App Launch 2.2.0, Conformance, §Metadata requires the
# `token_endpoint` it names.
#? issuer_metadata_file = ""
# The SMART platform base URL the discovery document hangs off (master04
# §Service Discovery: the document is served relative to the platform or
# gateway base, not the FHIR base). Unset, the REST root (`/ferroehr/rest`). A
# leading path segment is honoured, e.g. `/gateway/v1` →
# `/gateway/v1/.well-known/smart-configuration`.
#? platform_base_url = ""
# The server's externally reachable origin (scheme + host [+ port]), e.g.
# `https://cdr.example.com`. master04 §Services makes every `services.*`
# entry's `baseUrl` an "Absolute URL to the root of the API (required)", so the
# document prefixes this origin onto the served base paths. Required when
# `Self::discovery` is set.
#? public_base_url = ""
# Episode context (master09 §Experimental: Episode Context), advertised only:
# `episode_launch = true` adds `context-openehr-episode` to the document's
# capabilities and applies no episode filtering (openEHR has no first-class
# Episode resource; master09 calls the semantics "currently
# implementation-defined").
episode_launch = false
# The `client_id`s of the backend clients a `system/aql-*` grant counts for:
# master08 §Resource Scopes says such a grant "would grant access to all
# registered and ad-hoc AQL queries system-wide". Empty, no client.
backend_clients = []
# The issuers whose `patient/` grants count, each confined to the `ehrId` of
# the token's launch context (master07 §Context Selection: the `ehrId` names
# an EHR of the platform that issued it). Empty, a `patient/` grant grants
# nothing.
patient_issuers = []
# The `client_id`s that reach the DEMOGRAPHIC API. master08 §Resource Scopes
# defines no resource family for demographic data, so no SMART scope covers it:
# a listed client, or a caller holding the `[auth] product_scope`, reaches it
# (no openEHR spec governs this: our own design).
demographic_clients = []

# The SCIM 2.0 service provider and its provisioning clients; absent,
# `/scim/v2/` is not served.
#? [auth.scim]
# The externally reachable origin the SCIM base URL hangs off, such as
# `https://cdr.example.com`; every `meta.location` and discovery document names
# `<public_base_url>/scim/v2` (RFC 7643 §3.1: `location` is "The URI of the
# resource being returned"). Required.
#? public_base_url = ""
# The most resources one list response returns (RFC 7643 §5, the
# `ServiceProviderConfig` `filter.maxResults`).
#? filter_max_results = 100
# The most Users one client deactivates or deletes in one window; past it, a
# deactivation or a deletion is refused with `429`.
#? max_deactivations = 100
# The length of that window.
#? deactivation_window = "1h"
# How long after a User's deletion the contacts of every version of its
# `PERSON` are erased (GDPR Art. 17), at most 30 days; `"0s"` erases them in
# the deletion itself. The name, the binding key and the identifiers stay.
#? contact_erasure_delay = "0s"
# The most members one Group holds; an add past it is refused with `400`. Each
# membership change stores every membership of the Group again (RM demographic
# master02 §Versioning Semantics), so the cap bounds a Group's version
# storage.
#? max_group_members = 5000

# The provisioning clients.
#? [[auth.scim.client]]
# The issuer of the client's access tokens: the deployment's own authorization
# server, an `[auth.issuer]` of kind `machines`.
#? issuer = ""
# The client the token names (`client_id`, failing that `azp`).
#? client_id = ""
# The scope a token of the client must hold.
#? scope = ""
# The identifier issuer of the binding keys the client provisions, the
# `identifier_issuer` of an `[auth.party]` table; no two clients share one.
#? binding_issuer = ""

# RBAC, ABAC, assurance, the party binding, the system clients, the federation
# agreements and the registered origins.
[authz]

# Role-based access control.
[authz.rbac]
# Master switch of the coarse role gate, active only when auth is enabled
# (`FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ENABLED`, default `true`).
enabled = true
# The role required for Admin-class operations (default `ADMIN`).
admin_role = "ADMIN"
# The role marking a principal as read-only (default `READONLY`): a caller
# carrying it is refused on every write operation even when it also holds
# granting roles (a restriction overrides a grant). Supports the conformance
# catalogue's authorization-separation cases.
readonly_role = "READONLY"
# The role that may read the access log for ONE subject at a time
# (`FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__SUBJECT_AUDIT_ROLE`, default unset).
#? subject_audit_role = ""
# The role that may reach data under an EHDS Art. 8 access restriction in an
# emergency (`FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__EMERGENCY_ACCESS_ROLE`, default unset).
#? emergency_access_role = ""
# The roles of an EHDS Art. 10 access-service caller, held to an opt-out
# (`FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ACCESS_SERVICE_ROLES`; empty, the default, holds
# nobody).
access_service_roles = []
# The role that may read a party's protected national identifiers
# (`FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__IDENTIFIER_READER_ROLE`, default unset).
#? identifier_reader_role = ""
# The role that may import an EHR or an EHR extract (`message_import_ehr`,
# `message_import_ehr_extract`; default unset).
#? import_role = ""
# The issuers whose role claims may grant `admin_role`,
# `emergency_access_role`, `import_role` and `identifier_reader_role`, each a
# `persons` issuer; empty, the default, lets no token grant them.
role_issuers = []
# What an EHR carrying no `ACCESS_CONTROL_SETTINGS` admits (default `open`).
ehr_access_default = "open"

# Attribute-based access control (opt-in).
[authz.abac]
# Master ABAC switch (default `false`).
enabled = false
# Which PDP engine to use (default `cedar`).
engine = "cedar"
# The JWT claim carrying the caller's organization (default `organization_id`);
# resolved opportunistically (absent → no attribute).
organization_claim = "organization_id"
# The JWT claim carrying the patient id (default `patient_id`); its presence
# enables the local subject gate. Set to empty to disable the gate.
patient_claim = "patient_id"
# The subject namespace patient-claim ids are issued in
# (`EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref.namespace`, RM ehr master04 §EHR Status),
# default unset.
#? patient_namespace = ""
# Whether DIRECTORY (FOLDER) operations are submitted to the PDP (default
# `false`).
check_directory = false

# Embedded-Cedar settings.
[authz.abac.cedar]
# Directory of `*.cedar` policy files (required when `engine = cedar`).
#? policy_dir = ""
# Optional periodic hot-reload interval; off when unset.
#? reload_interval = "500ms"

# Remote-PDP settings.
[authz.abac.remote]

# `[authz.abac.remote.endpoint]`, the family's outbound endpoint: the PDP base
# URL (`url`; the policy name is appended, so it must end with `/`; required
# when `engine = remote`), the timeouts (a connect timeout keeps a PDP that
# blackholes packets from parking the request until the OS TCP timeout), the
# `retry` of a call that got no answer or a `5xx`, the TLS and the credential,
# such as the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant. Any `userinfo` in the URL is
# masked in every rendering.
[authz.abac.remote.endpoint]
# The service's URL (RFC 3986); required. It renders with its userinfo and its
# query masked, in `Debug` and when serialized.
url = ""
# How long one whole call may take; never zero.
timeout = "5s"
# How long opening the connection may take; unset, only `timeout` bounds it.
connect_timeout = "2s"

# How a failed call is tried again.
[authz.abac.remote.endpoint.retry]
# How many times one call is tried in all; 1 tries once.
max_attempts = 3
# The wait before the second try.
initial_backoff = "200ms"
# The longest wait between two tries.
max_backoff = "5s"

# The oldest TLS version the client speaks: `"1.3"` unless lowered to `"1.2"`,
# as for the listener.
min_version = "1.3"
