  • One instance, one organisation
  • Version signing
  • ATNA audit trail

Configuration follows the same pattern throughout: the server reads defaults, then the single ferroehr.toml file, then environment variables, with __ separating nested keys. The security configuration groups live in distinct sections of ferroehr.toml: [auth] (authentication), [authz] (authorization), [privacy] (the pseudonymisation boundary), and [audit] (the ATNA audit trail). Any key can be overridden with the matching FERROEHR_* environment variable shown below.

Authentication

Authentication is on by default (FERROEHR__AUTH__ENABLED=true). Setting it to false lets all requests through unauthenticated, a development-only mode.

There is no single “mode” switch. The server offers two mechanisms and enables each by the presence of its configuration. Both are checked by ferrohealth-smart, the resource-server crate every FerroHEALTH product shares; FerroEHR checks tokens and never issues them.

  • HTTP Basic is active when [[auth.basic.users]] lists a user. Each user has a user-id, an Argon2id password hash (a PHC string beginning $argon2id$) or a password_hash_file pointing at one, and the SMART on openEHR scopes it holds, and its RBAC roles (a user with none holds no role). Because it is a list of users, the Basic store is normally supplied through the TOML configuration file rather than environment variables.
  • OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens are active when [auth] names an issuer. The server reads the issuer’s metadata and key set at boot and validates every token’s signature (asymmetric algorithms only), issuer, audience, lifetime and type under RFC 9068.

Every person a request comes from is bound to a demographic PERSON, and the server writes each version’s committer from that party: Who is the committer.

Both mechanisms are validated at startup, and a configuration the server cannot honour refuses to boot rather than degrading at the first request:

ConfigurationBoot outcome
auth.enabled = true with no mechanismerror: a 401 challenge must name a scheme the server implements (RFC 9110 §11.6.1)
an issuer with no audienceerror: a server with no declared audience cannot reject another server’s token (RFC 9068 §4, RFC 8725 §3.9)
an issuer not https (plain http is accepted on a loopback host only), carrying a query or fragment, or a user name or passworderror: RFC 8414 §2, §6.2; OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §1.2
an issuer whose metadata or key set cannot be readerror: the start is refused rather than the first request
clock_skew above "5min"error: leeway may be “no more than a few minutes” (RFC 7519 §4.1.4)
algorithms naming an HS* algorithm, or emptyerror: the server accepts asymmetric algorithms only (RFC 8725 §3.1, §3.2)
a jwks_file holding a symmetric key or a private-key membererror: a verifier holds public keys only
a product_scope that is neither a full URI nor starts with __error: SMART App Launch 2.2.0, Scopes and Launch Context, §Extensibility
a password_hash below m=19456,t=2,p=1 argon2iderror: the OWASP Argon2id floor
[authz.assurance] minimum with an empty levels map, or with no mapped value at or above iterror: every patient-data request would be refused
an [authz.assurance] levels value that is blank or carries whitespace, a quote or a backslasherror: the step-up challenge names the values in one quoted acr_values parameter (RFC 9470 §3)
[authz.professional]error: removed; the issuer’s kind and profile classify the caller
a persons issuer with no [[auth.party]] table, two issuers sharing an audience, or no [authz.party_binding] providererror: every person is bound to a party, under the provider the deployment acts for
a Basic user with no [[authz.party_binding.basic_user]] mappingerror: a Basic user is a person, bound by its key
an [authz.rbac] role_issuers entry that is not a persons issuererror: only a person holds an administrator or emergency role

Successfully verified Basic credentials are cached for FERROEHR__AUTH__BASIC__CACHE_TTL (default 5min; 0s turns the cache off and checks every request) so a busy client pays the deliberately expensive Argon2 verification once per TTL instead of on every request. The cache names each entry by a keyed hash of the credential, never the password, and an entry exists only after a successful verification; the TTL bounds how long a removed user can still authenticate, exactly like a session lifetime.

The bearer settings:

Environment variableDefaultMeaning
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUERunset (required for bearer tokens)the first [[auth.issuer]] table’s expected iss, and where the metadata is read: RFC 8414 §3 first, OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 §4 after a 404; index 1 is the second table
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__KINDrequiredpersons, patients, machines or federation: whose tokens the issuer signs
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__PROFILErfc9068the preset of the issuer’s token shape: rfc9068, entra, keycloak, okta or nl
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCEunset (required with an issuer)accepted aud values
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTSunsetthe deployment’s own clients, the only ones a persons token is admitted through beside delegates
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ALGORITHMSRS256,RS384,PS256,PS384,ES256,ES384accepted signing algorithms, asymmetric only
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__CLOCK_SKEW60sleeway on exp, nbf and iat; capped at 5min
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__JWKS_FILEunseta static JWK Set of public keys, read instead of the issuer’s metadata
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__JWKS_MAX_AGE10mina key set older than this is read again
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__JWKS_REFRESH_INTERVAL1minan unknown kid reads the key set again at most once per interval
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__TIMEOUT10sone call to the authorization server
FERROEHR__AUTH__REALMferroehrthe realm every challenge names
FERROEHR__AUTH__PRODUCT_SCOPE__ferroehr.platformthe scope that admits the ADMIN and DEMOGRAPHIC APIs

There is no separate key-set URL to set: the server reads the jwks_uri from the issuer’s metadata unless you supply a JWKS_FILE. A rotated key is picked up on the first token that names it, bounded by the refresh interval, and a withdrawn key stops verifying within the max age.

Every route also enforces its SMART on openEHR requirement: a valid token or Basic user whose scopes do not grant the operation is refused with 403. See SMART App Launch.

Tip

Keycloak example. Point the issuer at your realm and let discovery do the rest:

export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUER=https://keycloak.example/realms/ferroehr
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__KIND=persons
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__PROFILE=keycloak
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCE=ferroehr-api
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTS=ferroehr-viewer

Keycloak’s access tokens carry typ: JWT, outside the RFC 9068 profile the server expects by default, which the keycloak profile admits. The client’s default client scopes put the SMART on openEHR scopes the routes need into each token’s scope claim.

The same pattern works for Active Directory or any standards-compliant identity provider; walkthroughs for Entra ID and AD FS (and the answer for plain-LDAP directories) are in Enterprise identity providers. User accounts, roles, and lifecycle are administered in the IdP; the CDR has no user API.

An unauthenticated request to a protected route is refused with 401; an authenticated request that lacks the required role or scope is refused with 403. Two outcomes are neither: a malformed Authorization header, or two of them, is a 400 (the server never read a credential), and an unreadable key set is a 503 (no token can be validated, so the server cannot decide; it is not a statement about the caller’s credential). The per-status table for client authors is in Using the API.

The 401 body deliberately says nothing about why, and neither does the challenge: every token that does not hold gets the one invalid_token answer (RFC 9068 §4), with no error_description. Rendering the rejection would tell an unauthenticated caller whether a token was expired or forged, which is exactly the distinction an attacker probes for; the reason stays in the debug log, where the operator can read it and the caller cannot. A 403 names no scope either, in its challenge or its body. A request that carried no credential at all, or one for a scheme the server does not admit, gets no error code: it has not made a mistake yet (RFC 6750 §3.1).

Assurance level and the natural person on patient data

Two optional blocks under [authz] judge how a professional authenticated and who stands behind a token. Both are off by default; with neither configured nothing below changes the wire.

[authz.assurance] reads the authentication assurance level from a token claim (claim, default acr) and maps each value your identity provider emits to an eIDAS level (levels: low, substantial or high). With minimum set, a patient-data request whose token maps below it, carries a value the map does not name, or carries no such claim is refused with 401 and the OAuth 2.0 step-up challenge of RFC 9470 §3:

WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="ferroehr", error="insufficient_user_authentication",
  error_description="patient data requires authentication at assurance level substantial or higher",
  acr_values="http://eidas.europa.eu/LoA/high http://eidas.europa.eu/LoA/substantial"

acr_values lists every mapped value at or above the minimum, so a client can send the user back to the identity provider with that request. EHDS Annex II 3.1 asks an EHR system used by health professionals for reliable identification and authentication of them; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2099 Art. 6(3) sets substantial for cross-border exchange, and high from 26 March 2032.

The natural person behind a token is the issuer’s to say. Each [[auth.issuer]] declares its kind, and ferrohealth-smart classifies every token by it and by the issuer’s profile: a persons token through one of the issuer’s first_party_clients is the person, a token through a client the issuer lists in delegates is that client acting for the person the token names, and an app-only token is a system. A persons token through any other client is refused with 401. The access record names the person by the profile’s person_key, and a delegated token as the client acting for that person; see Audit trail.

What counts as patient data: every API route except the definition family (/definition/...: templates, archetypes, stored-query texts), terminology, the aggregate counts under /admin/report, and the admin routes that manage configuration, the retention policy, templates and stored queries. The list of exceptions is closed, so a route added later is judged patient data until it is listed. The health family, /rest/status, discovery and /management are outside the API and never judged.

Basic credentials carry no assurance level and no issuer-asserted person. With minimum set a Basic request for patient data gets the same 401 step-up challenge; definition routes stay reachable with Basic. A Basic user is a person, bound by its key ([[authz.party_binding.basic_user]]).

The assurance level is judged before RBAC, so a caller below the level learns it must step up rather than that it lacks a role. A client token acting for a professional is held to the same level as any other token: the acr it carries is the one judged, so a client-credentials token needs your authorization server to put the professional’s assurance level on it.

Two limits worth planning around

Plain-HTTP issuers are accepted on a loopback host only. The server reads the issuer’s metadata and keys over TLS, because over plain HTTP an attacker on the network could serve their own signing keys (RFC 8414 §6.2); there is no switch that admits a plain-HTTP issuer elsewhere.

Revocation latency equals the access-token lifetime. Tokens are validated offline against the issuer’s published keys; the CDR calls no introspection endpoint (RFC 7662 defines that mechanism but does not require a resource server to use it), so a token revoked at the identity provider stays acceptable here until its exp passes. That is deliberate: introspecting per request would put the identity provider’s availability in the request path, and caching the results only shortens the lag. The control is therefore the token lifetime, which your authorization server owns: keep access-token lifetimes short (minutes, not hours) if prompt revocation matters, and use refresh tokens for session length. clock_skew_leeway_seconds adds at most its own value on top of exp.

Authorization

Authorization has three composable layers. The per-EHR EHR_ACCESS gate is the openEHR-specified base and is always on; the coarse role layer is active when authentication is enabled; the fine-grained attribute layer is opt-in. A request must clear every active layer. Deployments serving SMART apps can enable a fourth, token-scope layer on top; see SMART App Launch.

Per-EHR access control (EHR_ACCESS)

Every EHR carries a versioned EHR_ACCESS object, the openEHR access-decision authority for that record. A new EHR has no settings, and what that admits is a server-wide choice:

authz.rbac.ehr_access_defaultAn EHR with no settings
open (default)reachable by any caller the coarse layers already admitted
restrictedreachable only by authz.rbac.admin_role

open is the default because it is what every existing deployment runs, and changing it changes who can read existing records. restricted is object-level default-deny, and it is the setting to reach for if your threat model includes a caller enumerating record ids: a server-created ehr_id is a time-ordered UUIDv7, so it is not even unpredictable, and the OWASP Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention cheat sheet is explicit that an unpredictable identifier is not itself an access control.

Note

Under restricted, the admin role still reaches a setting-less EHR. That is deliberate: a plain deny would make such a record unreachable by everyone (including the operator who would author the settings that fix it) which is an outage rather than a control. Bind callers to patients with the ABAC layer below; this key decides only the default disposition.

Committing settings with the ferroehr.access_control.v1 scheme switches that EHR to explicit policy, and those settings always win over the server default, in both directions:

{
  "_type": "EHR_ACCESS",
  "name": { "_type": "DV_TEXT", "value": "access" },
  "archetype_node_id": "openEHR-EHR-EHR_ACCESS.generic.v1",
  "settings": {
    "_type": "FERROEHR_ACCESS_CONTROL_V1",
    "gate_keeper": "user:alice",
    "default_access": "restricted",
    "access_list": [
      { "principal": "user:bob",   "access": "full" },
      { "principal": "role:nurse", "access": "restricted_below", "max_level": 2 }
    ],
    "privacy": {
      "default_level": 0,
      "composition_overrides": [
        { "uid": "8849182c-82ad-4088-a07f-48ead4180515", "level": 3 }
      ]
    }
  }
}
  • Access list: with default_access: "restricted", only listed principals may touch the EHR: user:<login or OIDC subject> or role:<role> (matched against the caller’s roles). Everyone else gets 403. An EHR Extract export by manifest (POST /message/export) passes this gate for every EHR the manifest names before it reads any content, so one EHR the caller may not reach refuses the whole export.
  • Privacy levels: integer sensitivity levels with meanings you define for your jurisdiction. A composition’s level is its override entry or the default, and a caller may read it only when its level is strictly below their ceiling. full access has no ceiling; restricted_below uses the entry’s max_level; a caller with no access-list entry gets default_level + 1, so the default level stays readable and only raised levels are withheld. This gate applies to Composition read routes. An override’s uid is the VERSIONED_COMPOSITION uid, or a version uid whose first part is one; a CONTRIBUTION that writes any other uid is refused with 400.
  • Unreadable settings: settings that carry the scheme’s _type but do not parse hold the EHR closed. A request that names the EHR is refused with 500, no query reaches it, and the server logs an error naming it. A CONTRIBUTION, an EHR Extract import or an admin archive load that carries such settings is refused with 400 naming the setting that does not parse (the load names its EHR too, and writes nothing of the archive), so only settings stored before that check can hold an EHR. An administrator repairs a held EHR with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/ehr-access/repair, body {"ehr_id": "…", "settings": {…}}: the new settings must parse, the repair commits a new EHR_ACCESS version with its own commit audit and contribution, and it writes an access record (ehr-access-repair:<versioned object uid>) naming the administrator. The repair is refused with 409 for an EHR that is not held; such an EHR changes its settings with a CONTRIBUTION.
  • Gate-keeper: once set, only that principal may commit a new EHR_ACCESS version (via a CONTRIBUTION; there is no dedicated EHR_ACCESS endpoint in the openEHR REST API). Changes are versioned and audited like all record content.

The scheme is a FerroEHR extension: openEHR mandates the EHR_ACCESS object and its change control but publishes no concrete access-control scheme. The per-EHR decision also holds for AQL, ad-hoc and stored queries alike: an EHR the caller may not read contributes no rows, whether the query names it in its WHERE clause, in an EHR predicate, through the ehr_id parameter, or not at all, as in a population query. Query results are not filtered by privacy level.

Restriction of access by health professionals (EHDS Art. 8)

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 8 gives a person the right to restrict the access of health professionals and healthcare providers to all or parts of their data, and has the fact of the restriction stay invisible to healthcare providers. Art. 11(5) lets the restricted data be reached where necessary to protect the person’s vital interests, logged so the person can see it. No openEHR specification governs this; it is our own design.

  • Recording it. The controller records a restriction on the person’s instruction with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-restriction, for a whole EHR or for one versioned object, and lifts it with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-restriction/lift (the routes). A whole-EHR restriction covers data recorded after it too.
  • What a professional sees. Restricted data reads as absent: a restricted composition or EHR answers 404 exactly as an unknown one does, a query leaves it out at every scope (and a query scoped to a restricted EHR answers as for an unknown EHR), an export skips it, a CONTRIBUTION lists none of its versions, the event stream withholds it, and a write to it is refused as a write to an unknown target. No status, header or count says that a restriction exists.
  • What it does not change. Nothing is deleted, and storage and the controller’s own processing go on: the admin routes (dump, archive, erase, the registers) see everything. It is not the GDPR Art. 18 restriction of processing, which answers 403 and stops processing itself.
  • The emergency override. A caller holding the role authz.rbac.emergency_access_role names that declares one of [audit] emergency_purpose_codes reads the restricted data, and its access record carries the emergency mark. Either alone lifts nothing. Unset, nobody may override.
[authz.rbac]
emergency_access_role = "EMERGENCY"

[audit]
purpose_codes = ["TREAT", "ETREAT"]
emergency_purpose_codes = ["ETREAT"]

The grain is the versioned object, the whole EHR, or both. A finer grain (one entry inside a composition) is not built: an object is the unit the version reads, the queries and the exports already decide on, and splitting a composition would change what the stored, signed version holds.

Opt-out from the access services (EHDS Art. 10)

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 10(1) lets a Member State’s law give a person “the right to opt out from the access to their personal electronic health data registered in an EHR system through the electronic health data access services referred to in Articles 4 and 12”, and has the Member State “ensure that the exercise of that right is reversible”. Art. 10(2) lets the Member State admit “a healthcare provider or health professional” where processing “is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person”, even after an opt-out. No openEHR specification governs this; it is our own design.

FerroEHR ships the software part: a mark on the whole EHR that the callers you declare as the access services read as absent. Whether the right exists, how the person exercises it, and the rules and safeguards of Art. 10(2) are your Member State’s law and yours to apply. Where the Member State enforces the opt-out in its own services, leave the mark unused.

  • Declaring the access services. authz.rbac.access_service_roles lists the roles your Art. 4 access service (the person’s) and your Art. 12 health professional access service carry in their tokens or Basic users. It is empty by default, so the opt-out holds for nobody, and recording one is refused with 400.
  • Recording and reversing it. The controller records the opt-out on the person’s instruction with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-opt-out and reverses it with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-opt-out/reverse (the routes). A reversal keeps the row in the register with its reversal time, and stays open whatever the configuration, so an opt-out can always be reversed.
  • What an access service sees. A request from a caller holding one of the declared roles reads the EHR as absent: a route that names the EHR or an object in it answers 404 as for an unknown EHR, a population query leaves its data out, a query scoped to it answers as for an unknown EHR, an export and the lookup by subject find no such EHR, and a write to it is refused as a write to an unknown EHR.
  • What it does not change. Every other caller reads the record as before: your own care, through callers that hold none of the declared roles, and the controller’s admin routes. Nothing is deleted. It is not the Art. 8 restriction above, which reaches every professional route and leaves the person’s own access open.
  • The vital-interest override. An access-service caller that declares one of [audit] emergency_purpose_codes reads the EHR, unless it acts for the person (a SMART patient/ grant or the patient claim), because Art. 10(2) names a healthcare provider or health professional. Its access record carries the emergency mark, and a route that names the opted-out EHR, in its path or in a POST /message/export manifest, adds an access record access-opt-out-override:ehr-wide against it.
  • The record. Recording, reversing and reading the register are each an access record on the EHR (access-opt-out:ehr-wide) naming the administrator.
[authz.rbac]
access_service_roles = ["EHDS-ACCESS-SERVICE"]

[audit]
purpose_codes = ["TREAT", "ETREAT"]
emergency_purpose_codes = ["ETREAT"]

Information a person inserts (EHDS Art. 5)

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 5 lets a person, or their representative, insert information in their own EHR through the access services. That information “shall be clearly distinguishable as having been inserted by the natural person or by his or her representative”, and the person “shall not be able to directly alter the electronic health data and related information inserted by health professionals”. FerroEHR keeps both rules at the commit. No openEHR specification governs who may change what, so the rules are our own design; the marker is the RM’s own.

  • Who counts as the person. A bearer token with a patient/ scope and no user/ or system/ scope (for example patient/composition-*.cruds), from an issuer in [auth.smart] patient_issuers. The SMART scope grammar reserves patient/ for “applications acting in the context of a specific patient/EHR” and user/ for those acting for a logged-in practitioner, so a clinician’s app uses user/ scopes and keeps every professional right. The ABAC patient claim does not make a caller the person, because a professional’s token in a patient’s context carries it too. The rule is the FerroHEALTH family’s strict answer, shared through ferrohealth-smart; the Art. 3(3) delay below asks its broad one.
  • Who counts as the representative. A person bound to their own PERSON who acts for the patient through a representation relationship FerroEHR has recorded (how a login is looked up). The rules below hold for the representative exactly as for the person.
  • The marker. Every version and CONTRIBUTION the person commits records PARTY_SELF with no external_ref as AUDIT_DETAILS.committer, the RM’s way to say the committer is the record subject (RM common, Audit Details). A representative’s records PARTY_RELATED, naming the representative’s own PERSON and the coded relationship. FerroEHR writes this committer itself and refuses one the request states that differs, in the openehr-audit-details header or in a CONTRIBUTION body. Every read of the version carries it, an AQL query reads it with v/commit_audit/committer, the contribution list extension flags the change set with inserted_by_person, and the viewer names the committer “The person or their representative”. The marker is part of the stored version, so a dump and its restore keep it.
  • The composer. A COMPOSITION the person or the representative commits names the person (PARTY_SELF) or their representative (PARTY_RELATED) as its composer. Any other composer is refused with 403, so the person cannot present what they insert as a professional’s.
  • What the person may change. The person and their representative may update and delete a version whose committer is PARTY_SELF or PARTY_RELATED. An update or a deletion of a version anyone else committed, a professional or a system, is refused with 403 and a body that names EHDS Art. 5, whether it comes as a direct write or inside a CONTRIBUTION. Nothing is written. The marker is in the version, so the rule holds whatever became of the access record of the write.
  • What a professional may change. A professional’s writes are unchanged. A professional may update or delete an entry the person inserted; the new version is the professional’s, which the person may then no longer alter. The person’s own versions stay in the version history.

Delayed access by the person (EHDS Art. 3(3))

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 3(1) gives a person access to their data “immediately after the personal electronic health data have been registered in an EHR system”. Art. 3(3) lets a Member State restrict that right “by delaying access to their personal electronic health data for a limited period of time until a health professional is able to properly communicate and explain to the natural persons concerned information that can have a significant impact on their health”. Recital 10 gives the example: a diagnosis of an incurable disease should come first in a consultation, not through an electronic channel. This is the opposite direction of the Art. 8 restriction above: the data is withheld from the person, never from a professional. No openEHR specification governs it; it is our own design.

FerroEHR ships the software part. Whether the delay applies, to which data and for how long is the Member State’s rule, and you configure it in [privacy.access_delay]. It is off by default, so the person’s access stays immediate.

  • What is held. With the section on, every new COMPOSITION whose category (the [audit.categories] map, template first, then the root archetype) is listed in privacy.access_delay.categories is held from the moment it is committed, for privacy.access_delay.max_delay. Only the first version is held: a composition the person has already seen stays visible when it is amended, and a professional holds an amendment by hand if it needs explaining. A composition the person commits is never held from them.
  • Who it is held from. A request that may be the person’s own: a bearer token carrying a SMART patient/ grant, or the ABAC patient claim (authz.abac.patient_claim). A token that carries either is treated as the person’s, whatever user/ or system/ grant it also carries, so a mixed token is withheld from rather than shown the data too early. The rule is the FerroHEALTH family’s, shared with the other products through ferrohealth-smart. To that request a held composition reads as absent: a read answers 404 as for an unknown composition, a query and an export leave it out, a CONTRIBUTION lists none of its versions, and a write to it is refused as a write to an unknown target.
  • What a professional sees. Everything, as before. The hold changes no professional route, query or export.
  • Releasing it. The treating professional releases a composition once it has been explained, from the clinical surface with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/ehr/{ehr_id}/versioned_composition/{versioned_object_uid}/access-delay/release. The route takes the checks of a write to that EHR: the EHR access list, the ABAC check of a composition update and the SMART composition- update grant. A request that may be the person’s is refused with 403. The controller releases with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-delay/release, and holds one by hand with POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/access-delay, for at most privacy.access_delay.max_delay (the routes).
  • The limit. Every hold ends by itself when its period passes, released or not, because Art. 3(3) allows a delay “for a limited period of time” only.
  • The record. Placing a hold, releasing it and its expiry are each an access record: the release names the professional who made it, and the server writes the expiry record within a minute of the limit passing.
  • The person’s access trail (Art. 9). A record about a held composition would tell the person a result exists. The subject-scoped ITI-81 read, the one a patient portal serves the person’s own trail from, leaves out every record that names a held composition, its hold included, until the hold is released or expires; the records then appear unchanged, with their original times. The filter is ehds-logging’s, the FerroHEALTH family’s EHDS logging component. The controller’s unscoped read shows every record at all times.

Turning the section off makes every held composition readable to the person at once: the holds stay in the register, and no new one can be placed.

RBAC (role-based, coarse)

Every openEHR operation is classified as Public, Clinical, or Admin, and a role model gates each class. Roles are plain, case-insensitive strings; the defaults are USER and ADMIN.

Environment variableDefaultMeaning
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ENABLEDtruethe coarse role gate (active only when auth is enabled)
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ADMIN_ROLEADMINrole required for admin operations
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__READONLY_ROLEREADONLYrole marking a principal read-only: refused on every write
FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ROLE_CLAIMS["roles","groups","entitlements"]JWT claim paths mined for roles, per issuer; a Keycloak issuer adds realm_access.roles
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ROLE_ISSUERSemptythe persons issuers whose role claims may grant the administrator, emergency, import and identifier-reader roles; a token of any other issuer never holds them
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__SUBJECT_AUDIT_ROLEunsetrole that reads the access log for ONE subject at a time (GET /fhir/r4/AuditEvent with patient required). Unset, that log stays admin-only. See Audit trail

Roles come from the JWT claims listed in ROLE_CLAIMS, or from a Basic user’s configured roles. The defaults are the carriers RFC 9068 §2.2.3.1 names for conveying authorization state (roles, groups, entitlements, of which roles and entitlements are SCIM attributes), the default every FerroHEALTH product shares. A claim path may be dotted, so an issuer that nests them differently, such as Keycloak’s realm_access.roles, is configuration rather than a code change; a claim carrying a single string and one carrying an array are both accepted.

A Clinical operation needs at least one role of any name; an Admin operation needs the admin role. A Basic user holds the roles its roles list names and nothing else, so a user with none is refused every Clinical operation; roles = ["USER"] satisfies the Clinical class and no Admin operation. A bearer token whose SMART on openEHR resource scopes are all system/ scopes, such as system/template-*.r, is a backend client and needs no role for a Clinical operation: its scopes decide what it reaches. A user/ or patient/ token belongs to a person and still needs a role. The former user_role key is refused at boot. Disabling RBAC restores authentication-only behaviour.

Important

The management surface is not configured here. /management/* is governed entirely by [management.endpoints], one level per endpoint, and nothing under [authz.rbac] changes it. There is no global default beside it: an endpoint you do not name is off and is not mounted at all.

Each level means: off, not mounted, answers 404; private, any authenticated principal; admin_only, authenticated and holding authz.rbac.admin_role (the one place RBAC is consulted); public, no check at all, including no authentication.

The consequence worth internalising: prometheus = "public" is reachable by an anonymous caller whatever your RBAC settings say, because a public endpoint is mounted outside the authentication layer. Lock the surface down by raising the levels in [management], and read the effective set back from /management/env (or from the boot log line that names every mounted endpoint and its level) rather than assuming.

Important

The OAuth2 scope claim does not grant roles. A scope grants a client delegated authority (RFC 6749 §3.3); it asserts nothing about the subject’s roles. Reading it as one also made the at-least-one-role check pass for every OIDC token, since openid alone satisfied it. If your callers rely on a scope naming a role, move that role into one of the role claims above. Scopes remain on the principal and still drive SMART scope enforcement and ABAC policy.

Note

The downloadable Compose quickstart deliberately runs with RBAC off and a single user, so every surface works out of the box (see Docker Compose). Turn the role gate on with [authz.rbac] enabled = true (or FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ENABLED=true) and give each principal an explicit roles list.

A principal carrying the readonly_role (default READONLY) is refused on every write operation (creating an EHR, committing a composition, uploading a template, and any update/delete) even when it also holds granting roles such as ADMIN (a restriction always overrides a grant). Reads and AQL queries stay permitted, so a READONLY account is an authenticated, view-only principal. The repository’s from-source development stack ships one such account (ferroehr-readonly, password ferroehr) alongside ferroehr and ferroehr-admin, with RBAC at its default enabled = true, so the separation can be tried out; the downloadable quickstart file has neither (one user, no role gate).

ABAC (attribute-based, fine-grained)

For attribute-level decisions (“may this user touch this patient’s data, under this organisation, for this template?”) enable ABAC. A policy decision point is consulted per clinical operation with resolved attributes. An enabled ABAC block that cannot be built (a missing or invalid policy directory, an unreachable-by-construction PDP client) aborts server startup: a configuration that promises fine-grained authorization never silently runs without it.

Environment variableDefaultMeaning
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__ENABLEDfalsemaster ABAC switch
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__ENGINEcedarcedar (embedded) or remote (external PDP)
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__ORGANIZATION_CLAIMorganization_idJWT claim for the organisation attribute
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__PATIENT_CLAIMpatient_idJWT claim for the patient attribute (enables the subject gate)
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__CHECK_DIRECTORYfalsealso submit DIRECTORY (FOLDER) operations to the policy engine
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__CEDAR__POLICY_DIR— (required for cedar)directory of *.cedar policy files
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__CEDAR__RELOAD_INTERVALoffoptional policy hot-reload interval
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__REMOTE__ENDPOINT__URL— (required for remote)PDP base URL (must end with /)
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__REMOTE__ENDPOINT__CONNECT_TIMEOUT2sPDP connect timeout
FERROEHR__AUTHZ__ABAC__REMOTE__ENDPOINT__TIMEOUT5sPDP request timeout

Two engines sit behind one interface. Cedar is the embedded default: policies live in *.cedar files, are schema-validated at boot against a shipped schema built from the resource-kind and access-mode sets themselves (an invalid policy set stops the server rather than silently denying), and need no external service. The remote PDP option consults an external policy server over HTTP for deployments that already run one; it additionally requires an [authz.abac.policy.<kind>] binding for every resource kind it will be asked about, and a missing one is a boot error rather than a first-request surprise.

A policy sees the caller, not just the request: the authenticated subject, its roles (as the role layer above resolved them), its scopes, the resolved organization and patient, the resource’s patient, template, category and origin, and the operation id. So a rule can be written about one caller, a role, a scope, or a single operation; the shipped example policy shows a role-keyed break-glass permit and a scope-keyed write restriction.

An item tag is checked as the object it tags: a tag read where the read of its EHR, EHR_STATUS or composition is checked, and a tag write or delete where its target’s write is, with the same patient and the tagged composition’s template, category and origin. The action is the tag request’s own, so a tag put on a composition asks for composition.update and a tag delete for composition.delete.

Category and origin (EHDS Annex II 3.4 asks for access rights that take the origins and categories of the data into account). On a composition read, write or delete, a contribution and a query, resource.category holds each EHDS category of the data, spelt as the access record spells it: the <system>|<code> token of a priority or national category, [audit.categories] classifying the template, then the root archetype; none; or unclassified. resource.origin holds each origin the data came from, as the version recorded it at commit: a FEEDER_AUDIT originating-system id, the registered origin of the committing client, or this server’s system_id (keying on an origin declares the register). A write is decided on what its body names: its template’s category and the origin the commit will stamp. A FLAT or STRUCTURED write is converted only after the check, so it carries the category its template header implies and no origin attribute. A remote PDP receives both as the category and origin parameters of [authz.abac.policy.<kind>].

// Laboratory reports fed by the lab are readable by the lab's own staff only.
forbid (principal, action == Action::"composition.read", resource)
when {
  resource has category && resource has origin &&
  resource.category == "http://hl7.eu/fhir/health-data-api/CodeSystem/eehrxf-document-priority-category-cs|Laboratory-Reports" &&
  resource.origin == "lab.example" &&
  !(principal has organization && principal.organization == "lab")
};

A request whose patient, template, category or origin resolves to several values is evaluated over the full cartesian product of them, and every combination must permit; the first deny short-circuits. A request that resolves to no combination at all permits vacuously, because there is nothing to decide about.

Warning

Authorization is fail-closed in two distinct senses, and the difference shows up in the status code.

Nothing permits by omission: a gate reached without an authenticated caller refuses, an unconfigured resource kind on the remote PDP denies (and the missing rule is a boot error), and Cedar is deny-by-default with forbid overriding permit. A denied decision is a 403.

And a stage that cannot decide is never read as a decision. An unreachable policy engine, a policy server answering 5xx, or a policy that errors during evaluation is a 500: never a silent permit, and never a 403, which would claim a decision was made. (Cedar skips a policy that errors and reports it in its diagnostics; ignoring those would let an erroring forbid quietly stop forbidding.) A 4xx from a remote PDP is a decision, so it denies.

When a patient claim is configured, a local subject gate also rejects access to another patient’s EHR before any policy call. The EHR Extract import routes are checked as EHR writes, and the export routes as EHR reads. An export by manifest (POST /message/export) holds every EHR it names to that gate, and one EHR of another patient refuses the whole export.

Response security headers

Three surfaces, three honest answers: the set differs because what they serve differs.

The REST API carries, on every response including the transport-layer ones (413 from the body limit, 408 from the timeout, 503 from the overload bound, 500 from the panic handler), the health routes and the management listener on its own port. The family server stack sets them outermost (ferrohealth-server), each only where a response does not set its own:

HeaderValueWhy
Cache-Controlno-storeresponses carry patient data; the OWASP cheat sheet names no-store for exactly that. It does not affect openEHR’s ETag/If-Match concurrency control, which is a precondition mechanism, not a caching one
X-Content-Type-Optionsnosniffstops a proxy or browser re-guessing application/json as something executable
Referrer-Policystrict-origin-when-cross-originrequest paths carry ehr_id and version identifiers; this keeps them out of cross-origin Referer headers
Cross-Origin-Resource-Policysame-siterefuses cross-site embedding of API responses
X-Frame-OptionsDENYfor the HTML this origin can serve (Swagger UI)
Content-Security-Policydefault-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'the defensive minimum, applied wherever a response does not set its own; Swagger UI needs a real policy and brings one. The cheat sheet is explicit that CSP “might be meaningless in the response of a REST API that returns content that is not going to be rendered”, so this is not a policy pretending to govern scripts: it says nothing loads and nothing frames

X-XSS-Protection and X-Powered-By are absent because the cheat sheet says to remove them, and no Server header is sent at all.

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 is sent only when FerroEHR serves TLS itself ([server.tls]). RFC 6797 §7.2 requires a browser to ignore it over plain HTTP, which is how this server is commonly reached behind a terminating proxy, and forbids a server to send it there. Behind such a proxy, set it at the proxy or ingress that owns TLS. includeSubDomains is left out, because FerroEHR does not decide for the hosts beside it.

The viewer carries the FerroHEALTH console set instead, because it serves HTML: a CSP that admits scripts and styles from its own origin alone (script-src 'self'; style-src 'self', no nonce, no inline script or style), Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin (the viewer chapter lists them), with Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site from the API set beside them. Its Cache-Control has one scoped exception to no-store: FerroUI’s stylesheet, theme and scripts under /ferrohealth-ui/<version>/ are served no-cache, so the browser keeps them and revalidates them, and they hold nothing clinical (the viewer reaches the CDR from its own server, never from the browser). Every document carries no-store, because documents carry patient data. An asset response that is not a served body (a 404, a redirect) is never kept either.

The published documentation site cannot carry response headers at all: it is static files on GitHub Pages, so its policy travels as a <meta http-equiv> element, which is weaker by specification (frame-ancestors, report-uri and sandbox are ignored in meta form). Its img-src admits one outside path, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FerroHEALTH/FerroEHR/, for the conformance badges the Conformance workflow pushes. Anyone re-hosting these docs behind a real web server should send the headers properly instead.

Request limits and rate limiting

Four different protections, four different statuses, and an operator should be able to tell them apart from the status alone.

Connection bounds: [server] header_read_timeout. The limit that applies before a request exists, because a client that opens a socket and trickles headers, or sends nothing at all, reaches none of the others: a client that has not sent its request head in time, counted from accept, is disconnected, on the plain and the TLS listener alike. On a kept-alive connection the bound counts from the first byte of each later request head, and [server] idle_timeout (two minutes by default) closes a connection that waits that long for its next request. Keep it longer than the idle timeout of your clients (90 s for a Go client) and of any load balancer in front, so they close an idle connection first.

Body size: [server] body_limit and [api] body_limit. Two tiers: the routes that accept bulk by design (template upload and /message/import) take the listener’s limit, and the clinical surface the narrower [api] one when it is set. Over-limit is 413. The listener’s default is the family’s 1 MiB; a deployment that uploads operational templates raises it (the chart and the Compose files set 64 MiB), and one whose compositions embed large DV_MULTIMEDIA data raises the clinical tier deliberately.

Request rate: [server.caller_rate], unset by default and set by the chart and the Compose quickstart. It sits inside authentication, keyed on the authenticated subject, because a hospital behind one NAT is a single address and address-keying a clinical API would throttle a whole site for one busy client. Refusal is 429 with Retry-After.

Concurrency: [server] max_concurrent_requests, the admission bound. Refusal is 503 with Retry-After; the health routes are never refused.

So: 503 means the server is full right now, 429 means you are asking too fast, 413 means your payload is too big. Full key tables are on the configuration page.

If you benchmark this server, turn the rate limiter off first, or you will measure the limiter. Our own measurement lanes compose an overlay that disables it, and both instruments refuse to write a record if the server answered any 429: a performance number that is really a configuration key is worse than no number.

Operational surfaces: what is reachable, and by whom

Everything reachable without a credential is listed here, with the reason it is public. Every other route answers 401 to a request without one, and a test drives every mounted route to keep this list closed. A public answer says only what a client or probe needs; the detail behind it is on the authenticated /management surface.

SurfaceDefaultWhy it is public, or how it is gated
/health, /health/livenessalways on, unauthenticatedOrchestrator probes carry no credential. Liveness answers {"state":"up"} with no I/O behind it; /health answers the readiness status with the state alone.
/health/readinessalways on, unauthenticatedAn orchestrator probe: 200 while ready, 503 while the process boots or drains or an indicator is down. The body is the state, the phase and each indicator’s name and state, nothing more. The detail is /management/health.
{rest root}/statusalways on, unauthenticatedA documented client contract: status, server version, ITS-REST version, timestamp and the deployment profile. The licence, the deployment gaps and the support period are /management/status.
{rest root}/.well-known/smart-configurationmounted only with SMART onSMART App Launch service discovery, read before the client holds any token (ITS-REST SMART App Launch, Service Discovery).
OPTIONS {base path}always on, unauthenticatedThe ITS-REST System API’s options manifest, which its released OpenAPI document declares without security.
{rest root}/swagger-ui, {rest root}/api-docs/*private (api.openapi_ui)Public only if you set public; admin_only and off are the other levels.
/management/*not mounted at all (management.enabled = false)With the master switch off, every route is 404.
/management/{info,metrics,prometheus,env,loggers,flamegraph,health,status}each off individuallyEven with the master switch on, each endpoint stays unmounted until you name a level for it. There is no global fallback: silence means off, so a surface this privileged opens one endpoint at a time, by name.
management.listenunset (shares the API listener)Set it to serve ops introspection from its own listener on its own port. It binds all interfaces and always stays plain HTTP even with [server.tls] on, so treat it as an internal surface and keep it off any publicly routed port; the interface half of the separation is your network’s, not this key’s. Under deployment.profile = "production" setting it opens the plaintext_listener gap, so the server refuses to start unless the gap is accepted by name.

env and flamegraph deserve particular caution: env renders the effective configuration (redacted, but still configuration), and flamegraph starts a CPU profiler on request, which is both a disclosure and a denial-of-service lever. Both are off until you name a level, and the profiler additionally caps the window and sampling frequency, refusing an out-of-range request rather than clamping it silently.

Secrets: mount files, never bake values

Every secret this server reads has a *_file sibling, and the loader reads and trims the file at startup. Exactly one of a pair may be set; both is a boot error naming the pair:

SecretFile sibling
the database DSN, per storage domain, and the credential that prepares the schemadatabase.url_file, database.<domain>.url_file, db.migrate_url_file
a Basic user’s Argon2 hashauth.basic.users[].password_hash_file
the PGP signing-key passphraserecord.signing.key_passphrase_file
a terminology OAuth2 client secret[terminology].oauth.client_secret_file
the object-store secret keymultimedia.secret_access_key_file
the national-identifier root keyprivacy.identifier_protection.key_file

(The TLS certificate_file / client_ca_file settings and a static key set’s auth.jwks_file are paths by nature and have no inline form at all, which is the same property arrived at from the other direction.)

That is deliberately the shape Docker Secrets and Kubernetes Secrets deliver: a file mounted into the container. So the recommended posture needs no extra machinery.

services:
  ferroehr:
    environment:
      # Point the key at the mount path; the VALUE never appears anywhere.
      FERROEHR__RECORD__SIGNING__KEY_PASSPHRASE_FILE: /run/secrets/signing_passphrase
    secrets:
      - signing_passphrase

secrets:
  signing_passphrase:
    file: ./secrets/signing_passphrase.txt   # or `external: true` in swarm

Why files rather than environment variables: an environment variable is readable from /proc/<pid>/environ by anything in the container’s namespace, appears in docker inspect output, is inherited by every child process, and is routinely captured whole by crash reporters and process listings. A mounted file is none of those, and it can be rotated without recreating the container.

Two properties worth knowing because they are not obvious:

  • Redaction is a property of the type, not a list. Secret-bearing fields are a Secret/SecretUrl newtype whose Debug and serialization render ***, so a new secret key cannot be forgotten by a per-endpoint redactor: /management/env and ferroehr config check show *** because the type does, not because something remembered to hide it. A Basic password hash in [auth] is a secrecy secret of the shared crate’s section, rendered *** the same way.
  • A Kubernetes Secret is base64, not encryption. The cheat sheet is blunt about this: Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Enable encryption at rest or use an external manager; the chart mounts whatever you give it and cannot make an unencrypted store safe.

Warning

The downloadable quickstart carries an inline Argon2 hash for its throwaway ferroehr user, because a self-contained demo file cannot reference a secret you do not have. That is the one place a credential appears in our own artifacts, and it is a development credential by construction; replace it before any real use.

Verifying what you pulled

Release binaries, container images and the Helm chart carry signed build provenance, SBOMs and checksums, so you can establish that the bytes you are about to run came from this repository’s own pipeline and see what went into them. The commands, the SBOM formats, the SLSA levels claimed per artifact, and the published VEX justifications for scanner findings are all in Verifying releases. Enforcing image provenance at admission time inside a Kubernetes cluster is covered separately, in Images: build, provenance, scanning.

The pseudonymisation boundary

The pseudonymisation boundary separates a record from the person it is about, and it is enforced by PostgreSQL grants rather than by the server’s own routing: code that reaches for the wrong schema is a bug that can be fixed, while a database role able to read two domains defeats the separation however correct the code is.

GDPR Art. 4(5) defines pseudonymisation as processing where attributing data to a person requires additional information “kept separately and subject to technical and organisational measures”, and Art. 32(1)(a) names it a security measure for health data. EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 require that separation to hold against internal actors, operators with database access included.

Two domains hold the two parts, each behind its own role:

flowchart LR
    server["FerroEHR server"]
    server -->|ferroehr_clinical| ehr[("clinical<br/>versions and nodes,<br/>keyed by an opaque subject pseudonym")]
    server -->|ferroehr_party| demo[("party<br/>parties, and national identifiers<br/>sealed under a per-domain key")]
    server -->|audit writer| audit[("audit<br/>ATNA record repository")]
    ehr -. barred .- demo

Read one domain and you hold a clinical record whose subject is an opaque identifier, or a set of people with no records attached. Only the two together re-identify anything, and no credential the server uses holds both. The migrations create the roles, grant each its own schema, and revoke every other domain explicitly, in both directions; each role is NOINHERIT and a member of no other, so a grant cannot arrive through a membership.

The boundary is checked at startup, not assumed: the server reads the catalogue for every table, view, sequence and function each role can reach in a domain it does not own, and refuses to serve if it finds one, naming the role and the object. A misconfigured grant is a failed boot, not a silent weakening.

Two limits are worth stating plainly. The clinical schema holds a pseudonym only when [privacy] subject_namespaces declares the namespaces a subject reference may draw from — left unset, whatever a client sends is what gets stored, and no schema split saves you from a national identifier written into the clinical side; see Privacy and identifiers. And the split is a schema split by default: giving the demographic domain its own [database.party] url is what turns it into a credential split, which is the deployment step described in Operations.

Resolving across the boundary

One question needs both domains at once: which record belongs to this person? The server answers it in the application, over two connections, never in the database. An EHR names its subject in its own EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref, which the ehr relation copies into its subject columns on every EHR create and EHR_STATUS update. A cohort and the AQL demographic join read the parties on the party connection and the EHRs whose subject names them on the clinical connection, with a second search path and, when [database.party] url is set, a second database role. FerroEHR matches, links and merges no patients, and offers no lookup from a national identifier to its party.

No statement performs the join, because no credential could: the clinical role holds no grant in party and the party role holds none in clinical, both revocations are explicit and in both directions, and the boot check refuses to serve a database where either has been given one. The crossing exists as an application step that can be audited, rather than as a query anyone holding one password could write.

Every crossing records an access event in the linkage domain, naming who asked, the purpose of use they declared, and how many EHRs it reached. A miss is recorded like a hit: it says someone asked whether this deployment holds a record for that person. The event deliberately does not name the EHR that came back. A record pairing a party with its EHR would make the audit trail a map from parties to their EHRs, which the split exists to withhold.

Looking an EHR up by subject (GET /ehr?subject_id=…&subject_namespace=…) does not cross the boundary. That operation matches the EHR’s own EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref, which is the opaque pseudonym the privacy layer already constrains, so it resolves a pseudonym rather than an identity and reads no party. It records a linkage-domain access event all the same, naming the subject namespace and the EHR it found, because who resolved a subject to a record is worth knowing wherever it happened.

The lookup puts the subject identifier in the URL, because ITS-REST passes it as a query parameter. FerroEHR keeps it out of everything it writes: the request log and every trace span record the path and the matched route without the query string, and the 404 for an unknown subject names only the namespace. A reverse proxy or load balancer in front of FerroEHR sees the whole URL, so configure it not to log query strings on this route, or not at all. FerroPIX as the EHR index provider (IHE PIXm, planned in #3380) resolves a patient identifier to an EHR without putting it in a FerroEHR URL.

Declaring the posture

The separations above are each a configuration key, and a deployment that has made none of them is indistinguishable from one that has made all of them until something goes wrong. The top-level deployment.profile key (configuration) makes the posture explicit: production refuses to start while a separation is missing and not accepted by name, and reads the cluster each pool reached from pg_control_system() rather than trusting the DSN text; sandbox, the default, names every missing separation on the banner, in the boot log and on GET /management/status, reports the profile on GET /rest/status, and must not hold real patient data. The database keeps its own line of defence for the subject pseudonym too: once privacy.subject_namespaces is declared, a trigger on ehr refuses a subject reference that is not a UUID, whichever code path or session writes it.

One instance, one organisation

FerroEHR is single-tenant, and that is where openEHR puts the boundary. BASE architecture_overview/master06-design_of_the_ehr.adoc §The EHR System defines a system as “a distinct logical repository corresponding to an organisational entity that is legally responsible for the management and governance of the healthcare data contained within”, and says it is “distinct from any underlying virtualisation infrastructure or cloud computing facility, which may house multiple logical EHR systems in a multi-tenant fashion”. Multi-tenancy belongs to the layer that hosts several systems, not inside one of them.

So several organisations are served by several instances: one instance, one database, one set of domain roles each. That is a stronger boundary than a row predicate — a defect in a query cannot cross it, because there is nothing to cross — and it is what the §System Identity rule needs, since system_id “becomes embedded in the version identifiers of committed – and possibly signed – content” and “cannot easily be changed afterwards”. One system_id shared across organisations mints version identifiers that cannot tell the responsible parties apart.

There is therefore no tenant column on any relation, no row policy, no session variable to set and no [tenancy] configuration. What separates the clinical record from the identity of its subject is the pseudonymisation boundary above, which is a different question and stays.

Version signing

Every version the server commits can carry a VERSION.signature, computed inside the write transaction over the canonical form of the version itself. Signing is on by default in digest mode, and read-time verification of the server’s own signatures defaults to strict, so a served version that no longer matches its stored signature is a 500 rather than a silently served record.

The chapter Version signing covers the mechanism in two pages: Digest signing (what is signed, when, what the stored value proves, and how to reproduce it yourself) and PGP signing (key configuration and rotation, client-supplied signatures, and the signature an import wrapper carries). The [record.signing] keys are in the configuration reference.

ATNA audit trail

Separately from openEHR’s own provenance, FerroEHR keeps an IHE ATNA security audit trail of API access: on by default, persisted in the local Audit Record Repository (the dedicated audit PostgreSQL schema), rendered in both official formats (FHIR R4 AuditEvent per IHE BALP, and the DICOM PS3.15 audit message for the classic syslog feed), retrievable via the RESTful-ATNA ITI-81 FHIR search, and optionally forwarded to an external ARR over syslog and/or the ITI-20 FHIR feed. Node authentication (ITI-19) is available as native mutual TLS on the listener.

Stored records are tamper-evident: each is linked into a SHA-256 hash chain maintained by the database, the table refuses every rewrite path except the forwarding stamp, and SELECT * FROM audit.verify_audit_chain() names any record that was modified or removed. That is detection, not prevention: the controls that make it hard to forge wholesale are the least-privilege database role and the off-box sinks.

The full chapter (record content, sinks, tamper evidence, the ITI-81 search, fail-mode semantics, and mTLS) is Audit trail (IHE ATNA); every [audit] key is in the configuration reference.

Note

The ATNA trail is orthogonal to openEHR’s own CONTRIBUTION and AUDIT_DETAILS, which the server always writes in the same transaction as every change. openEHR audit records what a version says about its own authorship; ATNA records security surveillance of API access. Both coexist. Identified data never enters telemetry (metrics, traces, logs), so the audit trail is the single place where access to identified data is recorded; see Operations.

Verifying releases

Before you run a FerroEHR binary, image, or chart in a clinical environment, you should be able to answer two questions about the bytes you downloaded: did they arrive intact, and were they built by this project’s own release pipeline. This page is the operator’s procedure for both: one command per artifact kind, plus the deliberately-failing runs that prove your verification is actually checking something.

Every release publishes signed build provenance, a dependency SBOM, and a plain checksum alongside each artifact. Provenance is signed through Sigstore, so you can verify it yourself, and the signer identity is one you can pin to a single hardened workflow.

The repository moved to the FerroHEALTH organization on 2026-10-01, and v4.3.2 is the first release built there. Releases up to and including v4.3.1 were built and signed while it was rubentalstra/FerroEHR, so their attestations name that repository: verify them with -R rubentalstra/FerroEHR and --signer-workflow rubentalstra/FerroEHR/…. Their images and charts were published under ghcr.io/rubentalstra. The copies of v4.3.1 under ghcr.io/ferrohealth carry the same digests, so gh attestation verify accepts them with the old repository name. Their cosign signatures exist only beside the originals, so run cosign verify against the ghcr.io/rubentalstra path.
