How to use this

Copy the activity tables below into your own register and fill the three columns nobody but you can fill: the purpose your organisation processes for, the lawful basis it relies on, and the recipients it discloses to. Delete any activity your deployment has switched off. Activities 6 and 7 are off by default and only apply if you turned them on.

The identity fields Art. 30(1)(a) asks for are yours in every case:

FieldValue
Controller (name, contact)your organisation
Joint controllers, if anyyours
Representative in the Union, if applicableyours
Data protection officeryours
Processors engagedyours: the PostgreSQL operator, and any object store, outbox reader, terminology server or identity provider the deployment is configured against

Note

One transmission is on by default and is not a processor relationship: the usage report to FerroPULSE. It carries no patient data and no staff identities. Cadasto B.V. receives it as controller for its own purposes, and its collector stores the IP address each report comes from. Where that makes the report personal data (an instance run by one person from their own connection, for example), list Cadasto B.V. as a recipient in your record, or switch the report off.

1. Storing the clinical record

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
Purposeyours: the care or research purpose the repository serves
Categories of data subjectPatients and other record subjects; the health professionals recorded as composers, performers and participants
Categories of personal dataClinical content as the operational templates define it, in the clinical schema, its cold archival partitions included. Special-category health data under Art. 9. The subject appears as an opaque pseudonym once [privacy] subject_namespaces is declared
Recipientsyours: whoever the API is exposed to. The software discloses nothing on its own
Third-country transfersyours: wherever the deployment and its backups run
RetentionNo automatic expiry. Content leaves only by an administrator’s deletion; archiving moves it to the cold tier without expiring it
Security measuresLeast-privilege database roles per pseudonymisation domain; a data-minimisation pass over every write; one instance per organisation; TLS; authentication and layered authorization

2. Versioning and change control

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
PurposeKeeping the clinical record attributable and reconstructible, which openEHR’s change-control model requires
Categories of data subjectAs activity 1, plus the committing user
Categories of personal dataOne contribution and one audit entry per commit, naming the committer, the change type and the commit instant; every prior version of every object
Recipientsyours
Third-country transfersyours
RetentionIndefinite by design. A version is superseded, never overwritten
Security measuresContribution and audit written in the same transaction as the content; a temporal version table rather than in-place update; optional version signing

3. Query

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
Purposeyours: the reporting, cohort or operational purpose queries serve
Categories of data subjectAs activity 1
Categories of personal dataWhatever the query projects out of stored clinical content
Recipientsyours
Third-country transfersyours
RetentionResults are not stored. Stored query definitions are, as AQL text
Security measuresQueries run on the clinical credential only, so no query can reach the demographic domain; the planning gate refuses constructs the active specification generation does not define; result caps and statement timeouts bound one query’s reach

Note

Small-cell suppression applies to the cohort query only. A cohort result serving fewer distinct EHRs than privacy.cohort.small_cell_threshold has its rows withheld and is marked suppressed; an ordinary POST /query/aql takes no threshold, so a query returning one row about one rare condition is served like any other.

4. Identity and linkage

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
PurposeHolding who the record subjects are, and resolving a person to their record where a caller is entitled to
Categories of data subjectPatients, and the parties a record refers to
Categories of personal dataParties in the party schema with names, addresses and contacts as the template defines them; protected national identifiers sealed in national_identifier
Recipientsyours
Third-country transfersyours
RetentionParties leave only by an administrator’s deletion. The subject reference of an EHR leaves with the EHR that carries it
Security measuresTwo schemas under their own roles, revoked from each other in both directions and checked at boot; AES-256-GCM sealing with a keyed HMAC-SHA-256 digest for lookup, under per-domain subkeys; each crossing from a party or a subject to its EHRs runs in the application over two pools and writes an access record

5. Access logging

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
PurposeRecording who reached what, which EHDS Annex II 3.2 requires of an EHR system and which NEN 7513 specifies the content of for Dutch deployments
Categories of data subjectThe record subject, and the person who accessed the record
Categories of personal dataPer access: the accessing person and organisation, the roles held, the object and its domain, the outcome, the declared purpose of use, the configured legal basis and the time. Refusals are recorded too, unattributed where no principal was established
Recipientsyours: the local repository, plus any syslog or FHIR-feed Audit Record Repository configured
Third-country transfersyours
Retention[audit.store] retention, 0 meaning forever, reaped hourly otherwise. Where an active identifier rule names a jurisdiction with a registered floor, a shorter value is refused at boot
Security measuresRecords are hash-chained and verifiable with audit.verify_audit_chain(); the runtime role may insert and stamp delivery and nothing else; the audit schema sits outside both pseudonymisation domains; the syslog feed can run over RFC 5425 TLS with a client certificate

6. Change-event feed (off by default)

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
PurposeTelling downstream systems that a commit happened, when [record.change_feed] readers names a reader
Categories of data subjectRecord subjects, indirectly
Categories of personal dataA PHI-free envelope: the contribution id, the EHR id, the commit instant, and per version the object id, kind, version number, change type and template. No clinical content
RecipientsThe configured readers (FerroBRIDGE, for one), and whoever they deliver to
Third-country transfersyours: wherever the readers and their broker run
RetentionRows pruned [record.change_feed] retention after their commit, seven days by default, once every active reader has acknowledged them
Security measuresWritten in the same transaction as the commit it announces, so there is no event without its commit; read only by a caller holding the __ferroehr.outbox scope, one access record per read; the envelope carries identifiers, so a consumer still has to authenticate to the API to read anything

7. Workforce identity (off by default)

Art. 30 fieldWhat the software does
PurposeIdentifying the health professionals and the representatives who act on the record, so each version and each access names the natural person and the provider (EHDS Art. 13(4), Annex II 3.1 and 3.2), when [auth.scim] or just-in-time creation is on
Categories of data subjectThe deployment’s own professionals, its Basic users, and registered representatives
Categories of personal dataPer professional: the binding key (the identity provider’s immutable user id), the userName, the externalId, the name, the groups (care teams), the lifecycle state and the professional ROLE. Contact attributes only where the operator maps them; none are mapped by default. Just-in-time creation writes only the key, the userName and the name
Source (Art. 14(2)(f))The identity provider: Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak or another SCIM client, or the access token at the first login
Lawful basisyours. FerroEHR’s design assumes Art. 6(1)(c) for the attribution minimum (key, userName, name), since EHDS Art. 13(4) and the logging duties need the professional identified, and Art. 6(1)(b) or (f) for any contact attribute a deployment maps
Recipientsyours: everyone who reads a version’s committer or an access record
Third-country transfersyours
Retentionyours. In the Netherlands the attribution minimum is kept for the BW 7:454(3) horizon of the records it attributes (twenty years); EHDS Art. 13(4) sets the duty to identify, not a period. Elsewhere, name the national retention provision (GDPR Art. 6(3)). Contact attributes are erased [auth.scim] contact_erasure_delay after a User’s deletion, and the attribution minimum stays with the versions it attributes
Security measuresA professional’s PERSON and the groups are writable only by their SCIM client or an administrator; the binding key never changes once set; every SCIM request is an access record of the client naming the person; deactivations past max_deactivations are refused

Because the data come from the identity provider and not from the professional, give the professionals the information GDPR Art. 14 asks for: what is copied, from which source, for which purpose, and for how long.

Fields no software can fill

The record is not complete until these are answered, and they are answered by the organisation:

  • The purpose of each activity and the lawful basis for it, which for health data means an Art. 9(2) condition beside the Art. 6 one.
  • The recipients, including every category of person inside the organisation who can reach the API.
  • Transfers to third countries and the safeguard relied on, which follows from where the database, the backups and every configured peer run.
  • Time limits for erasure per category, which the software will not apply for you: it deletes when an administrator asks.
  • The general description of security measures in Art. 30(1)(g), for which the technical half is the DPIA page and the threat model.

Go-live checklist

Run this before a FerroEHR deployment holds real patient data. Every item is something you set and then read back from the running system, because a separation that was configured and never verified is a separation nobody has seen work.

None of it makes a deployment compliant with anything. It is the set of technical properties the software can hold, checked rather than assumed. The organisational half stays yours.

  • 1. Role separation, verified from outside
  • 2. The deployment profile is production, and the server boots
  • 3. Identifier scanning is on and strict
  • 4. The pseudonym namespaces are declared
  • 5. Backups, one per domain
  • 6. The audit trail is on, durable, and kept long enough
  • 7. Schema preparation runs on its own credential
  • 8. Callers are bound and rate-limited
  • 9. The paperwork exists
  • What this checklist does not cover

1. Role separation, verified from outside

Create the four domain roles, give each login role membership of exactly one, and point each pool at its own DSN:

[database]
url             = "postgres://app_ehr:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"
migrate_url     = "postgres://ferroehr_migrator:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"

[database.party]
url = "postgres://app_party:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"

Then check it:

ferroehr db verify

It exits 0 only when the database carries exactly this build’s migrations and no runtime role can read a domain it does not own, and it issues no DDL doing it. A breach names the role, the object kind and the schema-qualified object. The server runs the same check at every boot and refuses to serve on a breach, so this is the early warning rather than the only one.

The statements that create the roles, and what each one may reach afterwards, are Operations → Database roles and the threat model.

Warning

A login role that is a member of two domain roles crosses the boundary that ferroehr db verify reports as intact: the check measures the group roles. Give each login role one membership. The clinical login role’s membership in ferroehr_clinical also covers the local Audit Record Repository, which that role writes; it holds no grant in the other two domains.

  • Four domain roles exist, each NOINHERIT and a member of no other.
  • Each login role is a member of exactly one domain role.
  • ferroehr db verify exits 0.

2. The deployment profile is production, and the server boots

[deployment]
profile = "production"

Under production the server refuses to start while a separation is open and not accepted by name. The refusal lists every open gap with its finding and its remedy, so one boot tells you the whole list:

deployment.profile = "production" refuses to start: this deployment has not
made the separations production asserts. Make them, or accept each one by name
in deployment.accepts (which is then stated on every boot and on /management/status):
  - shared_credential: ...

The gaps are shared_credential, shared_cluster, open_subject_namespace, audit_off, audit_fails_open, no_category_map, open_ehr_access_default, migrate_on_runtime_credential, auth_off, rbac_off, plaintext_listener, plaintext_audit_feed and plaintext_object_store. shared_cluster is read from pg_control_system().system_identifier on each pool, the audit pool included, rather than from the DSN text, so two names for one cluster do not pass it.

Two of them are the shipped compatibility defaults, kept as they are because the conformance instrument and the development stacks need them: the EHR_ACCESS default is open, and the audit trail fails open. A production deployment either changes both, or names each in deployment.accepts and carries the decision.

plaintext_listener opens whenever the main listener speaks plain HTTP on an address reachable off the host. Behind a TLS-terminating ingress, accept it by name: the entry records that the ingress carries the encryption. It also opens when a separate management listener (management.listen) is set, because that listener binds every interface and never speaks TLS: unset the port so the surface shares the main listener, or accept the gap by name and keep that port off any network clinical clients or the internet reach.

The syslog feed has no gap of its own: it sends over RFC 5425 TLS only.

plaintext_audit_feed opens when the audit FHIR feed ([audit.fhir_feed]) is on with an http:// URL, and plaintext_object_store when the multimedia store is on with an http:// url = true. Use https:// for both, or accept the gap by name where the repository or the store is reached on a trusted segment.

A gap you have decided to run with goes in deployment.accepts by name. It is then stated on every boot and on GET /management/status, so it is run rather than hidden.

  • deployment.profile = "production" and the server starts.
  • [authz.rbac] ehr_access_default and [audit] fail_mode are the values this deployment intends, not the ones it inherited.
  • Every entry in deployment.accepts is a decision someone recorded, not a leftover.
  • GET /management/status shows the profile and an accepted-gap list you recognise.

3. Identifier scanning is on and strict

[privacy.identifier_scan]
mode  = "strict"
rules = ["ch-ahvn13", "ch-epd-pid", "de-kvnr", "fi-hetu", "gb-nhs-number", "nl-bsn", "no-fodselsnummer", "se-personnummer"]

Both are the defaults, so the check is that nothing turned them off. strict refuses a clinical write carrying a value one of the active rules claims, and names the RM path and the rule without echoing the value. Every rule the build ships is active unless you narrow the list.

Add patterns for the identifier kinds no build can ship a rule for: local medical-record numbers, payer references, a postcode paired with a house number. Each is a Rust regular expression compiled at boot, and one that does not compile is a boot error naming it.

If you are migrating existing content, run mode = "warn" first, read what it reports, then switch to strict. Going live in warn means the scanner observes and nothing acts.

  • mode = "strict".
  • The rules list covers every jurisdiction whose identifiers your content can carry.
  • Local identifier kinds have a patterns entry.

4. The pseudonym namespaces are declared

[privacy]
subject_namespaces = ["your-pseudonym-service"]

Empty is the default, and empty means the subject rule is out of force: whatever a client sends becomes the clinical subject reference. Declaring a namespace turns the rule on. From then on EHR_STATUS.subject.external_ref must name a listed namespace and carry a UUID, the server stamps ehr.posture, and a database trigger refuses a non-UUID subject whichever session writes it.

The name is a deployment fact: it identifies the service that mints your pseudonyms, and no server can invent it for you. FerroEHR mints none; under the IHE patient identity source it is the clinical domain’s assigning authority, pixm.assigning_authority.

  • subject_namespaces names at least one namespace.
  • The open_subject_namespace gap no longer appears on GET /management/status.

5. Backups, one per domain

Backups leave the database with none of the grants attached, so one dump per cluster undoes the split. Configure one per domain, each with its own credential and its own volume. On Kubernetes that is the backup values:

backup:
  enabled: true
  clinical:
    existingSecret: ferroehr-backup-clinical
    persistentVolumeClaim: ferroehr-backup-clinical
  party:
    existingSecret: ferroehr-backup-party
    persistentVolumeClaim: ferroehr-backup-party

Each credential is a read-only role on its own domain, and it cannot be the pool’s: each domain’s runtime role is revoked from the other domains, so a dump taken through one would be silently partial. The chart refuses to render when two domains name the same claim, which is the mistake that quietly puts the join back together.

Three things the chart does not do: it provisions no storage, it prunes no old dumps, and no network policy of ours selects the dump pods.

  • Two dumps, two credentials, two volumes, and a third set for the audit domain when it has a database of its own.
  • The demographic volume has the narrower audience.
  • A restore has been rehearsed, and the rehearsal is recorded.
  • Retention and pruning of the dumps is somebody’s job, and they know it.

6. The audit trail is on, durable, and kept long enough

[audit]
enabled = true
purpose_header = "x-purpose-of-use"

[audit.store]
enabled = true
retention = 0    # or a value at or above your jurisdiction's floor

Auditing is on by default with the local store as the sink. What a production deployment adds is a copy off the box, because a local repository shares the blast radius of the database it audits:

[audit.syslog]
url = "tls://arr.example:6514"

# or, for a RESTful ARR
[audit.fhir_feed.endpoint]
url = "https://arr.example/fhir"

Decide fail_mode deliberately. open logs a dropped record and serves the request; closed refuses an auditable operation with 503 when the record cannot be taken. closed is the posture that makes “no unaudited access” true.

Retention has a jurisdictional floor. Where one of your active identifier rules names a jurisdiction with a registered floor, a shorter horizon is a boot error naming the floor. Every EU Member State carries three years from each date of access (EHDS Art. 9(2)); the Netherlands five years, from the Besluit vaststelling bewaartermijn logging; Switzerland one year (DSV Art. 4 Abs. 5). The floors are in calendar years, so state the horizon as [audit.store] retention, which is compared exactly; a retention is held to the most days those years can span (1096, 1830 and 366). The audit trail page lists the floors with their sources. A deployment in a jurisdiction with no floor registered sets its own horizon and records why.

Verify the chain works before you need it:

SELECT * FROM audit.verify_audit_chain();
  • [audit] enabled = true with a durable sink.
  • A copy is forwarded off the box, to a sink the server’s own identity cannot rewrite.
  • fail_mode is a decision, not a default.
  • retention (or retention) is 0 or at or above the floor that applies to you.
  • audit.verify_audit_chain() returns no rows on a healthy trail.

7. Schema preparation runs on its own credential

Preparing the schema spans every schema at once: the DDL of all four migration sets under migrations = "apply", all four _sqlx_migrations bookkeeping tables under "verify". No least-privilege runtime role can do either, ferroehr_clinical included, so [database] migrate_url names the credential that can. Unset, it falls back to [database] url, which is the single-credential posture.

  • [database] migrate_url (or migrate_url_file) is set.
  • migrations = "verify" if the schema is applied out of band, with ferroehr db migrate run under the migrator DSN first.

8. Callers are bound and rate-limited

Every person is bound to a demographic PERSON before their issuer is trusted (Who is the committer), and each caller is held to a rate.

  • Every professional is provisioned through SCIM, adopted, or admitted by just-in-time creation before their persons issuer is added (bootstrap and migration).
  • [server.caller_rate] is set. It limits each authenticated caller on the clinical API, is kept per replica, and is off unless configured ([server.caller_rate]).
  • Every [[authz.federation.agreement]] carries its own caller_rate; boot refuses one without it.

9. The paperwork exists

  • A data protection impact assessment has been carried out and signed off. The technical half is the DPIA page; the purposes, the lawful basis and the organisational measures are yours.
  • The Art. 30 record of processing is written. The template is Records of processing.
  • The processor agreements are in place for the database operator and every configured peer.
  • Somebody has read what the software cannot do for a data subject.

What this checklist does not cover

  • Your identity provider. Every authorization stage reads claims it asserted. Its token lifetimes, binding and revocation are outside the software.
  • The platform. Host hardening, network policy, image admission and secret management are Cluster hardening.
  • Encryption at rest. FerroEHR stores queryable JSONB and does not encrypt clinical payload before it reaches PostgreSQL. That is the database operator’s layer.
  • Clinical governance. Validation checks structure, invariants and terminology bindings. It does not know whether a recorded fact is true.

Who is the committer

Every version FerroEHR stores carries an AUDIT_DETAILS, and its committer is the “identity and optional reference into identity management service, of user who committed the item” (RM common, AUDIT_DETAILS). FerroEHR writes that committer itself, from the caller it authenticated and the demographic party it bound the caller to. A client no longer says who committed. This page shows what the server writes for each kind of caller, what a client may still send, the refusals, and how a professional’s party gets the login identifier the binding matches.

  • Why the server writes it
  • The committer for each kind of caller
  • What a client may still send
  • The refusals
    • The deviation from ITS-REST
  • Imports
  • What the access record adds
  • How a party gets its login identifier
    • Who may set it
  • The identity provider side

Why the server writes it

  • RM common master04 §Referring to Demographic Entities: PARTY_PROXY.external_ref “will be non-Void” “where there is an entry in such a service for the party in question”. A professional is a PERSON in FerroEHR’s demographic store, so the committer names that PERSON.
  • RM common master04 §Audit Details lets the committer carry “a system login identifier”, and §Attestation names AUDIT_DETAILS.committer as “the identity of the attesting party”.
  • EHDS (Regulation (EU) 2025/327): Art. 13(4) asks the record to “identify the health professional and healthcare provider that carried out such registration or update”, Annex II 3.1 asks for “reliable mechanisms for the identification and authentication of health professionals”, and Annex II 3.2(a) and (b) ask the access record to name the provider and the natural person.

No openEHR specification governs how a login is matched to a party, when the match is made, or what happens when none matches. That is FerroEHR’s own design, configured under [authz.party_binding].

The committer for each kind of caller

ferrohealth-smart classifies every token by its issuer’s kind and profile (Who the caller is). The server then writes the committer from the bound party:

CallerCommitter the server writes
A person, at a persons issuer through a first-party clientPARTY_IDENTIFIED with the PERSON’s name, an external_ref to the PERSON, the login identifier {issuer = <token iss>, id = <person_key value>, type = "oauth2"} and the provider identifier {issuer, id, type = "healthcare-provider"}
A delegated person (a client or RFC 8693 actor in the issuer’s delegates)the person’s own committer, as above; the client and the actor go into the access record, never into the committer
A Basic userthe committer of the PERSON its [[authz.party_binding.basic_user]] table maps it to, with the login identifier {issuer = "ferroehr", id = <user>, type = "basic"}
A representativePARTY_RELATED naming the representative’s own PERSON in external_ref, their login identifier, and the coded relationship from the openEHR subject_relationship group (253|unknown| when no code fits)
A patient of a patients issuerPARTY_SELF with no external_ref (RM common master04, the first scheme of §Referring to the Patient)
A verified external person of a federation issuerPARTY_IDENTIFIED with no external_ref: the asserted name, the professional’s hp_identifier under "<country>:<issuing authority>", and the token’s iss and sub with type oauth2
A MyHealth@EU contact point’s professionalas the external person, with the HP Identity Assertion’s NameID under the assertion’s issuer and type hp_identifier:<NameID format>
A declared system client (relay or device)PARTY_IDENTIFIED named by the client, with {issuer = <token iss>, id = <client>, type = "client"} and no external_ref
An organisation of a federation issuernone: it commits nothing
An undeclared system clientnone: it commits nothing into an EHR (403)

A person’s version names the provider the deployment acts for, from [authz.party_binding] provider, so the version carries the Art. 13(4) provider without the access record. A PERSON with no name gives a committer with no name.

A system client commits clinical content only as declared:

  • a relay client relays another system’s record of a human act, such as an HL7 v2 message. The COMPOSITION names the professional in composer or in a context participation’s performer, and the committer stays the client (EHDS Art. 13(4)). FerroBRIDGE writes its HL7 v2 messages this way, with the clinician in the content and the facility from its mapping rules;
  • a device client registers a device act with no professional acting. The COMPOSITION names the device in composer. Treating such a registration as outside Art. 13(4) is FerroEHR’s reading of that article and of COMPOSITION.composer;
  • either one names a facility of its facilities in context.health_care_facility, or, without a context, in feeder_audit.originating_system_audit.location. The server checks the facility and never fills it.

The full rules are under [[authz.system_client]].

What a client may still send

A client keeps change_type, description and lifecycle_state, and its COMPOSITION content, the composer included. Where ITS-REST requires a committer (a CONTRIBUTION’s audit, each member’s commit_audit, an embedded attestation), send the placeholder, which names the authenticated caller and nothing else:

{
  "_type": "PARTY_IDENTIFIED",
  "identifiers": [
    { "_type": "DV_IDENTIFIER", "issuer": "<token iss, or ferroehr>", "id": "<sub, or the Basic user>" }
  ]
}

The server replaces it with the committer above. A committer that states nothing the server’s does not (the same name, the caller’s own login identifier, the bound PERSON as external_ref) is accepted too. On the header path, send no openEHR-AUDIT_DETAILS committer at all.

The refusals

RequestAnswer
A stated committer with another name, another identifier or another external_ref403 naming AUDIT_DETAILS.committer
A placeholder naming anyone other than the caller403
A stated PARTY_RELATED, or a PARTY_SELF from anyone but the record’s person403
A person’s committer stated by a system caller403
An attestation from a patient, a representative, a system caller, an external caller or an unbound caller403; only a person bound to a professional PERSON attests (RM common master04 §Attestation, “an explicit signing by one healthcare agent”; limiting it to professionals is FerroEHR’s reading)
A commit by an undeclared system client403
A system COMPOSITION outside its writes, or a person act from a client that is not relay403
A system COMPOSITION without a facility of its facilities, a relay act naming no professional, or an organisation composer422 naming the element
A patient-context token’s demographic write403
An import of a version whose committer names a local party, from a system [authz.import] trusted_systems does not list403

A login the binding cannot use is refused before any commit; the codes are under How a login is looked up.

The deviation from ITS-REST

The ITS-REST overview (Requests_and_responses.md, §openehr-version and openehr-audit-details) recommends that clients provision the audit headers “based on authentication and authorization runtime data”, and says a supplied value “MUST be merged”. Refusing a supplied committer that names someone other than the authenticated caller deviates from that merge rule, on purpose: a merged committer would let a client record another person as the author, which RM common master04 and EHDS Art. 13(4) rule out. The deviation is reported upstream in #5019.

Imports

POST /message/import… needs the role [authz.rbac] import_role names, or a system/ caller. An imported version keeps its wrapped commit_audit and attestations as received, so an IMPORTED_VERSION names who committed at the source. A wrapped committer that names a PERSON of this server, or carries a login identifier of its issuers, is refused with 403 unless the version was created by a system [authz.import] trusted_systems lists.

What the access record adds

The committer says who committed. The access record of the same request says how the caller was bound: binding (bound, provisional, external, organisation, system, self or a refused-* code), the party, its groups, the provider, the actor chain of a delegated token and the client. The values and their renderings are under The binding outcome.

How a party gets its login identifier

The binding matches the token’s person_key claim against the identifier at the binding-key selector of a mapped PERSON template, under the identifier_issuer of the issuer’s [[auth.party]] table. A PERSON binds a professional only while it performs a live professional ROLE, and a representative only while it is the source of a recorded representation relationship. The identifier gets there in one of four ways:

  1. SCIM. Your identity provider provisions the person through FerroEHR’s SCIM 2.0 endpoint at /scim/v2/, sending the key in urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:ferrohealth:2.0:User:loginIdentifier. FerroEHR creates the PERSON and its professional ROLE in one contribution.
  2. Just-in-time creation at the first login, off by default per issuer (configuration).
  3. The demographic API, under the administrator role.
  4. An existing PERSON that already carries the identifier, adopted as the migration describes.

In the openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-CLUSTER.person_identifier.v2 shape, the key is one DV_IDENTIFIER in the cluster PARTY.details holds, with the [[auth.party]] identifier_issuer as issuer and its identifier_type as type:

{
  "_type": "CLUSTER",
  "archetype_node_id": "openEHR-DEMOGRAPHIC-CLUSTER.person_identifier.v2",
  "name": { "_type": "DV_TEXT", "value": "Person identifier" },
  "items": [
    {
      "_type": "ELEMENT",
      "archetype_node_id": "at0001",
      "name": { "_type": "DV_TEXT", "value": "Identifier" },
      "value": {
        "_type": "DV_IDENTIFIER",
        "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>",
        "id": "<the Entra object id>",
        "type": "guid"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Who may set it

  • A professional’s PERSON, its professional ROLE and every provisioned GROUP are written only by the SCIM client that owns them or by an administrator. A professional editing their own PERSON cannot change their binding.
  • The binding key never changes once set (RFC 7643 §2.2): a version that changes it is refused with 403, and POST /admin/party/binding-key is the one change.
  • The professional ROLE is created or retired only by a SCIM client, just-in-time creation under its admission rules, or an administrator.
  • A representative’s PERSON and its representation relationship are registered by an administrator or by the proxy service’s registration, never by SCIM.

The identity provider side

FerroEHR is an OAuth 2.0 resource server and never speaks SAML. The walk-throughs, the generic standards path first, are on Enterprise identity providers.

Enterprise identity providers

FerroEHR does not manage users. There is no user table, no user API, and no plan to add one: identity administration is delegated to your identity provider (IdP), and the CDR consumes standard OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens. This page records that posture and walks through connecting an identity provider: the generic standards path first, then Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), AD FS, Okta, Keycloak, a SAML identity provider behind one of them, and the answer for plain-LDAP directories.

  • The posture: users live in the IdP
  • How the CDR consumes an IdP
  • Who the caller is
    • The MyHealth@EU contact-point route
  • The generic standards path
  • Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD)
    • Binding and provisioning with the entra preset
  • AD FS (on-premises Active Directory)
  • “We only have LDAP”
  • Okta
  • Keycloak
  • A SAML identity provider through Keycloak or Entra ID
  • Just-in-time creation
  • Serving SMART apps

The posture: users live in the IdP

A clinical data repository is the wrong place to store credentials. A user store would make the CDR an authentication product (password lifecycle, lockout policy, MFA, recovery flows, and the largest new attack surface the product could grow) duplicating what a dedicated IdP already does under your existing governance. So the split is deliberate and permanent:

  • The IdP owns identities: accounts, passwords, MFA, group/role membership, lifecycle (joiners/movers/leavers), and session policy.
  • The CDR owns authorization: it validates the token, mines roles from its claims, and enforces RBAC/ABAC and per-EHR access control on every request.

The HTTP Basic user list in ferroehr.toml holds persons only, and it is not a user store: each Basic user maps to the PERSON that carries its binding key, which the identity provider provisions through SCIM (bootstrap and migration). A machine authenticates with OAuth 2.0 client credentials under a declared [[authz.system_client]], and most people authenticate with bearer tokens from the IdP.

Note

The viewer follows the same rule: it authenticates against the same credentials the CDR accepts (the same OIDC issuer, or Basic) and has no user-management screens. To create, disable, or re-role a user, use your IdP’s own administration surface.

How the CDR consumes an IdP

Three things do all the work:

  1. Token validation ([auth]): the server reads the issuer’s metadata and key set at boot and validates each bearer token’s signature (asymmetric algorithms only), iss, exp/nbf, aud and typ; the audience list is mandatory, so a server with none refuses to boot rather than accepting another service’s token. See the bearer settings table.
  2. Role mining ([[auth.issuer]]): FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ROLE_CLAIMS (default ["roles","groups","entitlements"], the RFC 9068 §2.2.3.1 carriers; a Keycloak realm adds realm_access.roles) names the JWT claim paths whose values become the caller’s roles for the role layer. A path may be dotted to walk nested claims, and a claim holding a single string is accepted as readily as an array.
  3. SMART on openEHR scopes: every route requires a scope from the token’s scope claim (user/composition-*.cruds, user/aql-*.s and so on; see SMART App Launch). Your IdP has to mint them, for example as Keycloak client scopes assigned to the client. A token with roles and no SMART on openEHR scope authenticates and is then refused with 403 on every route.

Everything below is those three pointed at a different issuer.

Who the caller is

ferrohealth-smart classifies every token by its issuer’s kind and profile, and the server acts on the kind:

  • A person signs in at a persons issuer through a first-party client, or with HTTP Basic. The login is bound to the PERSON carrying its key, and the person commits under that PERSON.
  • A delegated person reaches the server through a client or an RFC 8693 actor that the issuer’s profile lists in delegates. The token’s subject is the person, so the request is bound and committed exactly as the person’s own; the client and the actor do not change who committed. The access record carries acting_mode = delegated, the client and the actor chain.
  • A Keycloak impersonation is a delegated person. Keycloak 26.8 puts the administrator who impersonates a user into an RFC 8693 act claim of every token of the impersonation session, {"sub": <the administrator's user id>, "preferred_username": …}, which “is always present and cannot be disabled” (Keycloak 26.8.0 release notes, Track impersonation across token lifecycle and downstream services). An impersonation is therefore refused like any undeclared actor, unless the issuer’s delegates lists the administrator as an actor ({ sub = "<user id>" }). Then the request is bound to the impersonated user and commits as that user, and the access record names the administrator as the actor (EHDS Annex II 3.2(b) asks for the natural person who accessed). Keycloak’s act names no issuer, so the actor is recorded under the token’s issuer. The impersonator claim (id, username) of Keycloak’s built-in IMPERSONATOR_ID and IMPERSONATOR_USERNAME session note mappers repeats act and decides nothing. To refuse every impersonation, add those mappers and set impersonation_marker = "impersonator" on the issuer: a token carrying the claim is refused before any actor is read. A Keycloak older than 26.8 writes no act, so there the marker is the only way to see an impersonation at all.
  • A guest, by the profile’s guest markers (Entra ID marks one with acct = 1 or an idp other than the issuer), is refused with 403 (refused-guest) unless the issuer’s [[auth.party]] table sets guests = true. Admit guests only for people acting under your own responsibility (GDPR Art. 9(3) and Art. 29), such as contractors.
  • A system caller is an app-only token by the profile’s app_only markers: sub equal to the client claim under rfc9068, idtyp = app without scp under entra, and the listed service-account subjects under keycloak. A Basic user is never one. A system caller acts for no person, so it holds system/ scopes only, and a token with a user/ or patient/ scope is refused with 403. It reads under its system/ scopes. It commits into an EHR only as a client an [[authz.system_client]] table declares (configuration), under the committer PARTY_IDENTIFIED{name = <client>, identifiers = [{issuer = <iss>, id = <client>, type = "client"}]} with no external_ref.
    • Each COMPOSITION it commits is of a template its writes lists, or the commit is refused with 403.
    • It names a facility of its facilities in context.health_care_facility.identifiers, or, for a COMPOSITION with no context, in feeder_audit.originating_system_audit.location.identifiers. Otherwise it is refused with 422 naming the element; the server fills neither.
    • A device act names the device in composer, with an identifier of one of the client’s device_identifier_issuers that is also feeder_audit.originating_system_audit.system_id, and is accepted only from a device client. Every other COMPOSITION records a person’s act: it is accepted only from a relay client (403 otherwise) and names the professional by an identifier in composer or in the performer of a context participation (422 otherwise). An organisation composer is refused with 422.
  • A verified external person or organisation of a federation issuer is admitted only under the [[authz.federation.agreement]] of its issuer and accessor, and refused with 403 without one or under the other accessor’s. Its rights come from the agreement, never from a role:
    • it holds only the patient/ scopes the agreement reads (beside openid, profile, fhirUser, online_access and launch), so a token with any other scope is refused, and it reaches only the EHR of its launch context, which needs the issuer in [auth.smart] patient_issuers;
    • it is an access-service caller by its kind, so an opted-out EHR answers 404 as an unknown one does (EHDS Art. 10(1)). Only an external person under an agreement with opt_out_override reaches one, under an emergency purpose, recorded as an override; an organisation never does;
    • a read under an agreement with a consent condition needs the consent decision reference for the patient (Wabvpz Art. 1(j) and Art. 15a(1)): the token carries it in the claim or authorization_details member its [[auth.federation]] table maps to consent.reference, as one string (a coded value refuses the token with 401), and its patient/ grant holds it to the launch-context patient. A read without it is refused with 403, and the access record carries the reference with the other external fields;
    • under an NL agreement, Wabvpz Art. 15f holds an insurer and an occupational or insurance physician out. A caller whose nl.role is the UZI role 01.008 (bedrijfsarts) or 01.048 (verzekeringsarts) is refused with 403 as refused-wabvpz-role, and a caller whose nl.organisation_type is missing or is not a care provider type of Nictiz’s OrganisatieTypeCodelijst is refused with 403 as refused-wabvpz-organisation-type, which is how an insurer is refused;
    • a chained organisation request carries the requester’s correlation id in the claim or attested authorization_details member its [[auth.federation]] table maps to correlation_id, as one string; a request without it is refused with 403, and a request header never stands in for it;
    • a caller above its agreement’s caller_rate is answered 429 with Retry-After before any patient lookup, a MyHealth@EU contact point’s included;
    • an external person commits only a COMPOSITION of a template the agreement’s writes lists; an organisation commits nothing, and neither attests or writes a demographic party. Neither deletes, except the discard of a dispensation described under the MyHealth@EU contact-point route;
    • an external person’s commit records the server’s committer, a PARTY_IDENTIFIED with no external_ref: the asserted name as one string, the professional’s hp_identifier under the issuer "<country_code>:<issuing_authority_name>" with type hp_identifier, and the token’s iss and sub with type oauth2. The country must be an upper-case ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code, and the issuing authority is NFC-normalised with its white space trimmed and collapsed and may hold no :, control or bidi character. A missing or failing field is refused with 403 naming it. Map the authority with a constant source in the [[auth.federation]] table when the token does not carry it;
    • the COMPOSITION names the healthcare provider the token asserts in EVENT_CONTEXT.health_care_facility, or with no context in feeder_audit.originating_system_audit.location: a DV_IDENTIFIER with the provider.healthcare_provider_identifier as id and the provider.issuing_authority_name as issuer. The server writes no facility and refuses a composition without it with 422 (EHDS Art. 13(4)). This is the domestic form; the MyHealth@EU contact-point form follows.
  • Attestations come only from a person bound to a professional PERSON. A patient, a representative, a system caller and an unbound caller are refused with 403 (RM common master04 §Attestation).

The MyHealth@EU contact-point route

A federation issuer with contact_point = true in its [[auth.federation]] table is a MyHealth@EU national contact point (NCPeH-A’s authorization server). Its person agreement names the service it serves in ehdsi_service (patient_summary, eprescription or orcd), and its issuer goes into [auth.smart] patient_issuers. Every request runs with a sender-constrained token (sender_constraint = "required"). On every patient-data route:

  • The token carries the patient of the treatment relationship confirmation in ehdsi.patient.id, as system|value, the patient identifier’s assigning authority and value, the form every family resource server reads. A token without it, or with a value of another form (an empty system or one with whitespace, or a value holding a control character, |, ^, &, ~ or a backslash), is refused with 403 whose detail opens with ERROR_SEC_DATA_INTEGRITY_NOT_ENSURED (MyHealth@EU Requirements Catalogue 10.0.0 requirement 11.01.02), recorded as refused-trc-missing, before the EHR index is asked.
  • The patient is resolved to its EHR through the deployment’s EHR index, compared on the value and the assigning authority, and the request must name that EHR: the route’s {ehr_id}, or a query’s ehr_id. The EHR stands in for the launch context the token does not carry (eHDSI XCA Profile 8.0.1 §4.2.1).
  • Another patient’s EHR, an EHR the server does not hold, an EHR an opted-out patient’s record keeps out of reach, a TRC patient no EHR belongs to, and a request that names no EHR all get one answer, 404 of type trc-patient-mismatch whose detail opens with the service’s *_NOT_FOUND code (ERROR_PS_NOT_FOUND, ERROR_EP_NOT_FOUND or ERROR_ORCD_NOT_FOUND), which the contact point answers as “No Data”. Each is recorded as a refused-trc-patient-mismatch security event, once per request and never summarised (eHDSI XCA Profile 8.0.1 §4.2.2).
  • Where the agreement sets discard, the person may discard a dispensation of a template its writes lists, as a logical delete (DELETE /ehr/{ehr_id}/composition/{preceding_version_uid}), within discard_window of its first commit (MyHealth@EU Requirements Catalogue 10.0.0, requirement 07.04). The eHDSI point of care is a name only, so the dispensation’s EVENT_CONTEXT.health_care_facility must carry every identifier the discarding token names its point of care by: the provider.healthcare_provider_identifier under the provider.issuing_authority_name, and the same identifier under the issuer urn:oasis:names:tc:xspa:1.0:subject:organization-id, the HCPO’s organization-id (eHDSI SAML Profile 10.0.0 §2.3). Any other discard is refused with 403.
  • The committer of a contact point’s caller names the professional by the HP Identity Assertion’s NameID: a DV_IDENTIFIER with the assertion’s issuer (ehdsi.assertion.issuer, NCP-B) as issuer, the NameID (ehdsi.professional.hp_identifier) as id, and hp_identifier:<NameID format> as type, such as hp_identifier:urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:X509SubjectName, because one string under two formats names two identifiers (eHDSI SAML Profile 10.0.0 §2.1). The token’s iss and sub follow with type oauth2, as on a domestic route. A discard is a logical delete under the same committer.
  • A contact point’s COMPOSITION carries, in EVENT_CONTEXT.health_care_facility.identifiers, the provider’s identifier under provider.issuing_authority_name and, as a second DV_IDENTIFIER, the HCPO’s organization-id under the issuer urn:oasis:names:tc:xspa:1.0:subject:organization-id. A commit without the second is refused with 422; the server writes neither.
  • A token that carries permissions (ehdsi.professional.permissions) records a dispensation and discards one only with PPD-046 among them, as the code or its urn:oasis:names:tc:xspa:1.0:subject:hl7:permission: URN (eHDSI SAML Profile 10.0.0 §2.5); otherwise it is refused with 403.

The generic standards path

Every walk-through on this page configures the same three things: an issuer of kind persons that signs your professionals’ access tokens, the [[auth.party]] table their logins are bound through, and a SCIM client that provisions their PERSONs. Configure them first against a standards-only authorization server; the vendor sections after this one are the same configuration through a preset (entra, keycloak, okta), each listing the preset’s deviations with their sources. Every preset key can be set on the issuer table, which wins over the preset.

  1. The issuer. The rfc9068 profile is the default: an RFC 9068 access token with typ at+jwt, the client in client_id and the scopes in scope.

    [[auth.issuer]]
issuer = "https://as.example.com"
kind = "persons"
audience = ["ferroehr"]
first_party_clients = ["ferroehr-viewer"]

  2. The binding, on sub. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.7 names iss with sub as the only stable identifier of an end-user, so the rfc9068 profile binds on sub. The [[auth.party]] table names the identifier the key is matched against:

    [[auth.party]]
issuer = "https://as.example.com"
identifier_issuer = "urn:example:staff-login"
identifier_type = "uuid"

    An email, phone_number, preferred_username or name is never a key.

  3. The SCIM client. Your authorization server issues the provisioning client an access token by the client credentials grant (RFC 6749 §4.4), or in exchange for a client assertion (RFC 7523 §2.2). Declare the authorization server as an issuer of kind machines, and the client in [[auth.scim.client]] with the binding_issuer of step 2. The SCIM client sends the key as urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:ferrohealth:2.0:User:loginIdentifier (RFC 7644).

  4. An onward caller. A service that calls FerroEHR for a signed-in professional, such as FerroBRIDGE, exchanges the professional’s token at the authorization server by RFC 8693 token exchange. List the service in the issuer’s delegates ({ client = "<its client id>" }, or { sub } for an RFC 8693 actor): the request is bound to the professional, and the access record names the service.

Who is the committer shows what the server records for each of these callers.

Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD)

Entra ID exposes a standards-compliant OIDC issuer per tenant.

  1. Register an application (Entra admin center → App registrations). Note the Directory (tenant) ID and the Application (client) ID.

  2. Define app roles (App registration → App roles): create roles named after the CDR roles you use (for example USER, CLINICAL, ADMIN) and assign users/groups to them (Enterprise applications → your app → Users and groups). Entra puts assigned app roles in the token’s roles claim.

  3. Expose an audience: either use the client ID as the audience or add an Application ID URI (for example api://ferroehr).

  4. Point the CDR at the tenant issuer and mine the roles claim:

    export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUER=https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__KIND=persons
# Entra ID mints no RFC 9068 tokens (`typ` JWT, the scopes in `scp`), which
# the `entra` profile reads.
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__PROFILE=entra
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCE=api://ferroehr
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTS=<the client id of your app>
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ROLE_CLAIMS=roles
# Its roles may grant the administrator role.
export FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ROLE_ISSUERS=https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0

  5. Verify: request a token for the app (any OAuth2 client credential or auth-code flow) and call the API. Read the status codes as a diagnostic:

    StatusWhat it tells you
    200-familyroles arrived and the operation was permitted
    401no credential, or one the server rejected (the body deliberately never says which)
    403the token is valid but carries no role or SMART on openEHR scope the operation needs: a clinical call needs a matching scope and, unless every SMART on openEHR scope it holds is a system/ scope, at least one role, an admin call needs the admin role and the product scope
    400the Authorization header itself is malformed; no credential was ever read
    503the CDR could not read your issuer’s key set again, so the token was never judged: check network egress, not the token

Important

A role must arrive in a role claim, not in scope. The OAuth2 scope claim grants a client delegated authority (RFC 6749 §3.3) and says nothing about the subject’s roles, so it is not a role source. If your IdP is configured to put role names in scope, map them into roles (or another entry of ROLE_CLAIMS) instead.

Tip

Group-based deployments can emit the groups claim instead and list it in ROLE_CLAIMS, but group claims arrive as object IDs unless you configure group names, so app roles usually read better in policy.

Warning

Two configuration mistakes are boot errors rather than runtime surprises, so you will find them the first time you start the server: an issuer that is not an https URL with no query or fragment, and an empty audience list. Both are deliberate: the second is what stops this server accepting a token minted for a different service. An issuer the server cannot reach at boot refuses the start too.

Binding and provisioning with the entra preset

The entra preset is the generic path with Entra ID’s deviations, each from Microsoft’s Access token claims reference (claims) or Optional claims reference (optional):

Preset keyValueSource
person_keyoidclaims, oid: “The immutable identifier for the requestor”; sub is a pairwise value per application and never a key
tenant_claimtidclaims, tid
token_types["JWT"]claims, header typ “always JWT”
scope_claim, app_only_scope_claimscp (string), roles (array)claims, scp and roles
client_claims["azp"]claims, azp
app_onlyidtyp = "app", and no scpoptional, idtyp; claims, scp “Only included for user tokens”
guestan idp other than the issuer, or acct = 1claims, idp; optional, acct
expectver = "2.0"claims, ver
user_claims["acct"]optional, acct, emitted only when the registration asks for it
unstable_claimsupn, unique_nameclaims, unique_name; optional, upn

Binding on oid is FerroEHR’s choice on Microsoft’s “immutable identifier” wording. For it to work, the app registration of FerroEHR’s API, and of every service such as FerroBRIDGE that calls it, needs:

  • the optional claims acct (the guest marker: the preset requires it on every user token, so a registration without it is refused at the first token, naming the claim), idtyp (the app-only marker), given_name and family_name, and the profile scope that oid needs;
  • "requestedAccessTokenVersion": 2 in the manifest’s api attribute (Understand the app manifest): FerroEHR accepts v2.0 tokens only, and a null value defaults to version 1.

Cross-tenant synchronisation and converted guests: a member-type user of another tenant carries acct = 0, but an idp naming their home tenant. The preset treats them as a guest by idp, so they bind only where the [[auth.party]] table sets guests = true, and never as staff.

A person in more groups than fit in a token (the groups overage: “150 for SAML tokens, 200 for JWT tokens”, claims) carries no groups claim, and the login is refused with 403 (refused-groups-unavailable) unless the issuer sets adapter = "idp-entra" with an [auth.idp.entra] table, which reads the groups from Microsoft Graph. Provision only the groups assigned to the application to stay under the limit.

Provisioning through SCIM. The non-gallery enterprise application, its Tenant URL https://<host>/scim/v2/ and the steps on FerroEHR’s side are in Provision from Microsoft Entra ID. On the Entra side:

  • Authentication. Use the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant against your own authorization server, or Workload Identity Federation, in which Entra presents a signed client assertion your authorization server exchanges. Never leave the Secret Token blank: Entra then sends its own test token, which every non-gallery application of the tenant receives.
  • Attribute mappings. Replace the tutorial’s mailNickname to externalId with objectId to externalId, because a mail nickname “may not be unique in the directory” (Develop a SCIM endpoint). Map objectId to urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:ferrohealth:2.0:User:loginIdentifier as well, and userPrincipalName to userName.
  • Matching precedence. Set externalId first and userName second.
  • Remove every other attribute the FerroEHR mapping does not carry: “Schema discovery isn’t currently supported on custom non-gallery SCIM application” (Develop a SCIM endpoint), so Entra cannot learn FerroEHR’s schema and sends what its defaults name.

AD FS (on-premises Active Directory)

AD FS 2016+ speaks OIDC. This is also the supported path for on-premises Active Directory in general: front AD with AD FS (or another OIDC-capable broker) rather than pointing anything at LDAP.

  1. Create an Application Group (AD FS Management → Application Groups → Web API template, or Server application + Web API for interactive clients). The Web API’s identifier becomes the token audience.

  2. Issue role claims: on the Web API’s Issuance Transform Rules, add a rule mapping AD group membership to the role claim (template: Send Group Membership as a Claim), one rule per CDR role.

  3. Point the CDR at the AD FS issuer and mine the role claim:

    export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUER=https://adfs.example.com/adfs
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__KIND=persons
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCE=ferroehr-api
# AD FS mints no RFC 9068 tokens: name the type and the claims its tokens carry.
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__TOKEN_TYPES=JWT
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__REQUIRED_CLAIMS=iss,sub,aud,exp
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTS=<the client id of your app>
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ROLE_CLAIMS=role
export FERROEHR__AUTHZ__RBAC__ROLE_ISSUERS=https://adfs.example.com/adfs

    Discovery works out of the box (https://adfs.example.com/adfs/.well-known/openid-configuration).

  4. Verify with the same status table as above: 401 without a token, 403 with a token that lacks the required role.

Note

AD FS emits a single string for one role and an array for several; the role-mining layer accepts both shapes on any configured claim path.

“We only have LDAP”

The CDR does not speak LDAP, by design: LDAP bind would put password handling back inside the CDR. Front the directory with an OIDC-capable broker and connect that instead:

  • Active Directory → AD FS (above) or Entra ID (if synced).
  • Generic LDAP → Keycloak with LDAP user federation (the Keycloak example then applies verbatim), or any other OIDC provider that can federate LDAP.

The broker owns the LDAP bind; the CDR sees only signed tokens.

Okta

The okta preset reads Okta’s access tokens (Okta, OpenID Connect & OAuth 2.0 API, the reserved claims of the access token):

Preset keyValueSource
person_keyuiduid: “A unique identifier for the user”
client_claims["cid"]cid: “Client ID of the client that requested the access token”
scope_claimscp (array)scp: “Array of scopes that are granted to this access token”
app_onlyno uiduid “isn’t included in the access token if there is no user bound to it”
token_typesnonethe page names no typ, so an okta issuer fails to load until you set token_types to what your Okta server writes
 
[[auth.issuer]]
issuer = "https://example.okta.com/oauth2/default"
kind = "persons"
profile = "okta"
token_types = ["<the typ header your server writes>"]
audience = ["api://ferroehr"]
first_party_clients = ["<the viewer's client id>"]

Read the typ header of one of your server’s access tokens and set it in token_types; the preset deliberately names none.

Keycloak

The keycloak preset reads Keycloak 26.8 access tokens: azp as the client, scope as a string, typ JWT (confirm it against your own server), and no app-only marker until you list your service accounts. Configure a realm for binding as follows.

  1. Two realms. An issuer has one kind, so professionals sign in at one realm (kind = "persons") and patients at another (kind = "patients").

  2. The binding on sub. Keycloak’s sub is the user id, which no user can change. A user-profile attribute can be the key instead only when its Who can edit permission is Admin ("permissions": { "edit": ["admin"] }, Server Administration Guide, Managing user attributes).

  3. Service accounts. “A client’s service account is a user account with username service-account-CLIENT_ID”, so its sub is a user id. List every service account of the realm by its sub in the issuer’s app_only; the empty list refuses the issuer at load. On a realm with just-in-time creation an unlisted service account would be read as a person, so the list must be complete.

    [[auth.issuer]]
issuer = "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/staff"
kind = "persons"
profile = "keycloak"
audience = ["ferroehr"]
first_party_clients = ["ferroehr-viewer"]
app_only = [{ subjects = ["<the sub of service-account-lab>"] }]

  4. The audience for an onward caller. Keycloak’s standard token exchange requires “the requester client set as an audience in the aud claim” of the subject token (Securing applications, token exchange). Add an audience mapper to the client scope your professionals’ tokens carry that puts the bridge’s or gateway’s client in aud, and let the onward caller name FerroEHR’s client id in the audience parameter. List the onward client in delegates.

  5. No impersonation on a binding realm. “Any user with the impersonation role in the realm can impersonate a user” (Impersonating users). Check that no user or group holds the realm impersonation role, or the fine-grained admin permission impersonate, and that no client holds the legacy token exchange’s impersonation permission; disable the legacy token exchange. Where an administrator must keep impersonation, add the built-in user session note mappers IMPERSONATOR_ID and IMPERSONATOR_USERNAME to the inbound client scope and set impersonation_marker = "impersonator", so every impersonation is refused. Whether Keycloak 26.8 adds those mappers by default is not verified here; check the client scope. Keycloak 26.8 also writes an RFC 8693 act claim into every impersonation token, so an impersonator your delegates does not list is refused even without the marker (Who the caller is).

  6. Realm hardening. On a binding or just-in-time realm: no self-registration, no social or other brokered identity provider without an explicit allow-list, and no automatic account linking (the first login flow’s “automatically set existing user”, or linking by email). Each of them would let a person choose which account, and so which PERSON, a login reaches.

  7. SCIM. Keycloak 26.8 promotes its SCIM API to supported, as a service provider for its own realm’s users and groups (release notes, SCIM API (supported)). It provisions nothing outbound, so it cannot create FerroEHR’s PERSONs or GROUPs: a deployment needs an upstream SCIM client, such as its identity governance or HR system, or just-in-time creation. Enabling Keycloak’s own SCIM adds a second SCIM endpoint to the deployment, which FerroEHR does not read.

A SAML identity provider through Keycloak or Entra ID

FerroEHR never sees SAML. It is an OAuth 2.0 resource server and validates only access tokens, so a SAML 2.0 identity provider reaches it through an authorization server that brokers it:

  • Keycloak brokers it by Web Browser SSO (OASIS SAML V2.0 Profiles §4.1) as the service provider, and issues its own OpenID Connect tokens after the login. Set the identity provider’s Principal Type to the Subject NameID with the persistent format (urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:nameid-format:persistent, Keycloak’s default NameID Policy Format) or to an immutable attribute, so the brokered user’s Keycloak sub stays the same from login to login. Keycloak refuses a Subject NameID principal with the transient format. Map the name attributes to given_name, family_name and name for just-in-time creation, and the group attribute to the group claim.
  • Entra ID federates the SAML identity provider for its tenant, and the entra preset reads the tokens it issues as above.

Never bind on email, phone_number, preferred_username, name, upn or unique_name, whatever the SAML assertion maps them from (OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.7).

Just-in-time creation

An issuer can let a professional with no party work at their first login: FerroEHR then creates a provisional PERSON from the access token and binds the login to it, as the configuration reference describes. It is off by default. What each identity provider must do for it:

  • Put the name claims in the access token. FerroEHR reads the person’s data from the access token only (RFC 9068 §2.2.2 lets an authorization server include resource owner attributes there), never from an ID token or the userinfo endpoint. A generic issuer emits the OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.1 claims your mapped attributes name (name, given_name, family_name).
  • Microsoft Entra ID (the entra preset): add the optional claims given_name and family_name to the access token of your app registration and request the profile scope: Entra documents both as v2.0 optional claims that “Requires the profile scope” (Microsoft identity platform, Optional claims reference). Admit logins by group (admit_groups, the object ids in groups) or by the idp claim, which “records the identity provider that authenticated the subject of the token” and differs from the issuer for a guest (Access token claims reference). The key is the object id oid, never upn or email, which Entra calls mutable.
  • Keycloak (the keycloak preset): the built-in profile client scope maps the name claims; check that its mappers add them to the access token. Make the name attributes administrator-controlled as the key is: in the realm’s user profile, set the attribute’s Who can edit permission to Admin only ("permissions": { "edit": ["admin"] } in the JSON editor), which Keycloak defines as writable only from the administrative context (Server Administration Guide, Managing user attributes, Permission). A professional who could edit their own name could change what their first login writes.

The userName comes from user_name_claim, or the key when it is unset, and never from a claim the user can change. SCIM completes a provisional PERSON later: a client whose binding_issuer is the issuer’s identifier_issuer finds it by userName, sets the externalId, and a complete PUT makes it complete.

Serving SMART apps

If your IdP is also the authorization server for SMART App Launch apps, the same [auth] issuer does double duty: the CDR validates the tokens those apps come back with, and the discovery document it serves is built from that issuer’s metadata, so the server it advertises to apps is the one it accepts tokens from. See SMART App Launch.

SMART App Launch

FerroEHR is the resource server of a SMART on openEHR platform: a clinical app is launched with an OAuth 2.0 access token from your authorization server (Keycloak or any standards-compliant identity provider), and the CDR checks the token, enforces the SMART on openEHR scopes it carries, and binds a patient/ grant to the EHR of the launch context. FerroEHR never issues tokens, registers clients, or serves the OAuth 2.0 endpoints itself; those remain your authorization server’s job. Token checking and scope enforcement run on ferrohealth-smart, the crate every FerroHEALTH product shares.

  • Scopes are enforced on every route
  • The scope grammar
  • What each route requires
  • Launch context: binding to one EHR
  • The discovery document
  • Configuration keys

Scopes are enforced on every route

Whenever [auth] is on, every route carries a SMART on openEHR requirement, and a credential whose scopes do not meet it is refused with 403 and the insufficient_scope challenge (RFC 6750 §3.1). There is no switch: a route the table does not know is refused too, so a route can never answer to a token that carries no grant for it. A bearer token’s scopes come from its scope claim; a Basic user’s from its scopes in [[auth.basic.users]]. With authentication off nothing is checked.

The scopes and the RBAC and ABAC layers are all checked: SMART only narrows, and never lets through what a role or a policy refuses (see Security).

The scope grammar

SMART on openEHR resource scopes have the form <compartment>/<resource>.<permissions>:

  • Compartment: patient (the launch context’s EHR only), user (what the user may see), or system (a backend service, no user).
  • Resource: one of three families, composition-<template-id>, template-<template-id>, or aql-<stored-query-name>.
  • Permissions: any combination of c create, r read, u update, d delete, s search/execute, in any order (.crud, .rs, .sr).

Resource ids accept wildcards: * matches within one ::-delimited namespace segment, ** matches across namespaces, and a bare * or ** matches every id. Every other character, :: and . included, is literal. The permission tail is split at the last dot, so template ids and query names keep their internal dots and versions.

ScopeGrants
user/composition-*.crudCreate, read, update, and delete any composition, and the EHR’s other data.
user/composition-MyHospital::*.rRead compositions of any template in the MyHospital namespace (not sub-namespaces).
user/template-*.crudsFull access to template definitions.
user/aql-*.sRun any query.
patient/composition-*.rRead the compositions of the launch context’s EHR only.
system/aql-org.openehr::bloodpressure.v1.sA backend service may run that one stored query.

The FHIR v1 suffixes (.read, .write) are not part of this grammar. A token may carry SMART on FHIR scopes beside these; they grant nothing on an openEHR route.

What each route requires

RoutesRequirement
COMPOSITION and versioned-composition operationscomposition-<template> with the operation’s permission, the template read from the body or the stored version
EHR, EHR_STATUS, DIRECTORY, CONTRIBUTION, the item tags, the EHR extract (/message)composition- with the operation’s permission over every template: they are the EHR’s data, and the draft names no family of their own
operational templates, archetypes and artefactstemplate-<template> with the operation’s permission, the template from the {template_id} path parameter
query executionaql-<query> with s, the query from the {qualified_query_name} path parameter
stored-query definitionsaql-<query> with the operation’s permission
the DEMOGRAPHIC APIa client listed in [auth.smart] demographic_clients, or the [auth] product_scope: no SMART on openEHR scope covers demographic data
the ADMIN APIthe [auth] product_scope
the terminology API, the ITI-81 audit retrievalan authenticated caller

Note

An unresolved resource id matches only a bare wildcard. A template upload or list, an ad-hoc query and an EHR-level operation name no template or query, so only a scope on every resource (* or **) covers them. Grant those scopes deliberately.

A system/aql-* grant “would grant access to all registered and ad-hoc AQL queries system-wide” (master08 §Resource Scopes), so it counts only for a backend client listed in [auth.smart] backend_clients.

Launch context: binding to one EHR

When an app is launched for a patient, your authorization server puts the openEHR EHR id of the launch context in the token’s ehrId claim (master07 §Context Selection). A patient/ grant then reaches that one EHR:

  • it counts only for an issuer listed in [auth.smart] patient_issuers, because an ehrId names an EHR of the platform that issued it;
  • an EHR route whose {ehr_id} names another EHR is refused, and so is an operation that names no EHR, such as creating an EHR;
  • a query runs only within the launch context’s EHR, named by its single-EHR ehr_id parameter or openehr-ehr-id header; a query naming no EHR, or another one, is refused;
  • it reaches EHR data alone, never a template definition;
  • a write under a grant of patient/ scopes alone is the person’s own: it is marked as inserted by the person and may not alter a version a professional committed (EHDS Art. 5).

user/ and system/ grants carry no such binding, and when a user/ grant covers the same operation the wider grant wins.

A system/ grant belongs to a backend client acting for no person. A token its issuer’s profile marks app-only holds system/ grants alone: one that carries a user/ or patient/ scope is refused with 403, because no person stands behind it. Such a client commits only as a declared [[authz.system_client]] (Who the caller is).

The discovery document

With [auth.smart] discovery = true, the server serves the SMART configuration document, unauthenticated, at:

GET /ferroehr/rest/.well-known/smart-configuration

(relative to the REST root, or to [auth.smart] platform_base_url when set). The document is built from the metadata of one [auth] issuer, read at boot: the first introspected issuer, else the issuer [auth.smart] issuer_metadata_file names, else the first issuer whose metadata is read from it, else the first issuer. It carries the authorization, token, registration, introspection and revocation endpoints, the grant types and client authentication methods it supports, and its jwks_uri. It therefore needs an issuer whose metadata names a token_endpoint, which the document requires (SMART App Launch 2.2.0, Conformance, §Metadata). An issuer read from a jwks_file has no metadata of its own: [auth.smart] issuer_metadata_file names a JSON file with its RFC 8414 §2 metadata, which must name an [auth] issuer read from a jwks_file and hold every endpoint to https (a loopback host excepted). The issuer it names may stand anywhere in the list, beside a Basic users’ issuer listed first. Without it, enabled = true refuses the start.

export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__ISSUER=https://as.example/realms/ferroehr
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__KIND=persons
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__AUDIENCE=ferroehr-api
export FERROEHR__AUTH__ISSUER__0__FIRST_PARTY_CLIENTS=my-smart-app
export FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__DISCOVERY=true
# The external origin absolute service URLs are built from; required.
export FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://cdr.example.com

A document looks like:

{
  "jwks_uri": "https://as.example/realms/ferroehr/certs",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://as.example/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://as.example/token",
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "private_key_jwt"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "client_credentials"],
  "scopes_supported": [
    "openid", "profile", "launch",
    "user/composition-*.cruds", "user/template-*.cruds", "user/aql-*.cruds",
    "system/composition-*.cruds", "system/template-*.cruds", "system/aql-*.cruds"
  ],
  "services": {
    "org.openehr.rest": {
      "baseUrl": "https://cdr.example.com/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1",
      "description": "The openEHR REST API baseUrl"
    }
  },
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "capabilities": [
    "permission-user", "client-confidential-symmetric",
    "client-confidential-asymmetric", "launch-standalone",
    "context-openehr-ehr", "openehr-permission-v1"
  ]
}
  • services names the openEHR REST service; org.fhir.rest is never advertised, because FerroEHR serves no FHIR API for clinical data. Each baseUrl is absolute, built by prefixing the CDR’s own base path with public_base_url, which is why that key is required.
  • capabilities carries what the server enforces: context-openehr-ehr and openehr-permission-v1 always, permission-user, and permission-patient only when patient_issuers binds an issuer; the client types and launch modes the issuer supports; sso-openid-connect, with the issuer member it requires, when the issuer’s metadata lists the openid scope; context-openehr-episode when episode_launch is on; and your [auth] capabilities, where launch-base64-json goes if your apps read it.
  • grant_types_supported names only authorization_code and client_credentials, whatever else the issuer advertises: the implicit and password grants are deprecated (master06 §Deprecated Flows).
  • code_challenge_methods_supported always carries S256 and never plain.
  • scopes_supported lists [auth] scopes_supported when set, otherwise the scopes the route table honours above, with the patient/ ones only when an issuer is bound. It never copies the issuer’s own list: “the server SHALL support all scopes listed here”.

With enabled = false the path is not mounted at all (404).

Configuration keys

The keys live in [auth] and [auth.smart]; see the configuration reference.

KeyDefaultMeaning
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__DISCOVERYfalseServe the discovery document.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__PUBLIC_BASE_URLunset (required when enabled)The external origin absolute services.*.baseUrl values are built from, e.g. https://cdr.example.com.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__PLATFORM_BASE_URLunsetBase the discovery document hangs off. Unset = the REST root (/ferroehr/rest). A leading path is honoured (/gateway/v1 → /gateway/v1/.well-known/smart-configuration).
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__BACKEND_CLIENTS[]The client_ids a system/aql-* grant counts for.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__PATIENT_ISSUERS[]The issuers whose patient/ grants count.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__DEMOGRAPHIC_CLIENTS[]The client_ids that reach the DEMOGRAPHIC API.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SMART__EPISODE_LAUNCHfalseAdvertise and accept episode launch context (experimental; advisory only, no episode filtering).
FERROEHR__AUTH__PRODUCT_SCOPE__ferroehr.platformThe scope that admits the ADMIN API and the DEMOGRAPHIC API.
FERROEHR__AUTH__CAPABILITIES[]Capabilities the discovery document adds.
FERROEHR__AUTH__SCOPES_SUPPORTED[]The scopes the discovery document lists.

Note

Episode context is experimental: enabling it advertises the capability and accepts launch/episode, but the server applies no episode-scoped filtering: openEHR has no first-class episode resource yet.

Audit trail (IHE ATNA)

FerroEHR keeps a full security audit trail of API access (who did what to which resource, with what outcome, from where, and when) following the IHE ATNA (Audit Trail and Node Authentication) profile, the standard the openEHR reference text points at (its platform service description names a system log “IHE ATNA-compliant”). It is on by default: every deployment records a queryable audit trail with zero external dependencies.

Warning

Two postures are legitimate to run and wrong to run silently, so the server says them at warn on boot (structured field posture = "audit"), in the audit_sender readiness indicator and on /management/info: auditing off ([audit] enabled = false) writes no access log and leaves the EHDS logging component off, and the shipped default fail_mode = "open" drops a record the audit queue cannot take while the request succeeds, so an access under load can go unrecorded. A deployment that must never serve an unrecorded access sets fail_mode = "closed", which answers 503 and Retry-After instead. A deployment declaring deployment.profile = "production" refuses to start with auditing off.
