The trail is orthogonal to openEHR’s own CONTRIBUTION/AUDIT_DETAILS change-control audit (which the server always writes in the same transaction as every version change): openEHR audit records what a version says about its own authorship; ATNA records security surveillance of access, including reads and rejected attempts.

The record, in both official formats

Every audited operation produces one record, rendered in the two formats the IHE standards define. Both are written by the shared audit crates of the FerroHEALTH products (FerroAUDIT): ehds-logging writes the EHDS access record, and ihe-atna writes the BALP AuditEvent and the DICOM audit message and sends them. FerroEHR decides which accesses are logged, what each record says and where it is stored.

  • FHIR R4 AuditEvent following the IHE BALP 1.1.4 (Basic Audit Log Patterns) content profiles: the modern RESTful-ATNA form and the canonical stored form. An access to clinical content is the EHDS access record: ehds-logging writes it on the RESTful pattern of its action, with the patient behind the EHR as the patient entity (PatientRead, PatientCreate and the other Patient* claims), the categories, the retention, the security labels and the origins. Every other record (an authentication, a template or party operation, a refused access) is a BALP exchange FerroEHR fills directly. The person is the agent:user slice, named by the token’s issuer and subject, with the token’s jti as its policy, the caller’s roles as its role and the client application as an agent of its own (BALP 1.1.4 §3:5.7.5.4); a Basic user is named by the account alone, with no issuer and no client. The ITS-REST operation id is a second subtype (urn:openehr:its-rest:operation). The object an access record reads, creates, updates or deletes is named by its openEHR object id as entity.what.identifier in the system urn:openehr:object-id, never as a what.reference, since it is no FHIR resource (FHIR R4 references.html §2.3.0.3). The outcome is stated in outcomeDesc, and source.type names an application server. Query executions carry the search expression.
  • DICOM Audit Message (DICOM PS3.15 §A.5 XML): the classic ATNA form, shipped as RFC 5424 syslog over RFC 5425 TLS per IHE ITI-20 when the syslog sink is enabled, with the optional EventOutcomeDescription, AuditSourceTypeCode (4, an application server) and each participant object’s ParticipantObjectDataLifeCycle. A record about a patient’s data names the patient (Patient Number) and, when it has one, its object as a System Object with the ID type URI (PS3.15 Tables A.5.1.2.2-1 and A.5.1.2.4-1), the same id the FHIR form names. Dedicated DICOM event ids are used throughout: Patient Record (110110), Query (110112), Export/Import (110106/110107, the EHR-Extract directions), User Authentication (110114, with the Login EventTypeCode 110122).

Both formats give the client and the server the same data-flow role: on a read the server is Source (DCM 110153) and the client Destination (110152), because the data moves from the server to the client (DICOM PS3.15 §A.5.2.7, the BALP Read profiles); on a create, an update and a query the client is Source (PS3.15 §A.5.3.20 for a query, the BALP Create, Update and Query profiles).

Every server operation is audited (an unrecognised extension operation fails closed to a generic audited class, so nothing is silently unaudited) and access refusals are always recorded: a 401, a 403, and the 400 a malformed Authorization header earns. A refusal is attributed to the caller only when one actually authenticated; an unattributable denial is recorded as unattributed rather than under a fabricated subject, so no audit record ever names an identity that did not authenticate.

Note

Successful-login records are suppressed by default ([audit] suppress_login_events = true). Set it to false to record them. Even then, a login record marks a genuine authentication event, not every authenticated request: it is emitted when credentials were actually verified: a Basic verified-credential-cache miss. A cache hit continues an established session, and a Bearer request authenticated out of band at your identity provider, so neither mints a per-request login record. Rejections are recorded regardless of this switch.

Reads are logged too, per record

A write leaves its own trail in openEHR’s contribution and audit chain. A read leaves nothing behind unless the server records it, and reads are what the access-logging rules are about: NEN 7513 requires per-access logging of who consulted which record and on whose authority, the Wabvpz gives the patient the right to know who consulted their record, and EHDS Art. 9 requires logging of access to electronic health data for primary use. No openEHR specification governs the read side, so this is FerroEHR’s own extension.

Every retrieval in the EHR, Query and Demographic APIs produces a record, and a test walks the generated route tables to prove it: a newly generated GET that emits nothing fails the build.

Each record additionally carries:

FieldWhat it holds
domainThe pseudonymisation domain read: ehr, demographic, linkage for a crossing that resolves a party or a subject to its EHRs, or system for an operation that touches no domain.
organisationThe organisation the caller acted for, read from the access token’s [authz.abac] organization_claim — the same claim the ABAC layer decides on, so no second setting can name a different one. The recording does not depend on that layer being switched on. A Basic-authenticated caller and an unconfigured claim both leave it empty.
purposeThe purpose of use the caller declared in the x-purpose-of-use header, when the deployment accepts it.
token_attributesThe purposes of use and the professional roles the access token states, each with its code system, for an issuer with an [[auth.attributes]] table (where the purpose comes from).
emergency_accesstrue when the declared purpose, or a purpose the token states, is one of [audit] emergency_purpose_codes: an emergency access (EHDS Art. 11(5)).
legal_basisThe basis the deployment processes under, from [audit] legal_basis.
result_countHow many records the operation served.
request_idThe x-request-id correlation id the response carried.

A query is the case a single record cannot describe. One AQL statement is one operation but potentially many disclosures, so it produces its own execute record plus one access record per EHR it served, each carrying that EHR’s served-row count. The served set is read off the rows the caller actually received rather than the rows the statement matched: a legal record of access must not name an EHR whose content was never disclosed. Two query shapes carry no per-EHR breakdown, because the shape makes it underivable — SELECT DISTINCT, where an extra column changes which rows are distinct, and an aggregate projection, where a per-row EHR is not valid SQL. Those record the statement and its row count.

NEN 7513 content, field by field

NEN 7513 §5 lists what a logged event has to contain. This is where each item lives in the record:

NEN 7513 asks forFerroEHR records it as
The identity of the person who accessed the recordprincipal — the authenticated Basic username or OAuth sub; an unattributable denial is recorded as unattributed, never under a fabricated identity. With [authz.professional] configured, professional_id names the natural person when the token names a client application
The identity of the patient whose record was accessedpatient_id — the resolved EHR subject, which under the pseudonymisation boundary is an opaque pseudonym
Which record, or which part of itresource_class + resource_id: the version uid, party uid or EHR id the operation touched
The date and timerecorded_at, the event time; stored_at is when the row was persisted
The kind of actionaction (DICOM C/R/U/D/E) plus operation, the released ITS-REST operation id. It equals the served OpenAPI operationId except for the demographic CONTRIBUTION pair, served as demographic_contribution_create and demographic_contribution_get because the released contribution_create and contribution_get also name the EHR operations and one document needs unique ids
Whether it succeededoutcome, the DICOM outcome indicator (0 success, 4 minor, 8 serious, 12 major)
Under which role or authorityroles — the roles the caller held at access time (the RFC 9068 §2.2.3.1 claim carriers for a bearer, the user definition for Basic), rendered as FHIR agent.role on the requestor and as a RoleIDCode per role on the DICOM requesting participant
On whose authority, and whypurpose and legal_basis, and permit, the identifier of the data permit a secondary-use caller declares it acts under (Secondary use)
Which system, and from whereAuditSourceID and the source participant’s network address (client_ip): the connection’s peer, or the client a peer in [server] trusted_proxies names in its forwarded_header (Server)
Who the person is in the demographic store, and for whom they actbinding and the fields beside it (the binding outcome): party (the bound PERSON), party_groups, provider, representation for a representative, and acting_mode (person, delegated, external or system); for a verified external accessor external_fields and agreement stand in for the party, and an organisation record names the organisation. The FHIR AuditEvent, the DICOM message and the syslog feed carry each in the ehds-accessor and ehds-relayed entities (the binding fields in the renderings)

Two of these are the deployment’s to supply. purpose is only as meaningful as the vocabulary you agree with your callers: set [audit] purpose_codes to that vocabulary and a code outside it is recorded as absent rather than as free text that reads at review time like an established purpose. legal_basis is a deployment-level fact and is recorded on every access once you set it.

Mapping the recorded fields onto your own retention schedule and review process stays yours: the software records the events and serves them back, and no supplier document discharges the obligation to review them.

The EHDS logging elements, mapped

Annex II 3.2 of Regulation (EU) 2025/327 lists five things the European logging software component must record “on every access event or group of events”. This is where each one lands, or does not. The elements were read from the published text on 2026-09-10; the regulation is the authority and the wording below is a paraphrase.

Annex II 3.2Access-event fieldDICOM PS3.15FHIR AuditEventState
(a) the healthcare provider or other individuals having accessedorganisation— (no such attribute)an agent whose who is a logical reference to an OrganizationRecorded
(b) the specific natural person or persons having accessedprincipal (+ token_id, client_ip), and professional_id + acting_mode for a caller its issuer classifies as a person or a delegateActiveParticipant/@UserID (the professional; a client application acting for one is a second, non-requesting participant; the token subject is @AlternativeUserID when it differs)the agent:user slice, who the token’s issuer and subject, the professional’s identifier as its ihe-otherId, and the client application as an agent of its own (BALP 1.1.4 §3:5.7.5.4)Recorded
(c) the categories of data accessedcategories + category_basis + category_evidence + category_map_digest, classified by ehds-logging through the [audit.categories] map (beside resource_class, domain and result_count)none (no such element)the entity named ehds-categories, with one ehds-category detail per category and its basis, each id the classification read and the map digest; each category is also a meta.security labelRecorded
(d) the time and date of accessrecorded_atEventIdentification/@EventDateTimerecordedRecorded
(e) the origin or origins of dataorigins + origin_count (the FEEDER_AUDIT originating systems of the served version bodies, or the server that created them, derived at commit onto version.origins)— (no such element)one entity named origin per origin, its system-id detail the originating systemRecorded

Read (a) beside (b): they are both about the accessing side, and the pair distinguishes the organisation on whose behalf the access happened from the natural person who made it. The principal answers (b); the organisation column answers (a), resolved from the same access-token claim the ABAC layer reads ([authz.abac] organization_claim) rather than from a second setting that could name a different claim. Sharing the setting is not sharing the switch: the organisation is recorded whether or not the ABAC gate is enabled, because the trail describes a caller rather than deciding anything about them. The FHIR rendering carries it as an agent of its own, a logical reference to an Organization, with no participation code, because AuditEvent.agent.type is optional and inventing a code would be worse than omitting one. The DICOM rendering carries nothing: PS3.15 §A.5 defines no organisation attribute on ActiveParticipant, and AuditEnterpriseSiteID is the reporting node’s own site rather than the caller’s organisation. Where no claim is configured or the caller authenticated with Basic, the field stays empty rather than being guessed.

Element (b) asks for a natural person, and a bearer token can name a client application instead. Each issuer’s kind and profile classify the caller, so every record says which it was and who stood behind it:

FieldMeaningDICOM PS3.15FHIR AuditEvent
acting_modeperson when the token names a natural person, client when it names a client applicationthe participant split belowthe agent split below
professional_idthe natural person: the person’s own claim, or the professional a client token acts forActiveParticipant/@UserID of the requesting participantthe ihe-otherId extension of the agent:user, typed NPI
principalthe token subject, as before: the client application in client modea second ActiveParticipant with UserIsRequestor="false" and the network address; @AlternativeUserID in person mode when it differs from the professionalagent:user who.identifier, with the issuer as its system; the acting mode is its first role
assurance_levelthe eIDAS level (low, substantial, high) the token’s assurance claim maps to under [authz.assurance]none (no such attribute)the ihe-assuranceLevel extension of the agent:user
assurance_valuethe raw claim value the level was read from, usually acrnonenone

PS3.15 §A.5 gives ActiveParticipant no assurance attribute, so the DICOM message and the syslog feed carry no level. The FHIR export carries the level as the BALP ihe-assuranceLevel extension (BALP 1.1.4 §3:5.7.5.4) and never the raw claim value, which lives in the local store’s column only. The tamper-evidence digest covers both columns, like every other column of the record (see Tamper evidence for records written before the digest was versioned).

For a system caller the mode and the professional stay empty and (b) is answered by principal, which names the client application. Without [authz.assurance] levels the level stays empty; the raw value is still recorded when the token carries the claim. A Basic credential records none of the four.

Element (c) asks for the priority category of the data, in the sense of Art. 14(1): patient summaries, electronic prescriptions, electronic dispensations, medical imaging, medical test results and discharge reports, plus any category a Member State adds in national law. AQL selects archetypes and templates, never categories, and no openEHR specification maps the one onto the other, so the deployment declares the mapping in [audit.categories]: a template id, or failing that the root archetype id, maps to a set of categories (a priority category by its code in HL7 Europe’s EEHRxFDocumentPriorityCategoryCS, such as Patient-Summaries or Laboratory-Reports, a national category as its <system>|<code>), or to none for content that holds no data of any category. While you declare no template and no archetype, the map FerroEHR ships applies: the published CKM templates and COMPOSITION archetypes whose data sit in one priority category (the shipped map). Your own map replaces it, and ehds-logging classifies each access through the map in force.

Each record is classified when the access happens, from what it served or wrote, and never at commit, because the map is your reading of your templates and can change:

  • a composition read or write is classified by the version’s template id, then by its root archetype id;
  • an AQL execution is classified by the template and root archetype ids of the versions its result page came from; where the answer carries no version (a DISTINCT or aggregate projection, or zero rows) by the query’s positive archetype and template constraints, so an operand under NOT CONTAINS or a predicate under NOT never counts. Every id the query constrains to must be mapped, and every content operand bound to an id, or the record is unclassified beside what did map. Each per-EHR record of a query carries the categories that EHR disclosed;
  • a logical delete writes no content, so it is classified by the version it deleted; a VERSIONED_COMPOSITION read by the composition it holds;
  • a CONTRIBUTION read, with or without Prefer: resolve_refs, is classified by the versions the contribution committed, a deleted version again by the version it deleted;
  • an EHR Extract export is classified by every version it carried, and an Extract import by the newest content of every versioned object it landed;
  • EHR, EHR_STATUS, EHR_ACCESS, the directory, item tags and revision histories are recorded as none, by resource kind.

An access the map cannot classify is recorded unclassified, with the template and archetype ids as evidence, and is never refused; the FHIR record says why (unmapped, unbound, named-nothing). A stored category is its <system>|<code> token. category_basis says what the classification was read from (returned, written, queried or resource-kind; records written before 5.3.2 carry template, archetype or query and the earlier spellings), and category_map_digest names the map that produced it, so a later map never rereads an old record. The map’s digest is also on the boot line and on GET /management/info under audit.category_map. The classification stays in the access log: it is never written to the request log, a span or a metric label. The DICOM rendering has no element for it (PS3.15 §A.5), so it travels in the local store and the FHIR export only.

Records in the demographic domain carry no classification, because no priority category lives there.

Element (e) asks where the DATA came from, which is not where the request came from. openEHR models that provenance as FEEDER_AUDIT on the content itself, so every committed version records the distinct set of FEEDER_AUDIT.originating_system_audit.system_id values found in its body, or this server’s own system id when it carries none. A composition, status or folder read then records the origins of the version it served, and an AQL execution the union over the version rows its result page came from. The record carries the true distinct count beside a set capped at 32, so a page drawing on more origins than that says how many rather than looking complete. A version committed before the column existed is assessed when it is read.

One further element, adjacent to the five: the declared purpose of use reaches one export of the two, and only one of them could carry it. It is stored on the record, served by ITI-81, and rendered as agent.purposeOfUse on the requesting person’s agent in the FHIR export. A declared code carries no system: the vocabulary is the one you agree with your callers in [audit] purpose_codes, which has no published code system URI, and attributing the code to a system it does not come from would misdescribe it. A purpose the access token states keeps the system the token gives it. The DICOM Audit Message schema of PS3.15 §A.5 defines no purpose element at all — EventIdentification, ActiveParticipant, AuditSourceIdentification and ParticipantObjectIdentification, and none of them carries one — so on that side it is a limit of the format, not something this code withholds.

Where the purpose of use comes from

The purpose of use reaches the record from two places:

  • The access token. An issuer with an [[auth.attributes]] table (mapping = "iua") states its professionals’ attributes in the token: the IHE IUA purpose_of_use and subject_role claims under extensions.ihe_iua (IHE ITI TF-2 §3.71.4.2.2.1.1), and with authorization_details_purposes the purpose_of_use of each RFC 9396 authorization_details entry. The record stores them in token_attributes, and both renderings write them with their code systems: the purposes at the requesting agent’s purposeOfUse, the roles at its role, beside the roles the caller held.
  • The [audit] purpose_header (x-purpose-of-use), which the caller sets. It works alone for an issuer without an [[auth.attributes]] table, as before.

The token is the authorization server’s statement, so it decides. A request whose header names a purpose the token, which states purposes, does not state is refused with 403, and the refusal is recorded as a failed authentication naming the caller and the token’s purposes. A header naming one of the token’s purposes is admitted and recorded with both. Which source wins is FerroEHR’s own design; no openEHR specification governs the purpose of use.

Note

Every row of this table is asserted by a test (app/ferroehr/tests/it/audit_ehds_mapping.rs), including the gaps: the tests that record an absence fail the day the field arrives, so the table and the code cannot drift apart in either direction.

The common specifications the regulation’s Article 36 provides for have not been adopted. When they are, this mapping is re-verified against them rather than assumed to still hold; see the EHDS readiness page.

The binding outcome

Every record of an authenticated request carries binding: how the caller was bound to a demographic party, or why the binding refused it. The committer the same request writes into a version is on Who is the committer. It answers Annex II 3.2(a) and (b) where the token’s subject alone does not. The columns beside it hold what each outcome needs:

bindingThe callerRecorded beside it
bounda person bound to a complete PERSONparty, party_groups, provider, guest for an admitted guest, representation for a representative, actor_chain for a delegated token
provisionala person bound to an incomplete PERSONparty, party_groups, provider
externala verified external person of a federation issuerexternal_fields, agreement, provider
organisationan organisation under an agreement with accessor = "organisation"external_fields, agreement (with its legal ground and access class, and for a chained request correlation_id and correlation_source), provider
systema client acting for nobodyprovider of its [[authz.system_client]], facilities of the compositions it committed
selfa patient token of a patients issuerthe principal
refused-*a refusal of the binding or of a caller kind: unbound, ambiguous, inactive, abandoned, deprovisioned, wrong-marker, representation-unrecorded, key-claim-missing, groups-unavailable, guest, external-incomplete, trc-patient-mismatch, trc-missing; and of a caller kind, system-personal-scope (a system caller holding a user/ or patient/ scope), no-agreement (no federation agreement admits the accessor) and scope-beyond-agreement (an external caller holding a scope its agreement does not read) and correlation-missing (a chained organisation request without an attested correlation id)party for a party refused for its state or marker, binding_detail for what else the refusal names (represented, the subject a representative asserted; claim, the name of the key claim a token lacked, never its value)

acting_mode is person, delegated for a person through a declared client or actor, external for a verified external accessor and system for a client acting for nobody (client remains on records written before). The FHIR AuditEvent writes each mode as the person’s agent.role. A record of a request with no authenticated caller carries no binding. The columns are in the chain digest: version 2 hashes them, version 3 adds token_attributes, a new record is version 3, and a record written before keeps verifying under its own version.

The binding fields in the renderings

Neither BALP 1.1.4 §3:5.7.5.4 nor DICOM PS3.15 §A.5 has an element for the binding fields beyond the bound person, so ehds-logging writes them as details of two entities it adds, and FerroEHR hands it every field. The FHIR AuditEvent carries each entity as an entity with its name and one detail per value. The DICOM message carries each as a ParticipantObjectIdentification of type 4 (Other) with the entity name as its ParticipantObjectName and one ParticipantObjectDetail per value (RESTful ATNA Rev. 3.6 Table 3.20.4.2.2.1-1), and the ITI-20 syslog feed sends that message. Both renderings take the detail list from ehds-logging, so they never disagree.

Recorded fieldRendered as
bindingehds-accessor: binding, with guest for an admitted guest and security-event for refused-trc-patient-mismatch and refused-trc-missing
partyehds-accessor: party as <namespace>|<type>|<id>; in the FHIR AuditEvent also the person’s otherId typed PRN
party_groupsehds-accessor: one group per group, in the party’s namespace with type GROUP
providerehds-accessor: acts-for as <issuer>|<id>
facilitiesehds-accessor: one facility per facility, as <issuer>|<id>
representationehds-accessor: represents, represents-ground and represents-relationship; a refusal’s represented as represents alone
actor_chainehds-accessor: one actor per actor, <issuer>|<subject>, outermost first
binding_detailehds-accessor: binding-claim for refused-key-claim-missing
external_fieldsehds-relayed, marked asserted and naming the issuer by relayed-issuer: each 2026/2099 Annex field and eHDSI SAML attribute at its own detail (hp-family-name, hp-identifier, provider-identifier and the others), consent.reference as agreement-consent, and every other field as asserted-field <name>=<value>
agreementehds-relayed: agreement-name, agreement-version, agreement-legal-ground and agreement-access-class
correlation_id, correlation_sourcethe FHIR AuditEvent: correlation-id and correlation-source of the request id’s entity; the DICOM message: the same two details of ehds-relayed, since it carries no request entity
acting_modethe FHIR AuditEvent: the person’s agent.role; DICOM: none

Every value goes through the renderers’ escape: a control character, a bidirectional control or a line separator is written as its code point, and no value is cut. A DICOM detail value is base64-encoded as given (PS3.15 §A.5.1.1). A binding record that lacks a field its code needs fails the rendering, and the sender reports the failure, never a record without the binding.

Refusal records and their budgets

Every refused request is recorded as a failed user authentication, through the same path as an operation record: under [audit] fail_mode = "closed" a refusal whose record the system log cannot take is answered 503. A refusal of the login binding or of a caller kind carries its refused-* code. Refusals are charged to one of two budgets, which never draw on each other, so a flood of invalid tokens cannot hide a verified caller’s probing:

BudgetCharged toPer caller in a windowPer window
Failed verificationthe source network: the /24 of an IPv4 address, the /64 of an IPv6 one101000
Verified callerthe token’s iss and sub101000

A window lasts 60 seconds. Past a caller’s 10 records the rest of its refusals in that window become one summary record, written when the window closes: it names the caller and carries summary, the count and the EHR ids the refused requests named (at most 64, while the count stays exact). Past a budget’s 1000 records, the refusals of every caller not yet recorded in that window become one summary record per issuer and outcome, naming no caller. A security event (refused-trc-patient-mismatch, refused-trc-missing) is recorded once for every answered request and never summarised. A federation caller above its agreement’s caller_rate, a contact point’s included, is answered 429 before any patient lookup, and every such refusal goes into that caller’s summary record from the first, with binding_detail naming caller-rate, so the count of security events stays bounded. A refusal record the system log cannot take is counted in atna_audit_refusals_unwritten and logged at error.

Note

The limits, the windows and the budgets are kept per replica. Behind a load balancer with three replicas, one caller can have up to 30 refusals recorded one by one in a window before the summaries begin, and each replica writes its own summary records.

Access through FerroBRIDGE’s FHIR facade

The openEHR REST API carries no end-user identity on a read, so when FerroBRIDGE’s FHIR facade reads or writes through FerroEHR, FerroEHR’s record names the bridge’s credential under (b) and cannot name the natural person behind the FHIR request. From FerroBRIDGE 0.0.16 the bridge records each facade access itself when its [audit] section is on: it writes the Annex II 3.2 record with the person, the categories, the time and the origin through the same ehds-logging crate, and sends it as an IHE BALP AuditEvent through ihe-atna over the ITI-20 FHIR feed to the Audit Record Repository you configure there. The bridge refuses a facade access whose record it cannot take. Read the two records together: FerroEHR’s says which data left the CDR and to which client, and FerroBRIDGE’s says which person asked for it. FerroBRIDGE’s access record page describes its record and its configuration.

Emergency access (EHDS Art. 11(5))

A natural person may restrict health professionals’ access to parts of their data (EHDS Art. 8). Art. 11(5) lets a professional reach restricted data where the person’s vital interests require it, and requires such cases to be “logged in a clear and understandable format” and “easily accessible for the data subject”. Art. 9(1) counts these accesses among the ones the person is told about.

You name the purpose codes your callers declare for an emergency in [audit] emergency_purpose_codes. Each one must also be on [audit] purpose_codes; the server refuses to start otherwise. An access whose declared purpose is one of them carries the emergency mark:

  • The stored record: the emergency_access column is true. It is false for every other access and for records written before the column existed.
  • The FHIR AuditEvent: the entity named ehds-emergency-access that ehds-logging writes, whose description states the mark in plain words (“Emergency access: the accessor declared that the access was necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art 11(5)).”) and whose ehds-emergency-purpose details name the purposes that marked it. The declared code stays on agent.purposeOfUse and on purposeOfEvent. A patient portal keys on the entity and shows its description.
  • The DICOM syslog feed: no mark. The PS3.15 schema has no purpose element.

The person reads their own log, the marked accesses included, through the subject-scoped ITI-81 retrieval.

[audit]
purpose_codes = ["TREAT", "ETREAT"]
emergency_purpose_codes = ["ETREAT"]

The mark records the declaration and lifts no restriction. A composition or EHR restricted under GDPR Art. 18 stays refused with an emergency purpose, because Art. 18(2) admits processing only with consent, for legal claims, for the rights of another person or for an important public interest, and the person’s own vital interests are not on that list. The refused attempt is still logged with the mark. An EHDS Art. 8 restriction of access by health professionals is different: a caller holding authz.rbac.emergency_access_role that declares an emergency purpose reads the restricted data, and its record carries the mark (restriction of access). An emergency the caller does not declare is not marked.

Retention, and who chooses it

[audit.store] retention decides how long the repository keeps a record: 0, the default, keeps them forever, and any other value sets the horizon. Every record stores the first date it may be deleted on, and the reaper deletes each record hourly on or after that date and never before it. An access record takes its end from the retention its categories and origins call for (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Annex II 3.4), so two records written the same day can end on different dates; every other record ends the day after its date of access plus the horizon. A record written before FerroEHR stored per-record ends is reaped by the horizon.

The default is deliberate. An access log is the evidence a data subject’s right of access is served from, and a repository that silently forgets is worse than one that grows — so the software keeps everything until an operator says otherwise, rather than choosing a horizon on their behalf.

Choosing that horizon is the deployment’s, and it is a legal question: EHDS Art. 9(2) makes the access information “available for at least three years from each date of access to the data”, and national law can ask for longer. NEN 7513 is the Dutch reference for this log and the Wabvpz for how long it must survive. The setting is per node, and one node serves one organisation, so two organisations needing different horizons run two instances.

A floor is enforced where a jurisdiction sets one. The jurisdictions a deployment answers to are the ones its [privacy.identifier_scan] rules name, and where one publishes a minimum retention for the access log the server refuses to boot with a shorter horizon, naming the configured value and the floor. 0 always passes. The floors are written in calendar years, as the law writes them: a horizon set as [audit.store] retention is compared against the years exactly, and one set as retention against the most days those years can span (the day count in brackets below). The floors registered:

JurisdictionFloorSource
Every EU Member State (AT, BE, BG, CY, CZ, DE, DK, EE, ES, FI, FR, GR, HR, HU, IE, IT, LT, LU, LV, MT, NL, PL, PT, RO, SE, SI, SK)three years from each date of access (1096 days, the most three calendar years can span)Regulation (EU) 2025/327 (EHDS) Art. 9(2); a longer national floor wins. Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway are not listed: EHDS reaches the EEA only through an EEA Joint Committee decision
NLfive years from the moment the entry is written (1830 days, the most five calendar years can span)Besluit vaststelling bewaartermijn logging (Stcrt. 2019, 38007), under Art. 5 of the Besluit elektronische gegevensverwerking door zorgaanbieders, which binds the period to NEN 7513
CHone year, and kept apart from the processing system (366 days, the most one calendar year can span)Datenschutzverordnung (DSV) Art. 4 Abs. 5, as amended on 1 December 2025, for the logs of a large-scale automated processing of sensitive personal data; the separate storage is the deployment’s, through the forwarding sinks

For the Netherlands the five national years win over the three EHDS years; Switzerland is outside the Union and keeps its one year. Of the other shipped jurisdictions, DE, FI and SE carry the EHDS floor, while GB and NO have no floor registered: an unknown requirement is never guessed at, and a deployment there sets its own. Art. 9 applies from 26 March 2029 for patient summaries, prescriptions and dispensations and from 26 March 2031 for the other priority categories (Art. 105). The floor is enforced from this release on, so a log kept today already meets it when Art. 9 applies. The effective retention is on the boot line beside the audit-enabled facts and on GET /management/info under audit. A record takes about 1.2 KB on disk, so the horizon decides how far the log grows (Storage sizing).

Getting the log out

Two routes, and they answer different questions.

  • ITI-81 retrieval — the audit search serves the records back as FHIR AuditEvent resources, filtered by patient, agent, date and outcome. This is the operator’s route and the one a patient portal would build on: everything Annex II 3.2 records is reachable through it, including the purpose and the organisation, which the syslog feed’s DICOM form cannot carry.
  • The BALP feed — records fan out to syslog and to a FHIR feed as they are written, for a SIEM or a central Audit Record Repository.

There is no patient-facing route in the product: a portal that shows a person who accessed their record builds on ITI-81 and authenticates the person itself. What the product gives that portal is a grant of its own size: authz.rbac.subject_audit_role reads the log for one subject at a time, with the patient parameter required, so the portal never holds an admin credential over every patient’s log (GDPR Art. 15 with Recital 63, under which the controller “should be able to provide remote access to a secure system” where possible; EHDS Art. 9; for Dutch deployments Wabvpz Art. 15e). The portal’s build is the deployment’s, and the shared-responsibility page says so.

Sinks

Records fan out to independently configured sinks ([audit] in ferroehr.toml; see the configuration reference):

SinkDefaultWhat it does
[audit.store]onThe local Audit Record Repository: records persist in the dedicated audit PostgreSQL schema (append-only and tamper-evident, strictly outside the EHR content), served back via the ITI-81 search below. retention prunes old records hourly (0 = keep forever).
[audit.syslog]offThe classic ATNA feed: DICOM PS3.15 XML as RFC 5424 syslog over RFC 5425 TLS to an external ARR, per IHE ITI-20.
[audit.fhir_feed]offThe RESTful-ATNA feed (ITI-20 ATX: FHIR Feed): each FHIR AuditEvent is POSTed to an external FHIR ARR. With the local store on, delivery is outbox-driven: an ARR outage loses nothing, pending records ship on recovery. The outbox holds the records written while the feed is configured; with the feed off, no record is owed. Records stored before FerroEHR kept an outbox and never delivered ship once a feed runs.

Emission never blocks the request path: a record is handed to a bounded queue (queue_capacity) and written by a background drain.

While a composition is held from the person

With [privacy.access_delay] on, a new composition can be held from the person under EHDS Art. 3(3) until a professional releases it or its period passes. Only one route honours the hold: the subject-scoped ITI-81 read, the one a patient portal serves the person’s own trail from, leaves out every record that names a held composition. Every other sink and stream is a feed to the controller’s own systems and carries those records and events while the hold is in force:

Sink or streamWhat it carries during a holdWhy it is not filtered
[audit.store], read without the patient scopeevery record, the hold’s own includedThe unscoped ITI-81 read is the controller’s, under the admin role
[audit.syslog]every record, sent as it is written: the commit, each read and the hold’s own record name the composition, the last as access-delay:<vo> beside the patientAn ITI-20 feed goes to an Audit Record Repository, which “receives event audit reports and stores them” (IHE ITI TF-1 §9.1.1.3)
[audit.fhir_feed]the same records as FHIR AuditEvent resources, POSTed as they are written, the hold’s own record naming the same access-delay:<vo>The same ITI-20 repository, over ATX: FHIR Feed; the reader of a BALP AuditEvent is an Audit Consumer (BALP §1:52.1)
Change events ([record.change_feed])the commit of the held composition: its vo_id, kind, change type and templateThe feed serves the deployment’s own readers; it withholds what binds them, a restriction or objection (GDPR Art. 18 and 21, EHDS Art. 8), and the Art. 3(3) hold binds only the person’s access

EHDS Art. 9(2) gives the person the access information “through electronic health data access services”, which are yours to run. A repository, a feed reader or anything built on them never reaches the person from FerroEHR, so none of them filters the hold: a filter there would also hide the record from the controller who answers for it. What you must not do, while a hold is in force:

  • Serve the person’s trail from the external Audit Record Repository the syslog or FHIR feed writes to, for example through that repository’s own ITI-81 query. Serve it from FerroEHR’s subject-scoped read instead.
  • Send the person a notification, under Art. 9(1) or otherwise, from a record on either feed or from a change event that names a held composition. Ask the hold first: a request in the person’s context reads the composition as absent (404) until the hold ends.

The shared-responsibility page puts the same duty on the deployment’s side.

The local store is the durability anchor. Under fail_mode = "closed", an operation whose audit record cannot be recorded answers 503 Service Unavailable: the deployment demanded an audit trail it cannot currently deliver, so no un-audited PHI access happens, and the same holds for the domain-level records the subject resolutions and the EHR-Extract transfers write. open, the default, drops-and-meters instead, and every loss path is metered (the atna_audit_* counters in Operations); the server announces that default at boot and on the readiness indicator as a stated caution, because a metered loss is still a loss. Login and rejection records never gate a response in either mode.

Tamper evidence

An audit trail that anything with the application’s database password can quietly rewrite is a log, not an accountability record. The local store is therefore tamper-evident: every record is linked into a SHA-256 hash chain maintained inside PostgreSQL, so each record commits to its predecessor and to its own content. The chain is built by the database itself, not by the server, which means it covers every writer: the per-event insert, the batched drain, and any statement typed by hand.

Each record’s digest covers every column of the record except the digest itself (row_hash) and the two per-sink forwarding stamps (delivered_syslog_at, delivered_fhir_feed_at). A column added by a later release joins the digest in the same release.

The store keeps a record’s facts in columns and renders its FHIR AuditEvent from them when the record is read (ITI-81) or delivered (the FHIR feed). What the rendering takes from the configuration (source_id, enterprise_site_id, server_host, value_if_missing, the store horizon, [audit.categories] and emergency_purpose_codes) is kept once per distinct configuration in audit.audit_render_policy, keyed by the SHA-256 of its text, and every record names the policy it was written under. A record therefore renders the same document after the configuration changes, and the verification below reports a policy whose text no longer matches its digest, as it reports a changed record. Release 5.6.0 starts on an empty audit store: its migration refuses a store that holds records written by an earlier release, and names the remedy.

Four controls sit on top of it, and they are separate on purpose:

  • The table refuses the ordinary rewrite paths outright. The only permitted change to a stored record is the per-sink forwarding stamp; an UPDATE of any other column, a DELETE, and a TRUNCATE are refused by the database. Retention pruning goes through the one sanctioned deletion path, which records which records it removed and what the surviving chain must link back to, so reaping does not look like tampering, and tampering does not look like reaping.

  • The privileges are narrow. The runtime role may record an event, stamp it forwarded, and read the trail back. It holds nothing that can rewrite a record, remove one, or alter the chain’s own bookkeeping. That posture is only fully in force with database.migrations = "verify"; see Operations, because a self-migrating server owns the schema and can therefore turn the enforcement off.

  • Verification is a query you can run yourself. It recomputes every digest, re-walks every link, and checks both ends of the chain:

    SELECT * FROM audit.verify_audit_chain();

    An empty result means the trail is intact. Any row names one record (its chain position, its id, when it was recorded) and what is wrong with it: content modified after it was written, a render policy changed or missing, records deleted with no retention record for the removal, or records removed from the end of the chain where no successor would have noticed.

  • The server runs the check itself, on a schedule. With the local store on, the check runs one minute after boot and then every [audit.store] verify_interval (default 3600, one hour; 0 turns it off). Each run verifies the records written since the newest link an earlier run found intact, and the chain head, so its cost follows the records written since rather than the size of the trail (audit.verify_audit_chain_incremental()). A full pass runs every [audit.store] full_verify_interval (default 604800, one week; 0 leaves it to the query above) and after every run that found damage, so damage to an older record stays reported. A run that finds damage logs at ERROR, one summary line with the finding count and one line per finding (the first 20), and adds the count to the atna_audit_chain_findings counter with kind = "damage". A run that cannot verify at all counts as kind = "unverifiable", because a trail that cannot be checked is never a pass. The latest result is the audit_chain indicator on GET /health/readiness: UP while intact and DEGRADED when damaged or unverifiable; its detail on GET /management/health names the first finding. It never flips readiness, because the trail keeps recording while the damage is investigated. Alert on the counter or on that component, and use the query above to see every finding. Each replica runs its own check.

Important

This is detection, not prevention, and the boundary is worth stating plainly. The chain is unkeyed, so a party with unrestricted write access to the audit schema (the database owner, or a superuser) can delete a record and recompute every hash after it. What closes that case is keeping the trail somewhere that party does not control. Enable [audit.syslog] or [audit.fhir_feed] so records leave the box as they are written, and give the server an app-role-only DSN so it is not that party.

Retrieving audit records (ITI-81)

The RESTful-ATNA ITI-81 Retrieve ATNA Audit Event transaction is a FHIR search on AuditEvent, so it is served at FerroEHR’s FHIR R4 base, /ferroehr/rest/fhir/r4, beside the openEHR API rather than under it, where a FHIR client or an IHE Audit Consumer expects [base]/AuditEvent. It is the one FHIR route FerroEHR serves:

GET /ferroehr/rest/fhir/r4/AuditEvent

It returns a FHIR searchset Bundle of the matching records’ AuditEvent documents, rendered from the store, newest first, with the full match total, a self link and a next link while more pages follow. The query is read by ihe-atna, the family’s audit crate. At least one date parameter is required (RESTful ATNA §3.81.4.1.2.1): a query without one is a 400. Every search parameter §3.81.4.1.2.2 says the repository shall support is applied. A parameter with several comma-separated values matches any of them, and every parameter of the query must match. A token takes the three forms of FHIR R4 Search §3.1.1.4.10: code, |code (recorded without a system) and system|code (or system| for any code of that system). FerroEHR records identifiers without a system, except the object of an access record, whose system is urn:openehr:object-id: entity.identifier=urn:openehr:object-id|<uid> and entity.identifier=<uid> find it, and a query that names another system for an identifier matches nothing. Every parameter answers through an index. A parameter on an element of the document (address and the .identifier, entity-type, entity-role, type and subtype parameters) matches the search tokens the store takes from the record’s rendered document when it writes the record (audit.audit_search_token, audit.audit_search_set and the record’s search_tokens), so the search finds what the served document says and renders only the page it serves. An entity.identifier that carries the record’s request id or the object it names (the version uid of a create) is read from the record’s own column instead, so a request adds no row to audit.audit_search_token. Retention deletes the tokens that no remaining record names, and never one a kept record names.

ParameterMatches
daterequired, repeatable: a FHIR date value with a prefix (eq when none, gt, lt, ge, le, sa, eb); a day such as 2026-07-12 covers the whole day, read in UTC
patientthe recorded patient (EHR subject) id
patient.identifierentity.what.identifier of the entity whose role is Patient
agentthe authenticated principal
agent.identifieragent.who.identifier
entitythe touched resource id
entity.identifierentity.what.identifier of any entity
entity-typeentity.type
entity-roleentity.role
source.identifiersource.observer.identifier, the audit source id
typetype
subtypesubtype (the REST interaction and the openEHR operation)
addressa part of agent.network.address, compared without regard to case
outcomethe outcome indicator: 0, 4, 8 or 12 (FerroEHR records 0, 4 and 8)
actionthe action code: C, R, U, D or E
_count / _offsetpaging; page size defaults to 50, capped at 1000; _count=0 returns the total alone

A malformed value is a 400 carrying a FHIR OperationOutcome with invalid; another FHIR R4 AuditEvent parameter, which §3.81.4.1.2.2 does not ask for, is a 400 with not-supported; a parameter the crate does not know is ignored (§3.81.4.1.3). Under RBAC the unscoped retrieval is admin-only; a caller holding the configured authz.rbac.subject_audit_role reads it scoped to one subject: one patient or patient.identifier with one value is required, and the caller is refused with a 403 that names the parameter when it omits it. Reading a subject’s log is itself recorded as an access naming that subject and the record count served. An emergency access in the subject’s log carries its mark as the ehds-emergency-access entity. The surface answers 404 when the local store is disabled.

# Who accessed patient-42's data this month?
curl -u admin:pw \
  "https://cdr.example.org/ferroehr/rest/fhir/r4/AuditEvent?patient=patient-42&date=ge2026-07-01T00:00:00Z"

This is also the openEHR “record demerging” instrument: when data lands in the wrong EHR, the patient-filtered audit search shows exactly who read it.

Note

Audit records are themselves sensitive (they name patients, subjects and actions) so this endpoint is a PHI-disclosure surface and is authorized like any other.

Node authentication (ITI-19, mutual TLS)

ATNA’s second half is node authentication. [server.tls] terminates TLS natively and can demand a verified client certificate:

[server.tls]
certificate_file = "/etc/ferroehr/server.pem"
key_file = "/etc/ferroehr/server.key"
min_version = "1.3"               # 1.3 (default) | 1.2
client_auth = "required"          # none | optional | required
client_ca_file = "/etc/ferroehr/client-ca.pem"

The protocol floor is TLS 1.3 only by default, as RFC 9325 §3.1.1 has it supported. Setting min_version = "1.2" enables 1.2 alongside 1.3, never instead of it, for a client that genuinely cannot do 1.3, such as an older integration engine or a pinned Java runtime. TLS 1.1 and 1.0 are refused when the configuration is read (RFC 8996).

With client_auth = "required", only clients presenting a certificate chaining to your explicit trust anchor complete the handshake: the IHE mutually-authenticated-node posture. Deployments terminating TLS at an ingress leave [server.tls] unset and enforce mTLS there instead.

Warning

The separate-port management listener (management.listen) stays plain HTTP even with [server.tls] set, and it binds all interfaces. Treat it as an internal surface and keep it off any publicly routed port. Under deployment.profile = "production" setting it opens the plaintext_listener gap, so the server refuses to start unless the gap is accepted by name.

Complete the posture with time synchronisation (IHE Consistent Time): run NTP/chrony on every node so audit timestamps align across systems.

Against independent ATNA implementations

The transactions above are tested by FerroEHR’s own suites, which read the profiles the way FerroEHR’s authors read them. EHDS Annex II 1.4 asks that a component meant to work with other products does so reliably, so scripts/interop/atna.sh runs the quickstart against software FerroEHR’s authors did not write, each from a published image:

TransactionIndependent implementationWhat the run requires
ITI-20 FHIR feedHAPI FHIR, an open-source FHIR R4 server, as the Audit Record Repository, with IHE BALP 1.1.4 loadedIt accepts every record, and its validator finds no error against base R4 and the BALP profile each record names
ITI-20 syslogsyslog-ng over RFC 5425 TLSEvery message parses as RFC 5424, and its payload is a well-formed DICOM PS3.15 A.5.1 AuditMessage (libxml2)
ITI-81HAPI FHIR’s AuditEvent search over the records the feed deliveredThe same searches answer the same records on both
 
cargo build --release -p loadtest
bash scripts/interop/atna.sh ghcr.io/ferrohealth/ferroehr:<tag> \
  ghcr.io/ferrohealth/ferroehr-postgres:<tag> atna-out

It prints every disagreement and exits non-zero on any. A disagreement is either FerroEHR’s or a shared crate’s defect, filed and fixed, or the other side’s, recorded with the profile text that shows it.

The run of 2026-10-29 found no disagreement: HAPI FHIR accepted and validated all 71 records of the window, syslog-ng parsed all 72 messages, and the ten ITI-81 searches answered the same records on both repositories (the record).

Configuration summary

Auditing defaults to on with the local store only; see the configuration reference for every [audit] key and its FERROEHR__AUDIT__* environment form. The syslog sink’s own keys are host and port under [audit.syslog], with its TLS material under [audit.syslog.tls]; the switches shared by every sink stay directly under [audit].

Note

There are no alternative spellings for any of these: an unrecognized FERROEHR_* variable or an unknown TOML key is a boot error naming the spelling it should have had, never a silently ignored setting. Validate a deployment’s configuration up front with ferroehr config check.

Version signing

Every version FerroEHR commits can carry a VERSION.signature: a value computed over the version’s own canonical form, inside the write transaction that stores it. openEHR defines two depths for that value, and FerroEHR implements both as first-class modes (RM Common IM, Change Control §Digital Signature).

ModeWhat is storedWhat it establishes
digest (the default)sha256: + base64(SHA-256(canonical form))the version has not been altered since committal
pgpan ASCII-armored RFC 4880 detached signaturethat, plus which key signed it

Signing is on by default, in digest mode, and read-time verification of the server’s own signatures defaults to strict: a served version that no longer matches its stored signature is a 500 rather than a silently served record.

The two pages

  • Digest signing covers the mechanism both modes share: what goes into the signed form, when it is computed, what a stored digest does and does not prove, how verification at read behaves, and how to reproduce a digest yourself from the served JSON.
  • PGP signing covers what changes when a key is involved: the key configuration and its fail-closed boot check, rotation and retired keys, client-supplied signatures versus server-generated ones, and the signature an import wrapper carries.

Read them in that order; the PGP page builds on the digest page rather than repeating it.

Where this sits

Version signing is openEHR’s own record-level integrity mechanism, and it is distinct from the two other integrity surfaces this book describes. The ATNA audit trail records security surveillance of API access, with its own hash chain over audit records. Verifying releases is about the artifacts you downloaded, not the data you stored. All three coexist and none substitutes for another.

Every [record.signing] key, with defaults and environment forms, is in the configuration reference.

Digest signing

Every version FerroEHR commits can carry a VERSION.signature. openEHR defines two depths for that value: hash the version and store the digest, or sign the hash with a private key. The openEHR RM Common IM, Change Control §Digital Signature puts it directly: “If only the hashing step is done, the digest acts as a data integrity check, indicating if the data have been tampered with after creation. If the signing step is carried out, it authenticates the user as the author of the content.”

This page covers the hashing depth, which FerroEHR calls digest mode and runs by default. PGP signing covers the other one.

  • What the digest covers
  • When it is computed
  • What a stored digest proves
  • Verification at read
  • Verifying a digest yourself
  • Switching modes later

What the digest covers

The signed value is the whole VERSION object as the server will serve it, with the signature attribute itself left out. Concretely, for a locally committed version that is the ORIGINAL_VERSION carrying:

  • uid, the OBJECT_VERSION_ID this repository allocated;
  • preceding_version_uid, when the version has a predecessor;
  • contribution, the OBJECT_REF of the enclosing CONTRIBUTION;
  • commit_audit, including its committer and time_committed;
  • lifecycle_state;
  • data, the clinical content;
  • attestations, the ones committed with the version.

The assembled object is reduced to a canonical string with RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme), and the digest is sha256: followed by the standard-base64 encoding of the SHA-256 of that string:

sha256:jtWX/CULavvzX0ehjowv2XZPICTQhN1t0+AXHfbEaNc=

The sha256: prefix is a FerroEHR addition. openEHR names the OpenPGP format for the signing depth, and says nothing about how a bare digest is spelled on the wire, so the prefix carries the algorithm and encoding that a raw radix-64 hash would leave unstated. It is also what lets a reader tell a digest from a PGP signature without a second stored column.

The RM section marks the exact serialization “To Be Determined” and notes that ODIN might be preferred because XML libraries differ. FerroEHR uses canonical openEHR JSON reduced by RFC 8785, which is deterministic and independent of the signature itself.

Note

A logically deleted version has no data attribute at all: openEHR deletes by committing a new version whose data is Void. Its digest therefore covers the identity, provenance and 523|deleted| lifecycle state, and nothing else. It is a signature over a real version, not an empty one.

When it is computed

At commit, inside the write transaction, before any row is inserted. The commit instant and the CONTRIBUTION id are both known up front (the commit instant is the transaction timestamp), so the server assembles the exact version envelope it will later serve, signs that, and writes the version row, the CONTRIBUTION and the audit together.

Two properties follow, and both matter for verification:

  • The signed bytes and the stored bytes are the same bytes. The content is decomposed into storage rows once and reassembled once; that reassembled value is what gets signed and what a read returns. There is no second serialization that could drift.
  • A version that fails to sign does not commit. Signing sits inside the transaction, so a canonicalization or signer failure rolls the whole change back rather than storing an unsigned version.
flowchart TD
    A["commit<br/>(direct write or CONTRIBUTION)"] --> B{"UPDATE_VERSION.signature<br/>supplied by the client?"}
    B -->|yes| C["stored verbatim<br/>signature_client_supplied = true"]
    B -->|no| D{"record.signing.enabled"}
    D -->|false| E["no signature stored"]
    D -->|true| F["assemble the VERSION envelope<br/>uid, contribution, commit_audit,<br/>lifecycle_state, data,<br/>at-committal attestations"]
    F --> G["canonical form:<br/>drop signature, RFC 8785 (JCS)"]
    G --> H{"record.signing.mode"}
    H -->|digest| I["sha256: + base64(SHA-256(canonical))"]
    H -->|pgp| J["RFC 4880 detached signature,<br/>ASCII-armored"]
    I --> K[("version row<br/>same transaction")]
    J --> K
    C --> K
    E --> K

What a stored digest proves

It proves that the version served today canonicalizes to the same bytes it did at commit. Any change to the content, the committer, the commit time, the lifecycle state or an at-committal attestation moves the digest, so a row edited behind the server’s back is detected the next time that VERSION is read.

It proves nothing about who wrote the version. A digest needs no key, so anyone holding the bytes can compute the same value, and an attacker who can rewrite a version row can rewrite its digest with it. Digest mode is a tamper-detection control against accidental corruption and against an actor who reaches the data but not the write path. Authorship and non-repudiation need a key, which is PGP mode.

It also covers one of the two copies FerroEHR stores. Every version’s content is written twice in the same transaction: as the materialized document a point read serves, and as the decomposed rows the AQL engine queries. The digest is computed over the first one, and read-time verification recomputes it from the same place. The decomposed rows are never recomputed on a read, so a row edited behind the server’s back is invisible to this check and can still reach a client through an AQL scalar result.

That copy has its own channel: POST /ferroehr/rest/extensions/v1/admin/integrity/verify re-derives every stored version from its decomposed rows and reports any that no longer match the stored document. It is an admin route, it runs outside the request path, and it reports by identifier rather than by content. The admin API reference documents the report and its five defect values.

Verification at read

record.signing.verify_on_read resolves to strict whenever signing is enabled, so the default deployment checks its own digests. On a VERSION read the server rebuilds the envelope from the stored row, recomputes the canonical form, recomputes the digest, and compares.

verify_on_readOn a mismatch
strict (the default while signing is enabled)500; the record is provably corrupt and is not served
warnlogs at error level, increments version_signature_invalid_total{verdict="digest_mismatch"}, still serves
offno check at all

Verification runs where the server serves a VERSION object: the versioned_composition and versioned_ehr_status version routes, their version_at_time forms, the demographic version reads, and the versions a CONTRIBUTION read resolves under Prefer: resolve_refs. A plain content read (GET /ehr/{ehr_id}/composition/{uid_based_id}) returns the COMPOSITION rather than the VERSION that carries the signature, and runs no check. AQL reads the decomposed storage rows directly and runs no check either; the storage-parity sweep is what covers those.

Warning

A strict mismatch is a 500 on purpose. The alternative is serving a record the server can prove was altered after committal, which in a clinical repository is worse than an outage on that one version. If a deployment needs reads to continue while an integrity problem is investigated, warn is the deliberate downgrade, and it is metered so the downgrade is visible.

Two cases are never verified, whatever the setting says:

  • A client-supplied signature. A VERSION.signature a caller sent in a CONTRIBUTION is stored verbatim and served verbatim. The author may have signed another agreed serialization, which this server cannot recompute, so treating a non-match as corruption would be wrong. The stored row records which of the two it holds.
  • The ORIGINAL_VERSION wrapped inside an imported version. Its signature belongs to the system that created it. See PGP signing.

Verifying a digest yourself

The digest is reproducible from the served JSON. Fetch the VERSION:

BASE=http://localhost:8080/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1
curl -u ferroehr:ferroehr -o version.json \
  "$BASE/ehr/$EHR_ID/versioned_composition/$VO_UID/version/$VERSION_UID"

Then, over version.json:

  1. read the stored value, jq -r '.signature' version.json;
  2. drop that member, jq 'del(.signature)' version.json;
  3. canonicalize the result per RFC 8785 (the served bytes are canonical openEHR JSON, whose member order is _type-first, so they are not already in JCS order; this step is the one that decides whether the comparison works);
  4. openssl dgst -sha256 -binary, base64, and prefix sha256:.

Step 3 needs an RFC 8785 implementation. FerroEHR ships no command-line tool for it, so use a canonicalizer from your own language’s ecosystem.

Note

One case does not reproduce. openEHR allows an attestation to be added “at any time after committal”, and such an attestation post-dates the signature. FerroEHR appends those to the served attestations list after verification, so the served list can hold more entries than the signed form did, and the wire carries no marker separating the two. The server’s own check uses the at-committal set; an outside recomputation over a version attested after committal will not match. Versions with no after-committal attestations reproduce exactly.

Switching modes later

The stored format decides how a signature is checked, so a mode change does not invalidate history: a sha256: digest keeps verifying after the server moves to pgp mode, because the check keys off the value’s own prefix. The reverse direction is weaker. A PGP-signed version read by a server in digest mode has no key to verify against, so it is served without a verdict rather than failing. Keep the certificate configured if those versions must stay checkable.

Every key in [record.signing], with defaults and environment forms, is in the configuration reference.

PGP signing

pgp mode replaces the stored SHA-256 digest with an OpenPGP (RFC 4880) detached signature made with a key the server holds. openEHR names that format directly: the signature “is generated according to the openPGP standard”, and where a digest only detects tampering, a signature “authenticates the user as the author of the content to readers of the content” and “acts as a non-repudiation measure, since the signature is stored permanently with the data” (RM Common IM, Change Control §Digital Signature).

Read Digest signing first: what gets signed, when, and how the canonical form is built are identical in both modes. This page covers what changes.

  • What differs from digest mode
  • Configuring the key
    • Retired keys and rotation
  • Server-generated versus client-supplied signatures
  • Imported versions carry two signatures
  • Read-time verification

What differs from digest mode

digestpgp
Stored valuesha256: + base64(SHA-256(canonical form))ASCII-armored RFC 4880 detached signature
Key materialnonean armored secret key the server loads at boot
HashSHA-256SHA-256, inside the OpenPGP signature
Provesthe version was not altered after committalthat, plus which key signed it
Boot behaviournothing to validaterefuses to start without a usable key
Verification at readrecompute and compareverify against the configured certificate

The bytes being signed do not change. The server assembles the version envelope, drops the signature attribute, reduces it to its RFC 8785 canonical form, and hands that string to the signer. Only the last step differs.

Configuring the key

pgp mode needs a key_file pointing at an armored secret key, and the passphrase that unlocks it if it has one:

[record.signing]
enabled = true
mode = "pgp"
key_file = "/etc/ferroehr/signing.asc"
key_passphrase_file = "/run/secrets/pgp-pass"
retired_key_files = ["/etc/ferroehr/signing-2025.pub.asc"]

The same settings as environment variables:

FERROEHR__RECORD__SIGNING__MODE=pgp
FERROEHR__RECORD__SIGNING__KEY_FILE=/etc/ferroehr/signing.asc
FERROEHR__RECORD__SIGNING__KEY_PASSPHRASE_FILE=/run/secrets/pgp-pass
FERROEHR__RECORD__SIGNING__RETIRED_KEY_FILES=/etc/ferroehr/signing-2025.pub.asc

Prefer key_passphrase_file over the inline key_passphrase: it is the shape Docker Secrets and Kubernetes Secrets deliver, and the passphrase then never appears in the environment. Setting both of the pair is a boot error. The full key table, the Kubernetes config.files mount, and the rotation walkthrough are in the configuration reference.

Boot is fail-closed. The server loads the key, then signs a fixed test string with it. A missing key_file, an unparseable file, a wrong passphrase, or a certificate with no usable signing component all stop startup with an error rather than leaving a running server that cannot sign.

The signing component is chosen at boot. No subkey signs while the primary key is revoked (RFC 9580 §5.2.1.11: “A revoked key is not to be used”) or past the Key Expiration Time its self-signature states (§5.2.3.13). RFC 9580 does not say in so many words that a subkey inherits its primary key’s revocation or expiry, so applying it is FerroEHR’s own choice: the primary key’s binding is what vouches for the subkey. Otherwise a subkey qualifies to sign when all of these hold:

  • its newest valid Subkey Binding signature (RFC 9580 §5.2.3.10) carries the data-signing key flag 0x02 (§5.2.3.29);
  • neither that binding nor the subkey has expired (§5.2.3.13);
  • no valid Subkey Revocation signature covers it (§5.2.1.12: “A revoked subkey is not to be used”).

Of the qualifying subkeys, the one created last signs; on equal creation times, the later one in the file. RFC 9580 gives no rule for choosing among several signing subkeys, so preferring the newest is FerroEHR’s own choice. It is what makes adding a signing subkey a rotation. An encryption subkey never signs.

When no subkey qualifies, the primary key signs, provided the certificate lets it:

  • its governing self-signature carries the signing flag 0x02. RFC 9580 keeps the primary key’s flags in a Direct Key signature or, by version 4 convention, in a User ID self-signature (§5.2.3.10), so the governing one is the newest valid Direct Key signature when it carries key flags, else the newest valid self-signature on the primary User ID. A Direct Key signature that a valid Certification Revocation created at or after it revokes is cancelled and not chosen (§5.2.1.13, §5.2.3.10: “Revoking a Direct Key signature cancels that signature”). A version 6 key without a valid Direct Key signature in force is not used at all, as §5.2.3.10 requires. A self-signature with no key flags grants no signing, since §5.2.3.29 counts an unstated flag as zero. RFC 9580 gives no precedence between the two places, so preferring the Direct Key signature is FerroEHR’s own choice;
  • neither that self-signature nor the primary key has expired (§5.2.3.13, counted from the primary key’s creation);
  • no valid Key Revocation signature covers it (§5.2.1.11: “A revoked key is not to be used”).

When neither a subkey nor the primary key may sign, the server refuses to start and names the signing flag. It never signs with a key the certificate does not authorise. Add a signing subkey (gpg --quick-add-key <FINGERPRINT> ed25519 sign), or re-issue the primary key’s self-signature with the signing flag.

The choice holds until the next restart, so restart after adding, revoking or expiring a subkey, and before the chosen component expires.

Sign with Ed25519. It is the one algorithm the server signs with that has neither a refusal nor a warning.

An ECDSA or Ed448 signing key is refused at boot. The private-key arithmetic of both runs on crypto-bigint 0.5, whose operations meant to be constant-time can branch on secret values (RUSTSEC-2026-0387), and the 0.5 line has no fixed release. That covers ECDSA on every curve (P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1, Brainpool). The server stops before it makes a single signature and names the advisory. Only the signing component counts: a certificate whose primary key is ECDSA and whose chosen signing subkey is Ed25519 is accepted. Such a certificate stays usable for verification as a retired key, since verifying uses only public values.

An RSA signing key is accepted with a warning. Every commit would then perform an RSA private-key operation, the operation the Marvin timing sidechannel (RUSTSEC-2023-0071 / CVE-2023-49092) concerns, and the underlying rsa crate has no fixed release. The server warns at boot and keeps working, because a repository whose history is RSA-signed still needs that key to verify it. An Ed25519 key keeps that code off the signing path.

Retired keys and rotation

A stored VERSION.signature records no key identifier, and it is an immutable committed fact that cannot be re-issued. Rotating a key therefore has to keep the old one verifiable. Two mechanisms do that:

  • A new signing subkey on the same certificate. After a restart the server signs with the newest qualifying subkey (see above), the certificate retains the previous one, and verification tries the primary key and every subkey. Revoking the old subkey stops it signing and keeps it verifying. Nothing else changes.
  • retired_key_files. A replaced certificate’s public half is listed there and consulted during verification. A public key verifies and can never sign again, so a retired entry cannot become an active signer.

A retired certificate may use any algorithm the server can verify, ECDSA, Ed448 and RSA included, so moving off a refused signing key keeps every version it signed verifiable.

Server-generated versus client-supplied signatures

A VERSION.signature in this repository is one of two things, and the distinction is recorded on the row rather than guessed from the value.

Server-generated is the ordinary case. The direct write routes (POST/PUT/DELETE on a composition, the EHR status, the directory, a demographic party) carry no signature field at all, so every version they commit is signed by this server when signing is enabled.

Client-supplied reaches the server through one route: an UPDATE_VERSION.signature inside a CONTRIBUTION commit. When a member carries one, the server stores it verbatim and does not sign that version itself, whatever record.signing.mode says. openEHR models the signature as a fact created by the committer and carried with the data, potentially in another agreed serialization, so the server has nothing to recompute it against. Such a signature is never re-verified at read, and no verify_on_read setting changes that.

Note

A client-supplied value is stored as sent, so an opaque or invalid one is served back unchanged rather than refused. It is a claim by the committer, and this server neither vouches for it nor mistakes it for its own. Only signatures the server generated are covered by read-time verification.

Imported versions carry two signatures

An EHR Extract import wraps each received ORIGINAL_VERSION in an IMPORTED_VERSION, and openEHR is explicit about what happens to signatures there. The wrapped original “is never modified”, and the wrapper is signed like any other version: “all attributes of the object are serialised and then used to generate a signature. The result will be that the IMPORTED_VERSION instance will carry its own signature which signifies the act of importing and making available locally an ORIGINAL_VERSION from another system.”

FerroEHR implements exactly that:

  • The wrapper is signed by this server, over the whole IMPORTED_VERSION including the wrapped item, using the configured mode. An import is a local act of committal, so it is signed like one.
  • The wrapped original’s signature rides inside item untouched. It belongs to the source system’s key, which this server does not hold, so it is served verbatim and never verified.

Reading such a version verifies the wrapper and leaves the wrapped signature alone. Reading the same version as an ORIGINAL_VERSION (the form an EHR Extract export carries) reproduces the received original with its foreign signature and verifies nothing, which is what makes a re-export a faithful copy.

Read-time verification

The stored signature’s own format decides how it is checked, which is why a mode change does not strand history. The full path:

flowchart TD
    R["read a VERSION resource"] --> A["rebuild the envelope from the stored row<br/>(a deleted version carries no data attribute)"]
    A --> B{"signature_client_supplied?"}
    B -->|yes| S["serve"]
    B -->|no| C{"verify_on_read"}
    C -->|off| S
    C -->|"warn / strict"| D{"a stored signature?"}
    D -->|no| S
    D -->|yes| E["recompute the canonical form<br/>drop signature, RFC 8785 (JCS)"]
    E --> F{"stored value's format"}
    F -->|"sha256: prefix"| G["recompute the digest and compare"]
    F -->|"PGP armor"| H{"a PGP key configured?"}
    F -->|"anything else"| I["client_foreign: serve"]
    H -->|"yes (pgp mode)"| J["verify against the certificate,<br/>its subkeys and the retired ones"]
    H -->|"no (digest mode)"| I3{"does the armor parse?"}
    I3 -->|yes| I
    I3 -->|"no: pgp_invalid"| L
    G --> K{"verdict"}
    J --> K
    K -->|"match"| S
    K -->|"failure"| L{"verify_on_read"}
    L -->|warn| M["log + version_signature_invalid_total,<br/>then serve"]
    L -->|strict| N["500 integrity failure"]
    S --> T["append attestations added after committal"]
    M --> T
    I --> T

The server reaches one of five verdicts: digest_match, digest_mismatch, pgp_valid, pgp_invalid, client_foreign. Two of them are failures, digest_mismatch and pgp_invalid, and those are the ones counted, under the verdict label on version_signature_invalid_total.

Three parts of the path are worth stating in prose:

  • Attestations added after committal are appended after verification. openEHR allows an attestation “at any time after committal”, so such an attestation post-dates the signature and cannot be inside it. The server verifies the at-committal form and then extends the served list.
  • A version with no stored signature is served normally. Versions committed while signing was disabled carry none, and their absence is not a failure.
  • strict is the default while signing is enabled. A mismatch is a 500 rather than a served record that is provably altered. warn downgrades that to a logged and metered event, which is a deliberate reduction in an integrity guarantee rather than a setting to leave on.

FerroEHR Viewer

ferroehr-viewer is a standalone web UI for managing an ITS-REST-1.1.0 CDR, this server or any other. It is a pure REST client: everything it does goes through the CDR’s public API (never the database), so what you see in the viewer is exactly what the API serves. The whole application is Rust, drawn on the server as plain HTML with FerroUI, the component library the FerroHEALTH consoles share; the only scripts are FerroUI’s own small modules, and there is no hand-written JavaScript anywhere, including its browser tests.

  • Running it
    • On Kubernetes
  • Signing in
    • Your access
    • When your session ends
  • The deployment profile
  • Configuration
    • Commands
    • Browser security headers
  • How the pages work
    • Paging
    • Preferences and the keyboard
  • Audit log
  • Acknowledgment

Running it

The quickstart compose ships the viewer as the ferroehr-viewer service on port 3000, behind the viewer profile, so it is opt-in and does not start with a plain docker compose up:

docker compose --profile viewer up
# → http://localhost:3000  (log in with the quickstart user ferroehr/ferroehr)

Standalone, point it at any CDR:

docker run -p 3000:3000 \
