  -e FERROEHR_VIEWER__CDR__BASE_URL=https://cdr.example.org \
  ghcr.io/ferrohealth/ferroehr-viewer

On Kubernetes

The Helm chart deploys the viewer as its own Deployment, Service and ServiceAccount, with an optional Ingress and a NetworkPolicy that confines its egress to the CDR and DNS: the viewer is a REST client of the CDR by mandate, so the chart enforces that rather than trusting it. Off by default, and off renders nothing:

# values.yaml
viewer:
  enabled: true
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    hosts:
      - host: viewer.example.org
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
  auth:
    oidc:
      enabled: true
      issuer: https://keycloak.example/realms/ferroehr
      clientId: ferroehr-viewer
      publicBaseUrl: https://viewer.example.org
  # the OIDC client secret is MOUNTED from a Secret you create, never env-borne
  existingSecret: viewer-oidc

It needs no database credential and never reaches the database. Before you enable OIDC: a registered client whose redirect URI matches publicBaseUrl, and a Secret holding its client secret. To turn the viewer off, set viewer.enabled: false and upgrade; every viewer object is removed and the CDR is untouched.

Note

To scale the viewer past one replica, set session.store = "sealed" and the same session.key (or session.key_file) on every replica: the session is then a sealed cookie any key-holding replica can serve. The default memory store keeps sessions in one process, which is right for exactly one replica. A sealed store with no key refuses the start.

Signing in

The sign-in page offers exactly the methods that can actually work: the viewer’s configured login modes intersected with the authentication schemes the CDR advertises (its WWW-Authenticate challenge). A Basic form is never shown against a bearer-only CDR, and vice versa. If the CDR cannot be reached at all, the page falls back to the viewer’s own configuration and renders anyway, and the outage then surfaces on the login attempt instead of hiding the page. A username or password the CDR refuses brings you back to the sign-in card with the refusal under the password.

The viewer verifies the CDR and the OIDC issuer against the platform trust store and the extra certificate authorities its configuration names: a CDR or an identity provider whose certificate comes from a private CA is trusted once cdr.tls.trust_roots_file or oidc.tls.trust_roots_file names a PEM bundle holding that CA, on Linux and macOS alike. A file that cannot be read, or holds no certificate, refuses the start.

The viewer manages no accounts of its own: it authenticates you against the CDR (Basic) or your identity provider (OIDC), and there are no user, role, or password screens to find; those live in the CDR’s configuration and in your IdP.

The button with your name at the end of the top bar opens the user menu: who is signed in and how, Your preferences, Your access, the theme, Keyboard shortcuts and Sign out.

Your access

Your access (/access) answers what may this session do, and who says so: the principal and how it signed in (a Basic session replays its CDR account and carries no SMART scopes; an OIDC session carries an access token whose scopes are listed), every scope on the session read as its parsed grant (the compartment, the resource family and id pattern, and which of create, read, update, delete and search it permits, with a broad access marker on a bare *; an identity or launch scope such as openid, profile or launch/patient reads as the request it makes), and a previewer: paste any scope or a whole claim, press Read it, and read the same rendering. A malformed scope says what the grammar expected. The user menu and Server’s SMART tab link here.

The reading parses with the same grammar the CDR’s SMART on openEHR enforcement reads, so the two cannot drift. Scopes narrow access and never grant it; the CDR remains the enforcer.

When your session ends

A session ends when you sign out, when its idle window (session.idle_timeout, an hour by default) passes with no request from your browser, when its lifetime (session.absolute_timeout, 12 hours after you signed in by default) runs out whatever you do, or when the CDR stops accepting the credential behind it (an expired or revoked token). The pairing of an idle timeout with an absolute one follows the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.

Each signed-in page watches its session. Two minutes before the idle window ends, a dialog says when the session ends and offers Stay signed in or Sign out; typing or clicking on the page also keeps the session going, at most once a minute. Nothing extends the lifetime, so near its end the page gives no warning and leaves when it runs out. When the session has ended, the page leaves for the sign-in page, which says the session ended, and signing in again (Basic or OIDC) returns you to the page you were on. Every other tab of the viewer in the same browser leaves with it, and signing out in one tab ends the others.

The idle window slides on each request your browser makes for a page or a post. The watch’s own reads of the session do not slide it, so a tab left open and untouched idles out after session.idle_timeout_s like a closed one. With FerroUI’s scripts refused, the next page you ask for is where the viewer notices.

The deployment profile

The status pill at the end of the top bar says whether the CDR answers. A deployment that declares the sandbox profile (deployment.profile in its configuration, reported on GET /rest/status) raises a band under the top bar on every signed-in page: this deployment must not hold real patient data, with the number of production separations the server reported as open (a shared database credential, a shared cluster, no subject pseudonym namespace, no durable audit trail, schema preparation on the runtime credential). Its Details opens Server’s Overview, which names each one. A production deployment raises no band. The quickstart and the composed stacks run as sandbox; a CDR older than the profile reports none and the viewer claims nothing. See the deployment profile in the server configuration.

Configuration

One TOML file (ferroehr-viewer.toml, read from the path --config or FERROEHR_VIEWER_CONFIG names; with none named, no file is read), with FERROEHR_VIEWER__<SECTION>__<KEY> environment overrides and --set key=value pairs over both. Unknown keys and unknown FERROEHR_VIEWER_ variables are refused at startup. The CDR refuses only an unknown FERROEHR__ override, because the viewer’s variables share its prefix:

KeyDefaultMeaning
server.listen127.0.0.1:3000 (0.0.0.0:3000 in the image)The socket address the viewer listens on.
server.tlsunsetThe listener’s certificate and key, as the CDR’s [server.tls] table; unset, the viewer speaks plain HTTP behind a terminating proxy.
server.request_timeout / body_limit"1min" / "16MiB"How long one request may take, and the largest body it may post (a template or composition posts whole).
server.drain_delay / shutdown_timeout"0s" / "10s"On SIGTERM the viewer withdraws readiness, waits the drain delay, then gives the requests in flight the shutdown bound.
server.*as the CDR’sThe other keys of the CDR’s [server] table (header_read_timeout, idle_timeout, max_concurrent_requests, retry_after, trusted_proxies, forwarded_header, compression, compression_min_size) apply as they do there. base_path and caller_rate are refused: the viewer’s pages are served at /, and it mounts no per-caller limit.
telemetry.*as the CDR’sThe CDR’s [telemetry] section: format (auto, json or pretty), filter (default info,hyper=warn,tower=warn,h2=warn, refused at startup when it does not parse; RUST_LOG is a lower-priority fallback, as on the CDR), logged_query_parameters, environment and the [telemetry.otlp] export. A viewer request line has the CDR’s fields, and a panic writes the CDR’s one fixed line. The service.name is ferroehr-viewer; the viewer serves no Prometheus surface, so its http.server.request.duration histogram leaves only over OTLP with otlp.metrics.
cdr.base_urlhttp://localhost:8080The CDR origin (cdr.base_path is appended).
cdr.base_path/ferroehr/rest/openehr/v1The CDR’s ITS-REST base path. Mirror of the CDR’s own api.base_path: set the same value here when a deployment shortens it, or the viewer calls paths the CDR does not serve. The status document, the OpenAPI documents and the SMART discovery document are derived from it by the same rule the CDR uses.
cdr.timeout"30s"How long one request to the CDR may take.
cdr.tls.trust_roots_fileunsetA PEM bundle of certificate authorities trusted for the CDR beside the platform’s roots, for a CDR behind a private PKI.
cdr.tls.client_identity (_file)unsetThe client certificate chain and its private key, in one PEM, presented to a CDR that asks for mutual TLS.
cdr.tls.min_version"1.3"The oldest TLS version the CDR client speaks; "1.2" lowers it.
cdr.management_base_urlderived from cdr.base_urlThe CDR’s management surface, base path included; set it when the CDR serves management on its own internal listener (management.listen) or under a renamed base path. Drives Server’s management tabs.
auth.basic_enabledtrueOffer the username/password form (validated against the CDR; held server-side).
auth.oidc_enabledfalseOffer the OpenID Connect sign-in (authorization code + PKCE) at the provider [oidc] names.
auth.public_base_url—The viewer’s externally visible origin: the origin the same-origin check compares a post with, the base of oidc.redirect_uri (<public_base_url>/auth/callback) when that is not set, and the base of oidc.post_logout_redirect_uri (<public_base_url>/sign-in?signed-out=1, the signed-out page) when that is not set.
oidc.issuer / client_id / client_secret (_file) / redirect_uri / post_logout_redirect_uri / scopes—The viewer’s client at its OpenID Provider (ferrohealth-session’s [oidc]). The provider must allow the redirect URI <public_base_url>/auth/callback and the post-logout redirect URI <public_base_url>/sign-in?signed-out=1 (OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §3). With auth.oidc_enabled, an issuer that is not https off loopback, a missing client id or redirect URI, and scopes without openid are startup errors, and the provider’s metadata is discovered at the start.
oidc.resolveemptyhost=ip:port entries for split-horizon DNS: the viewer reaches each provider host at its address, while browsers and tokens keep the canonical URL.
oidc.tls.trust_roots_file / client_identity (_file) / min_versionunset / unset / "1.3"The family’s outbound TLS table for the provider: a PEM bundle of certificate authorities trusted beside the platform’s roots, for a provider behind a private PKI; the client certificate chain and its private key in one PEM, for mutual TLS (RFC 8705 §2); and the oldest TLS version of the provider connection ("1.2" lowers it).
login.noticeemptyInformational text on the sign-in card, line breaks preserved. A demo or evaluation deployment states its public credentials and usage expectations here.
login.linksemptyLinks under the sign-in card, each { label, href } — an API reference, a documentation page.
session.storememoryWhere sessions are kept (ferrohealth-session’s [session]): memory in the one viewer process, or sealed in one AES-256-GCM cookie every replica holding the key opens.
session.idle_timeout"1h"Session idle expiry: the window slides on each page or post the browser asks for and on Stay signed in, never on the session watch’s own reads.
session.absolute_timeout"12h"The session’s lifetime from sign-in, which no activity extends. Zero, or a value below session.idle_timeout, is a startup error.
session.secure_cookietrueThe cookies carry Secure and with it the __Host- prefix; set false only for plain-HTTP local development.
session.key / session.key_fileunsetThe sealing key of a sealed store: base64 of at least 64 bytes (openssl rand -base64 64), the same on every replica. A sealed store without one, or a key beside a memory store, is a startup error.
ui.localeenThe language a page renders in when the browser’s Accept-Language names none the viewer ships. English is the one language that ships today. A language is added as a catalog file under app/ferroehr-viewer/locales/<tag>/ (the viewer’s words) beside FerroUI’s (the components’ words) with no code change; the catalogs are embedded when the viewer is built, so a new one reaches a deployment in a rebuilt image, never at run time. A value that is no BCP 47 language tag is a startup error.

Commands

ferroehr-viewer (or ferroehr-viewer serve) serves until SIGTERM or SIGINT. ferroehr-viewer config check reads the configuration, checks [oidc] and [session] and builds the CDR client and the session store, reading every TLS file, without reaching the CDR or the provider. ferroehr-viewer healthcheck, the image’s HEALTHCHECK, asks the viewer beside it for GET /health/readiness over the loopback (over TLS when server.tls is set) and exits 0 only on 200. The viewer serves the family’s health routes: /health/liveness, /health/readiness and /health.

Every command exits 78 (EX_CONFIG of sysexits(3)) when the viewer refuses its configuration (an unknown or invalid key, a TLS file that does not read, an [oidc] or [session] table it cannot use) and 1 on any other failure, with the whole cause on stderr. A command line clap cannot parse exits 2.

Browser security headers

Every response carries a Content-Security-Policy that admits scripts and styles from the viewer’s own origin alone (script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'), with no nonce and neither 'unsafe-inline' nor 'unsafe-eval', beside X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site; when the viewer serves TLS itself (server.tls), Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 as well. Every document is Cache-Control: no-store; FerroUI’s stylesheet, theme and scripts under /ferrohealth-ui/<version>/ are no-cache, so a browser revalidates them. A request that is not a safe method (a form post, the search panel’s answer) is refused 403 unless the browser’s Sec-Fetch-Site says it came from the viewer’s own pages; without that header its Origin or Referer must name auth.public_base_url.

The viewer is stateless: it has no database and keeps no local files of its own. Everything it shows, including how stored queries are grouped, which is derived from the namespace in each query’s qualified name, lives in the CDR and is read over ITS-REST, so nothing here needs backing up and every replica shows the same repository. The sign-in and the session are ferrohealth-session’s: with session.store = "sealed" the session is a sealed cookie (AES-256-GCM, keyed by session.key), so any replica holding the key can serve any signed-in visitor.

Sign-in and sessions live in the viewer’s server; the browser stores only the session cookie, an opaque id or ciphertext: CDR credentials and bearer tokens never reach it in readable form. The sign-in page is /sign-in, and the sign-in routes are /login (which begins the OpenID Connect sign-in), /auth/callback, /logout and /session.

How the pages work

The viewer draws every page on its server and sends it complete. Every link is a link and every action is a form that posts to the page it sits on, so the whole viewer works with JavaScript off. The browser then loads FerroUI’s small script modules, which add behaviour to a few parts of a page (the code editor, the path trees, the chart legend, the date pickers, the search panel’s suggestions, the user menu’s keyboard handling, the subject reveal and Copy buttons); nothing on a page waits for them. There is no hand-written JavaScript.

An editor (a new EHR, a composition, the EHR status, the directory, a party, a template upload) ends in a bar docked at the foot of the page: what has changed, Discard, and the save. A save that the CDR refuses keeps what you typed on the page beside the CDR’s own words.

The screens are listed in the sidebar; below 48 rem it folds into a drawer behind the menu button.

  • Dashboard: record counts, the compositions committed per day, and the stored queries by namespace. See Queries.
  • EHRs: find, create and delete EHRs; each EHR’s compositions, directory, status, contributions and tags. See Templates and EHRs.
  • Parties: the demographic parties, their versions, relationships and tags. See Parties.
  • Templates: upload and read ADL 1.4 and ADL 2 operational templates. See Templates and EHRs.
  • Terminology: the terminologies the CDR serves. See Terminology.
  • Stored queries and Query: build or write AQL, run it, chart and export the rows, save it to the CDR. See Queries.
  • Server: what the CDR is, how it runs and what it serves, and the Audit log. See Server and audit log.
  • Configuration: the CDR’s redacted running configuration, by section.
  • About: the viewer, the CDR and their versions, the manufacturer and the CDR’s conformance manifest.

The top bar’s search takes an EHR id, a composition or party uid, a subject id, a template id or a stored-query name. From the second character a panel under the field shows what matches, five of a kind; the arrow keys move through it, Enter opens a hit and Escape closes it. Submitting the search opens the find page, which lists every match, or the other ways to find a record when nothing does.

The footer under every page names the viewer and its version, the manufacturer (Cadasto B.V.), and an About link.

Paging

A listing that can show patient data (the EHRs, an EHR’s compositions and contributions, the audit log) pages with First, Previous, Next and Last under the table and keeps its page in a cookie for the browser session, never in the address or the history, as FerroUI asks of every family console. A filter stays in the address, so a filtered view is still shareable; the page you were on is not. Each step is a form that posts to /paging and comes back to the listing, so paging works with JavaScript off.

Preferences and the keyboard

Your preferences keeps the viewer’s display choices, each in its own cookie for that browser: the theme, the reading choices, and the keyboard shortcuts. See Preferences and the theme.

Audit log

The audit log has its own section in Server and audit log.

Acknowledgment

The viewer’s feature set (the Template Manager, the point-and-click Query Builder, and saved, grouped and cohort queries) is inspired by EHRServer by Pablo Pazos and CaboLabs Health Informatics (Apache-2.0). The interface is reimplemented in Rust over FerroEHR’s own AQL engine, and no code is copied.

Dashboard & queries

The dashboard opens the viewer, and Query and Stored queries cover AQL end to end: build a query from a template or write it, run it, read the rows as a table or a chart, export them, and save the query to the CDR as a versioned stored query.

  • Dashboard
  • Query
    • Build
    • AQL
    • Results
  • Stored queries
    • Saving and versions

Dashboard

What the CDR holds, as it answered just now: the EHR, composition, template and stored-query counts (each a link to its screen), the compositions committed per day over the last 30 days, read by commit time with one AQL query, and the stored queries grouped by namespace.

Query

Query has two tabs over one form: Build and AQL. Run in the page header runs whichever tab is open; Save to the CDR beside it stores the query.

Build

Build lowers a template and a few choices into AQL you can read:

  • Template, the operational template the query reads, and Returns: data points, whole compositions, a count, or the EHRs (a cohort). Apply redraws the form for a new template or shape.
  • Data points, each a path from the template’s Web Template and an optional column name; Add a data point adds a row.
  • Conditions, in groups that match all or any of their conditions, each negatable. A condition is a path, an operator for that data type and a value: a quantity takes a number with its unit, a date a date, a coded text one of the codes the template allows. Add a condition and Add a group close each group.
  • Order and limit.

The AQL the form lowers to is shown under it, and is what Run sends.

Every control is a field of the page’s form, and Add and Remove post it, so Build works with JavaScript off.

AQL

The AQL tab is a code editor with line numbers and the AQL grammar’s findings beside the line they name, before anything is sent. A $parameter in the query gets a row under Parameters: its name and the value Run binds. Open in Build appears when the query is one Build can represent, and opens it there.

Results

Results come back under the form: how many rows, whether the query carried its own LIMIT, and the rows as a table.

Chart in the Results heading runs the query again and draws the numeric columns as lines over the first time column (or over the row order when there is none), one series per column with a legend; Table goes back, and the next Run keeps the view you chose. The table under the chart names each point by its time. With FerroUI’s scripts loaded, pressing a legend entry hides that series; the last one shown stays.

Export in the Results heading opens a menu of the formats: CSV and JSON download the rows. The query runs again on the viewer’s server and the file arrives as aql-export.csv or aql-export.json. The menu works with JavaScript off, and with no row Export is unavailable. The viewer keeps no results between requests, so an export is always the CDR’s answer at that moment.

Stored queries

Stored queries lists every stored query the CDR holds, grouped by the namespace of its qualified name (org.example.vitals::latest-weights sits under org.example.vitals): its versions, its parameters, and Run, Open in Query and Delete this version from each row’s menu.

A stored query’s page has three tabs. Definition shows its AQL and facts.

Run runs it on the CDR with a value for each parameter. Which version runs is the openEHR resolution choice: the latest (no version sent), a version prefix (1 or 1.1, the latest matching it) or an exact version; the line under the choice names the request it sends. Numbers and true/false are sent as they are; quote a number to send it as text.

Versions lists every version.

Saving and versions

Save to the CDR takes a namespace, a name and a version. An empty version lets the CDR assign one. A stored (name, version) pair cannot change: saving the same pair again is refused and the popover says so. Opening a stored version in Query fills Save with its namespace, its name and the next minor version.

Deleting a version needs the CDR’s ADMIN role and asks first: Delete version… on the query’s page or in its row menu.

Templates & EHRs

Templates holds the operational templates the CDR validates compositions against, and EHRs opens every EHR with its compositions, directory, status, contributions and tags.

  • Templates
    • Uploading a template
    • A template
    • ADL 2 templates
    • Deleting a template
  • EHRs
    • An EHR
    • Deleting an EHR
    • Committing several changes at once
  • Compositions

Templates

The list has a tab per family, ADL 1.4 and ADL 2, each with its count, a find field over id, concept and archetype, and a row per template with Build a query and Delete… in its menu. The releases of one template share a group: the newest release leads with the number of releases, and the earlier releases follow under it, each its own row. Releases belong together when their ids differ only in the .v version at the end; an ADL 1.4 template whose id has no version joins the templates with the same concept and root archetype.

Uploading a template

Upload a template opens an editor for one source: choose or drop a file (.opt or .xml for ADL 1.4; .adl, .adls, .adlt, .adl2 or .txt for ADL 2; up to 16 MiB) or paste the source, then Upload this template. The CDR validates it; a refusal keeps the source on the page beside the CDR’s diagnostics, for ADL 2 the openEHR-ADL engine’s own words. With JavaScript off, paste the source.

A template

A template’s page has four tabs, and a fifth, Compare, when it has more than one release. Overview reads its identity, its releases with the number of compositions committed against each, and how to query it. The release you are reading is named beside the title; with more than one release it opens a list of the others, the newest marked, each a link that works with FerroUI’s scripts refused too.

Paths is its Web Template as a tree: pick a node to read its path, type and codes, and on a COMPOSITION template Build a query on this path. A demographic template’s nodes offer no query, since the query builder reads compositions. With FerroUI’s scripts loaded the tree folds in place and answers the arrow keys; without them each node is a link.

Source is the template as stored, with line numbers and Copy; Download in the More menu saves it as a file. Example is the composition the CDR generates for it, in the format, type and detail you pick.

Compare reads two releases, the one you are reading and the one before it unless you choose others, and lists each path the later release adds, removes or changes, with what it was and what it is.

ADL 2 templates

An ADL 2 template’s page opens on its latest release, and the JSON tab beside Source shows the OperationalTemplateV2 document. An older release opens on its Overview, says which release you are reading, and links back to the latest.

A template whose archetypes the CDR no longer holds says so on every tab, names each missing archetype and links to uploading them. Its Paths, JSON and Example tabs stay empty until the archetypes are back.

Deleting a template

Delete… in a row’s menu opens the template with the confirmation inline; on the template’s page it opens a dialog. The CDR refuses while compositions use the template, and deleting needs its ADMIN role; either refusal arrives in the CDR’s words.

EHRs

The list shows every EHR the CDR holds, newest first, and finds one by its subject id and namespace. The subject is shown masked.

New EHR creates one with its status: an optional subject (an id the CDR keeps without reading it, and its namespace) and an optional EHR id; leave the id empty and the CDR mints a UUID. An id that is no UUID is refused before anything is sent; an id the CDR already holds is refused with a link to that EHR.

An EHR

An EHR’s page names it, its subject masked until you press Reveal (with JavaScript off the reveal is a link), and its Queryable and Modifiable badges, on every tab. A revealed subject hides again after the time set in Your preferences (30 seconds unless you change it). New composition and More (Commit several changes, Create the directory, Copy EHR id, Delete EHR…) sit in the header.

The tabs:

  • Compositions: the EHR’s compositions, filtered by composer, template and start date; the filters stay in the address.
  • Directory: the folder tree, Show one folder by path, and the directory’s versions with Restore… on each older one. Edit opens the editor: add, rename and remove folders and add references to the EHR’s compositions; nothing reaches the CDR until you save. Older versions reads further back than the newest ten.
  • Status: the current EHR_STATUS and its versions; Edit status sets Queryable, Modifiable and the other details as one new version.
  • Contributions: the contributions per day over the last 30 days and every contribution, each opening its versions.
  • Tags: every tag in the EHR, on a composition or on the EHR status, by key and value; a row opens the object it tags.

Every save names the version it supersedes (If-Match). A save over a version someone else replaced meanwhile is refused with the CDR’s 412, and the editor offers to reload the newer version.

Deleting an EHR

Delete EHR… asks for the first eight characters of the EHR’s id, then removes the EHR and everything in it; it needs the CDR’s ADMIN role.

Committing several changes at once

Commit several changes builds one contribution: stage a new composition, an amended one or the EHR status, each with its document in an editor of its own, as many as you need, then commit them together with a description. The CDR takes all of them or none: a refused change keeps every staged change on the page beside the CDR’s words.

Compositions

A composition’s page has four tabs. Reading shows it as a person reads it, label and value, by section.

Document shows it in the format you pick (JSON, XML, FLAT or STRUCTURED), as the CDR converts it. Versions lists every version and reads the VERSIONED_COMPOSITION and the chosen version’s envelope; At a time opens the version that was current then. Tags lists the composition’s tags and sets or removes one; a tag stays on the composition across its versions and commits no version.

Edit as a new version opens the document in an editor; the save writes the next version. Delete composition… marks it deleted with a new version; its versions stay readable and it leaves the EHR’s list.

Parties

Parties reads and writes the demographic parties the CDR holds (people, organisations, groups, agents and roles), their versions, the relationships between them, and their tags.

Note

Parties follow the released RM 1.1.0 demographic model. The openEHR REST API for them is still in development, and the relationship routes are this server’s own extension: a different openEHR server will not serve them.

  • Finding a party
  • Creating a party
  • A party
  • Relationships
  • Tags
  • Contributions

Finding a party

Pick a kind and type a party’s uid, then Open. There is no list of parties: the demographic API publishes no “list all people” endpoint, and AQL reads EHRs. A versioned object uid opens the latest version; a version uid opens the object it belongs to. Open is a plain form and works with JavaScript off.

The one demographic collection the API publishes is the tag index, under Open: every tag on any party, each row opening the party it tags.

Creating a party

New party opens an editor with a starting document for the kind you pick (Start over swaps it for another kind’s). Every attribute in it is one openEHR requires: the party’s name, which openEHR uses for its type (the names a person goes by live in identities), the archetype_details and the root archetype_node_id, at least one identity, and for a role its performer. Fill in the identity, replace the archetype ids with your own demographic archetypes’, and create. The document is sent as you wrote it; a refusal comes back with the CDR’s words and the path it names, the document still on the page.

A party

A party’s page has five tabs. Overview reads its facts and identities.

Document shows it as the CDR serves it. Versions lists every version, each opening its envelope and its contribution; At a time opens the party as it stood then. Relationships lists the relationships the party is the source of. Tags lists its tags and sets or removes one.

Edit opens the whole party as JSON; the save writes the next version with the opened one as its If-Match, so a party someone else changed meanwhile is refused with the CDR’s 412. Delete party… marks it deleted; its versions stay readable.

Relationships

A relationship joins a source party to a target: an employment, an authority, a care relationship. openEHR models it two ways, and both are visible here:

  • inside the source party, which carries the relationships it is the source of; its Relationships tab lists those, each row opening the target;
  • as an object of its own, with its id, versions and history, the shape this server’s relationship routes serve.

The target side cannot be listed: openEHR defines “relationships pointing at this party” as a derived attribute the CDR does not populate, and the tab says so where you would look.

Relate this party opens a new relationship with this party as its source: a type (openEHR stores it as the relationship’s name), the target’s kind and uid, and optional details. A relationship’s own page links both ends, reads its facts, versions and document, and edits its type and details; the ends do not change, since a relationship between other parties is another relationship.

Tags

A tag is a key, an optional value and an optional target path. Setting one re-sends the party’s whole tag collection, as the openEHR tag update does: the viewer reads the current tags and merges yours in, so a tag another client added between your read and your save can be lost; read again before editing a busy party. A tag stays on the party across its versions and commits no version.

Contributions

Every write here commits a contribution, openEHR’s record of one change set: who committed it, when and why. A version’s contribution link opens it, with the versions it touched, each linked to the object it belongs to.

Terminology

The Terminology screen browses the coded vocabularies the CDR can answer questions about: which terminologies it serves, what a code means, which codes a value set holds, whether a given code is one of them, and whether one code subsumes another. Everything on it is a read of the CDR’s public API; nothing is stored on the viewer’s side.

  • Switching it on

Note

The terminology API is this server’s own extension. openEHR’s REST release publishes no terminology contract, so the operations, URLs and JSON envelopes are this server’s own design over the openEHR TERM specification. A different openEHR server will not serve them.

Switching it on

The surface is opt-in and off by default. While it is off the CDR answers its terminology routes as if they were not mounted, and the screen says so in one card instead of pretending to work:



[api]
terminology = true```

or, as an environment override, `FERROEHR__API__TERMINOLOGY=true`.

Turning it on exposes only lookups over terminologies the server already holds:
the bundled openEHR terminology plus the external code sets beside it. Wiring
the FHIR terminology server is a separate setting, and it changes what
these lookups can answer; both are covered in
[Terminology servers](../beyond-core/terminology.md).

## The terminologies

**Terminologies**, the first of four tabs, lists exactly what the CDR reports:
the internal `openehr` vocabulary and the external code sets beside it
(languages, countries, character sets, media types). A row opens the
terminology's descriptor: publisher, identifying URI, version, and the fields
an extract may ask for, with links to look a code up in it and to expand one
of its groups. Fields the server does not publish are left out.

## Look up

Pick a terminology, type a code and **Look up**. A defined term comes back with
its text, the language it is written in and whether it is the preferred term.
An **effective date** is optional: supplied, it asks for the definition as it
stood that day; the openEHR bundle is one pinned release, so a date changes
nothing there, while an external terminology server can answer differently.

A code the terminology does not define is an answer, not an error: the page
says so, naming the code and the terminology.

![Look up](img/terminology/lookup.png)

> [!NOTE]
> openEHR terminology codes are scoped to their group: `532` is `complete` in
> one group and `completed` in another. A lookup reads the `openehr`
> terminology as flat and returns the first group's rubric, so expand the
> group under Value sets whenever the group matters.

## Value sets

Pick a terminology and a value set (for `openehr`, a vocabulary group such as
`audit_change_type`, offered as you type) and **Expand** it into its members.
Under them, **Validate** answers whether a code is a member, as a sentence
either way; a value set the CDR does not know has no members.

![Value sets](img/terminology/valuesets.png)

## Hierarchy

**Test** asks whether one code is broader than another. The test is strict,
so a code is never broader than itself, and the openEHR vocabulary defines no
hierarchy, so for any two openEHR codes the answer is no; the page says why.
Hierarchical answers come from an external terminology server when one is
bound.

Every tab is a GET form: the question stays in the address, so an answer is
shareable, and every tab works with JavaScript off.

## In the query builder

A condition on a coded text in [Build](queries.md#build) offers the codes the
template allows as a select, so a coded criterion is never typed from memory;
the query carries the bare code.

Server & audit log

Server says what the CDR this viewer reads is, how it runs and what it serves, as six tabs, and the Audit log browses its security audit trail. Everything on them comes from the CDR’s own endpoints over HTTP; the viewer has no privileged channel.

  • Overview
  • Health, Metrics and Logging
  • API and SMART
  • Configuration
  • Audit log

Overview

The CDR’s state, its deployment profile and version, and how it was built: the version, the git commit, the build date and rustc, the PostgreSQL target, the audit posture (whether auditing is on, its fail_mode, the local store and the retention), the active spec_profile with the openEHR specification versions it selects, the manufacturer, and the end month of the release’s support. The conformance manifest the CDR answers at OPTIONS on its base path (its product, vendor, conformance profile and the API groups it mounts) is on About.

Health, Metrics and Logging

These three tabs read the CDR’s management surface, and appear only when the CDR serves it. To get them, enable the surface and give each endpoint an access level (Operations → The management surface); every endpoint ships off:

[management]
enabled = true

[management.endpoints]
info = "admin_only"     # the probe the tabs appear on; enable it with the rest
metrics = "admin_only"
env = "admin_only"
loggers = "admin_only"

If the CDR serves management on its own internal listener (management.port) or under a renamed base path, point the viewer at it with the full prefix (FERROEHR_VIEWER__CDR__MANAGEMENT_BASE_URL); unset, the viewer derives {cdr.base_url}/management. Being allowed to read an endpoint is the CDR’s decision per request, and a refusal is reported on the tab that asked.

Health lists what the CDR depends on (the database, the migrations, the audit chain and sender, and any optional components) with each one’s state and the CDR’s detail. It reads the public readiness probe (GET /health/readiness). The pill in the top bar answers a different question: whether the API answers at all.

Metrics has three tiles (compositions committed, AQL queries, database connections in use) over the whole metric registry: pick a metric and Show its current samples with their labels. The choice stays in the address (/server/metrics?metric=db_pool_connections). For dashboards and alerts, scrape GET /management/prometheus.

Logging shows the filter in effect and the boot filter, and changes the live filter without a restart: type tracing directives (ferroehr=debug,sqlx=warn), Apply…, and confirm in the dialog; Reset to the boot filter puts the startup value back. The tab then reads the CDR’s answer, so what you see is what the server confirmed.

Important

A log-filter change applies to that CDR instance only and lasts until it restarts. Behind a load balancer each instance is set on its own; for a lasting change, set log.filter in the server configuration.

API and SMART

API lists the OpenAPI documents the CDR serves for itself, one family at a time: pick one (openEHR EHR, Query, Definition, Demographic, Admin, and the FerroEHR extensions, or the complete surface) and read its endpoints by tag. The family stays in the address (?family=query).

SMART reads the CDR’s SMART discovery document: the scopes it supports as parsed grants, the grant types and PKCE methods, and the document itself. Your access shows the scopes your session holds.

Configuration

Configuration in the sidebar shows the CDR’s redacted running configuration by section, each key with what it means; secrets show as their reference, never their value.

Audit log

The Audit log browses the CDR’s security audit trail (who accessed what, with what outcome) through the IHE ITI-81 retrieval (GET /fhir/r4/AuditEvent; see the Audit trail chapter). Filter by principal, outcome, action, date window and patient; the filters stay in the address, so a filtered view is shareable. The page lives in the session, as on every listing that can show patient data.

A row opens its record: the event, who, the patient, what was done and the outcome, and the stored FHIR R4 AuditEvent with line numbers and Copy.

A filter that matches nothing says so, with the filters named and a way to clear them.

The audit trail is an operator surface: the screen needs the CDR’s ADMIN role, and a session without it is refused in the CDR’s words. When the CDR’s local audit store is off, the screen says so.

Preferences & the theme

Your preferences (in the user menu) keeps the viewer’s display choices for you, in this browser: each one is its own cookie, read when the server draws a page, so a choice applies from the first paint and nothing is kept in browser storage. Nothing here names a patient, and nothing changes what you may do. Reset to defaults… clears them all.

  • Appearance
  • Reading
  • Keyboard
  • The dark theme

Appearance

  • Theme: light, dark, or the one your system uses. The user menu sets it too.
  • Density: comfortable (the default) gives rows and forms room; compact fits more rows in every list.
  • Reduce motion: follow the system, or always reduce.

Reading

  • Language: follow the browser, or one of the languages the viewer ships (English today; see ui.locale under Configuration).
  • First day of the week in the date pickers.
  • Show a revealed identifier for 15 seconds to 2 minutes: how long a subject id stays shown after Reveal.

Keyboard

Shortcut hints, the key caps after a label: on wide screens with a keyboard (the default), on all wide screens, or never. Phones never show them. The keyboard shortcuts themselves are listed under Keyboard shortcuts in the user menu.

Operations

Running a clinical data repository in production means more than starting the binary: the database must be backed up and least-privileged, traffic must be encrypted, upgrades must be safe while the service stays up, and you need to see what the system is doing. This chapter is a production checklist (database roles, TLS, backup and point-in-time recovery, upgrades and migrations, observability, the health probes, and the management surface) drawn from how the container image and Helm chart are built to run. The operator-facing HTTP surfaces have their own page: Admin & messaging APIs.

Database roles and least privilege

FerroEHR connects to an external PostgreSQL 18: a managed service or an operator-run cluster, never a chart-side sidecar, because a database holding PHI must be independently backed up and recoverable. The server carries only a connection string, ideally sourced from a secret.

The database never runs as a superuser at runtime. Two roles cover provisioning and migration:

RolePurposeUsed by
ownerowns the databaseprovisioning only
ferroehr_migratorruns the schema migrations; owns the helper functionsthe migration step

and four cover serving, split by pseudonymisation domain, the clinical record and the identity of its subject:

RoleReads and writesBarred from
ferroehr_clinicalclinical, archival tier includedparty
ferroehr_partyparty, archival tier includedclinical
ferroehr_clinical_readerread-only over clinicalparty
ferroehr_party_readerread-only over partyclinical

The migrations create these roles idempotently, apply the per-schema grants, and revoke every other domain explicitly in both directions, and revoke the ability to create objects in the public schema. All four are NOINHERIT and none is a member of another, so a boundary cannot be crossed by picking up a membership. GDPR Art. 4(5) defines pseudonymisation as processing where attribution to a person needs additional information “kept separately and subject to technical and organisational measures”, and Art. 32(1)(a) names it a security measure for health data (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj); EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 require that separation to hold against internal actors, operators with database access included.

Each serving role holds SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on its own domain’s tables, EXECUTE on the ext helper functions, and MAINTAIN on its store’s partitioned tables (and ehr, for ferroehr_clinical), and nothing else: it is not a superuser, does not bypass row-level security, and cannot create, alter or drop a table, index, schema or role. On the audit trail it is narrower still: it may record an event and stamp it forwarded, and it holds no privilege that can rewrite or remove one (see Audit).

MAINTAIN is there so the server can keep those tables’ planner statistics (see Planner statistics of the partitioned tables). It also allows VACUUM, CLUSTER, REINDEX and LOCK TABLE on exactly those tables. The role can already write every row of them, so what it adds is the locks and index rebuilds those commands take. The reader roles do not hold it.

Turning the schema split into a role split

The schema separation is unconditional: the server always reads and writes parties in party, whatever it authenticates as, and each of the three pools carries only its own schema on its search_path. The role separation is a deployment choice, and it is one configuration table per domain:

[database.party]
url = "postgres://ferroehr_party:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"

(or url_file, for a mounted secret). With a domain’s url set the server opens that pool on that credential, and a flaw that reaches one of them reaches one domain. Left unset, the domain uses [database].url and the separation is schema-only. Set both domains and no credential the server uses can join a party to its EHR in SQL; the crossing happens in the application, over two connections, and is recorded as an access event (see Security → Resolving across the boundary).

A DSN that names another host moves the domain to a database or cluster of its own, which is the separation a schema cannot make: a base backup, WAL archiving and physical replication carry every schema of a database together (PostgreSQL 18, Backup and Restore).

Two boot checks make the posture honest. Two domains configured on different DSNs that authenticate as the same database role are refused — a separation that exists only in the configuration reads as one that holds, which is worse than none. And a domain role that does not exist is a warning under deployment.profile = "sandbox" and a refusal under production: absent roles mean absent grants, and the boundary check would otherwise pass by having nothing to measure.

Which credential prepares the schema

None of the domain credentials. Preparing a database spans every schema in it at once: the DDL of each resident migration set under [database] migrations = "apply", and their _sqlx_migrations bookkeeping tables under "verify" — a read, but a read across the whole database. Each runtime role holds exactly one domain, so none can do it, and verify is not the exception: a role that is a member of ferroehr_clinical and nothing else is refused on the very first set: it cannot read the ext, party or audit bookkeeping.

So the credential that prepares the schema is named separately, and the server uses it for that one boot step:

[database]
url = "postgres://ferroehr_clinical:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"
migrate_url = "postgres://ferroehr_migrator:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"

[database.party]
url = "postgres://ferroehr_party:***@pg:5432/ferroehr"

migrate_url prepares every domain that reaches the same DATABASE it does, which is all of them in the posture above: three credentials, one database. A domain whose DSN reaches a DIFFERENT database is prepared there on that database’s own migrator, [database.<domain>] migrate_url, because migrate_url names one database and a relocated domain is not in it; unset, it falls back to the domain's own DSN, which a DML-only role cannot use. Which case a domain is in is read from the server itself (pg_control_system()andcurrent_database()`), never from the DSN text — two DSNs that differ only in their credential reach the same database.

(or migrate_url_file, for a mounted secret). The connection is opened for preparation and closed again: no pool is held on it, and no request is ever served through it. Left unset it falls back to url, which is exactly what a single-credential deployment has always run — its behaviour is unchanged by this key existing.

A credential that cannot read a set is told which schema and which role, so the fix is visible from the message:

database role `app_ehr` cannot read the migration state of schema
`ext`: … point `[database] migrate_url` (or `migrate_url_file`) at the credential
that prepares the schema — unset, it falls back to `[database] url` — and, for a
domain in a database of its own, `[database.<domain>]` migrate_url` at that
database's migration credential

Either way the server refuses to boot when the grants themselves are wrong: a self-check enumerates every table, view, sequence and function in each domain and fails, naming the role and the object, if either runtime role can read across the boundary. ferroehr db verify runs the same check. When the four roles do not exist at all (the development, compose and test-harness case, where the migrator holds no CREATEROLE) the check warns rather than inventing a failure — under deployment.profile = "production" it refuses, because absent roles mean absent grants and there is then nothing to measure.

On Kubernetes the same choice is chart values, mounted as files the same way the clinical DSN is, so no credential enters the pod’s environment:

database:
  existingSecret: ferroehr-db                 # postgres://ferroehr_clinical:…
  party:
    existingSecret: ferroehr-db-party         # postgres://ferroehr_party:…
  audit:
    existingSecret: ferroehr-db-audit         # the audit repository's own DSN
  migrateExistingSecret: ferroehr-db-migrator # postgres://ferroehr_migrator:…

Leave a domain’s block unset and that pool uses the shared DSN, which is the schema-only posture.

Provisioning the four roles is yours in both cases. The migrations create them only when the migrator holds CREATEROLE and skip them with a NOTICE otherwise, so on a managed database — where the migrator usually does not — create them before the first deploy:

CREATE ROLE ferroehr_clinical NOLOGIN NOINHERIT;
CREATE ROLE ferroehr_party NOLOGIN NOINHERIT;
CREATE ROLE ferroehr_clinical_reader NOLOGIN NOINHERIT;
CREATE ROLE ferroehr_party_reader NOLOGIN NOINHERIT;
-- The released grant files still name this role, so a first install needs it
-- while they apply. The last migration drops it again where it may; a migrator
-- without CREATEROLE may not, so drop it yourself after the first boot.
CREATE ROLE ferroehr_linkage NOLOGIN NOINHERIT;

then give each login role membership of exactly one of the first four. ferroehr db verify tells you whether the boundary holds afterwards.

The local Audit Record Repository is written on its own pool ([database.audit]), and the audit schema is granted to ferroehr_clinical (record an event, stamp it forwarded, run the retention reaper, verify the chain) and to ferroehr_clinical_reader (read it and verify the chain). A clinical login role that is a member of ferroehr_clinical alone writes its own access log; no extra membership is needed. The audit trail is not a pseudonymisation domain, so this grant adds no reach into party.

The compose stacks create the four domain roles, and ferroehr_linkage for the released grant files, and grant the clinical and party domains to the single dev login role, which owns the database. That demonstrates the schema separation and exercises the boot self-check; it is deliberately not the credential separation, because one container with one DSN cannot show that half honestly.

Which of these postures is exercised, and which is not

A recommendation nothing runs is a guess. This is what the suites cover.

Exercised against a real PostgreSQL 18:

  • Two runtime credentials serving both domains through the assembled router, each of the server’s own pools refused every relation of the other domain (app/ferroehr-rest/tests/it/credential_separation.rs), and the single-DSN fallback still serving both.
  • All four domain roles refused every relation in the domain they do not own, enumerated from information_schema rather than from a written list (app/ferroehr/tests/it/pseudonymisation_boundary.rs).
  • The boot sequence on separated credentials with [database] migrate_url, under both verify and apply, and the single-DSN fallback under both (app/ferroehr/tests/it/schema_preparation_credential.rs).
  • The party domain relocated to a second database, prepared and verified there on [database.party], and the refusal when the domain’s two DSNs reach different databases (app/ferroehr/tests/it/relocated_domain_preparation.rs).
  • The chart’s production overlay on three PostgreSQL clusters, one per domain, prepared by the migration Job and booting under production (scripts/deploy-probe-k8s.sh --production-only, probes P-K8S-PROD-BOOT and P-K8S-PROD-SHARED).
  • The compose stack’s grant boundary read back from the running database by scripts/deploy-probe.sh, which also records that the stack is single-credential by design.

Not exercised by anything, and stated rather than left to inference:

  • A real deployment on separated DSNs: a container booting with the DSN files mounted, and the chart wiring them through database.party.existingSecret and database.migrateExistingSecret. What is covered is the in-process half.
  • Role provisioning on a managed database where the migrator holds no CREATEROLE and the roles are created by the manual step above.

Which posture you actually get depends on [database] migrations, because the server’s embedded migrations are DDL: a self-migrating deployment necessarily runs as a role that can execute DDL. The single-container quickstart takes that path: its DSN authenticates as a non-superuser role that owns the database and is a member of ferroehr_migrator, ferroehr_clinical and ferroehr_party.

Applying migrations

[database] migrations decides who runs the schema:

  • apply (the default): the server applies its embedded migrations at boot. This is what makes a fresh checkout and an empty database work with no configuration at all, and it is the right choice for development and for small single-tenant deployments. The runtime DSN must be a member of ferroehr_migrator, so the serving process holds DDL rights for its whole life. Least isolation.
  • verify: the server issues no DDL at all. At boot it checks that the database carries exactly this build’s migrations and refuses to start otherwise, naming the schema and what is wrong with it. The pools can then hold no schema rights at all, which is the least-privilege production posture: an application-level SQL flaw can reach rows, never the schema. The check itself still reads every schema’s bookkeeping, so it runs on [database] migrate_url — see which credential prepares the schema, and set that key whenever database.url is a role that holds one domain.

Migrations are append-only, so upgrading an existing database in place is the supported path and always has been the one your data takes. A released migration is never edited: sqlx records a checksum of each applied file and refuses a database whose recorded checksum no longer matches, so a corrected schema arrives as a new migration rather than as a change to an old one. A CI guard fails any pull request that modifies, renames or deletes a migration the base branch already carries.

With verify, something else has to run the migrations first. Use the binary’s own subcommand under the migrator DSN: a CI/CD stage, a one-shot job, or the Helm chart’s migrations.job.enabled pre-install/pre-upgrade hook Job, which Helm waits on so a failed migration fails the release (it takes its own migrations.job.existingSecret holding the migrator DSN, deliberately a different credential from the runtime one, and rendering fails without it):

FERROEHR__DATABASE__URL='postgres://ferroehr_migrator:***@pg:5432/ferroehr' \
  ferroehr db migrate     # applies; exits when done
FERROEHR__DATABASE__URL='postgres://ferroehr_clinical:***@pg:5432/ferroehr' \
FERROEHR__DATABASE__MIGRATE_URL='postgres://ferroehr_migrator:***@pg:5432/ferroehr' \
  ferroehr db verify      # read-only check; exit 0 iff the schema is current

db verify splits the same way the boot sequence does, and for the same reason: the schema state is read on migrate_url, while the pseudonymisation boundary is measured on the runtime DSNs — asking the migrator credential whether it can reach every domain would answer yes by design and tell you nothing about the roles that serve requests.

Gate the rollout on the migration step so two server versions never race the schema. Note the difference in failure shape: a verify server refuses to boot against an unmigrated database (loud, immediate), while an apply server that loses its schema later stays up and reports readiness DOWN, the warning below.

Warning

Migration is a boot step, and nothing re-runs it. A running instance whose database is replaced, wiped, or reachable-but-empty does not migrate. It reports

{"state":"down","phase":"serving","indicators":[{"name":"db","state":"up"},
 {"name":"migrations","state":"down"}]}

on /health/readiness (503), with the detail core schema tables missing (migrations not applied) on /management/health, leaves the load balancer’s rotation, and keeps passing liveness (correctly, since the process is healthy) so nothing restarts it. Under Kubernetes that is a Deployment sitting at 0/N ready with no error after the first one.

The readiness check re-tests the schema on every probe, so recovery does not require a restart of that instance: it goes back to UP within one probe interval of the schema existing, whoever created it. What needs a restart is the case where the only thing that would migrate is the instance itself: then kubectl rollout restart deploy/ferroehr (or a migration job) is the remedy.

For the out-of-band flow this means: the migration step must complete before the first instance starts, or that instance sits unready until the schema appears, harmless but confusing, and it delays the rollout rather than failing it. Gate the rollout on the migration job.

Planner statistics of the partitioned tables

node, version and vo_attestation are partitioned by storage tier in both stores, and PostgreSQL estimates a join over them from the statistics of the partitioned table itself. Autovacuum analyzes the partitions and never the partitioned table (PostgreSQL 18, §24.1.3 Updating Planner Statistics), so FerroEHR runs ANALYZE ONLY on the partitioned tables itself, and on ehr while autovacuum has never analyzed it:

  • after it applies the migrations, as the migration credential;
  • after load_ehrs loads an archive;
  • at boot and then every hour, as each store’s serving role.

Without these statistics an AQL CONTAINS can read every COMPOSITION’s nodes. ANALYZE needs the MAINTAIN privilege on the table, and the migrations grant it to ferroehr_clinical on clinical.node, clinical.version, clinical.vo_attestation and clinical.ehr, and to ferroehr_party on the three partitioned tables of party. When a serving role still lacks it, for example because the roles were absent when the migrations ran, the hourly refresh logs a warning naming the tables it could not analyze. Grant the role MAINTAIN on those tables, or run the same ANALYZE ONLY from a scheduled job as the migration role.

Recovering a partially wiped database

A wipe that removes some of the server’s schemas is not a fresh start, and the server cannot tell it from one.

The server owns four schemas: ext, clinical, party and audit. A fresh start drops all four. Each domain’s cold archival tier is a partition of the relation it archives, inside that domain’s own schema, so a DROP SCHEMA clinical CASCADE takes the archived rows with the live ones. There is no separate mirror schema left to survive a wipe of the tier it mirrors.

Dropping some of the schemas is not a supported reset, because they are not independent. ext holds the helper functions the clinical and party relations depend on, so DROP SCHEMA ext CASCADE drops them with it, and those sets, still recorded as applied, never recreate them. The next boot rebuilds the dropped schemas, and its migration check reads each set’s bookkeeping only, so it passes over a database that has lost those guarantees.

A database written by a release before the storage rewrite is refused outright:

this database predates the storage rewrite: schema `ehr` carries its own
migration bookkeeping, which only a release before the rewrite wrote.

The new migration sets replace the old ones rather than upgrading them, so there is no in-place path. Dump anything worth keeping, recreate the database, and start the server against it.

Tip

When you wipe a FerroEHR database deliberately, drop the database, not a schema. DROP DATABASE cannot leave half a repository behind, and it is the only wipe with no partial-state failure mode. ferroehr db erase drops all four schemas of a database in one transaction, for taking an instance out of service (Decommissioning).

Upgrading past the linkage domain

Releases before 5.6.0 ran a third storage domain, linkage, with its own schema, role (ferroehr_linkage), [storage.linkage] and [storage.migrate.linkage] configuration, pool and backup job. It held no relation once which EHR belongs to which subject became the EHR’s own EHR_STATUS.subject, and this release removes it.

Before you upgrade, delete [storage.linkage] and [storage.migrate.linkage] from the configuration, and the linkage blocks under database and backup from the chart values: the server now refuses both tables as unknown keys, and the chart schema refuses both blocks.

On a co-located database (no [database.<domain>] naming another database) the first boot does the rest. Migration audit/0021_drop_linkage_domain.sql drops the linkage schema, revokes what the role held on ext, drops the role when nothing else in the cluster names it, and drops the btree_gist extension. When it cannot drop the role or the extension, it says so in a NOTICE and the boot carries on.

The migration runs in the database that holds the audit domain, so it does not reach every layout. Run the following by hand, as a superuser or a member of ferroehr_linkage, when either applies:

  • the linkage domain lived in a database of its own, or [database.audit] names a database other than the one that held linkage;
  • the cluster holds more than one FerroEHR database, which keeps the role named in the others.

In every such database:

DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS linkage CASCADE;
REVOKE ALL ON SCHEMA ext FROM ferroehr_linkage;
REVOKE ALL ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA ext FROM ferroehr_linkage;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA ext REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM ferroehr_linkage;
DROP OWNED BY ferroehr_linkage;
DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS btree_gist;

Then, once per cluster:

DROP ROLE ferroehr_linkage;

A database that held only the linkage domain holds nothing the server reads any more; drop it with DROP DATABASE once you no longer need it. Drop the login roles that were members of ferroehr_linkage as well.

TLS and database security

These are database-side settings that belong to whoever provisions PostgreSQL; the deployment references them but cannot enforce them:

  • TLS in transit. Require hostssl on the server and put ?sslmode=verify-full in the DSN so the client verifies the server certificate.
  • pgaudit. Run pgaudit as the database-layer complement to the openEHR audit and the ATNA trail (for example pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role, connection' globally plus object-level audit on the PHI tables) and ship the audit log to an immutable store with long (roughly six-year) retention.
  • Encryption at rest. Encrypt at the volume or disk layer. Do not encrypt the stored clinical JSON with pgcrypto: it would break AQL’s ability to query inside the data.

Backup and point-in-time recovery

Enable WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery from day one (pgBackRest or a managed PITR), because a CDR’s data is not reconstructible. Clinical and audit tables are never UNLOGGED. Test your restore, not just your backup.

Dump each domain separately

A logical backup is where the two pseudonymisation domains are easiest to re-join by accident. One pg_dump of the whole database produces a single file holding the pseudonymised clinical record beside the identities of its subjects, and whoever can read that file can re-identify every record in it, which is the separation the schema split and the database roles exist to maintain. Two domains, two dumps, into targets with different access control.

How many dumps, by DSN layout. The number of dumps follows the domains, not the databases: co-located, the three domains share one database and are dumped --schema by --schema as below; relocated, each database is dumped for the domains that live in it. What never changes is that the clinical record and the identities land in two different artefacts with two different audiences. ferroehr config check prints the resolved layout, which is the list a backup runbook is written from. The audit repository travels with the clinical dump while it shares that database (--schema=audit below) and needs a dump of its own once [database.audit] names another one. On Kubernetes that third dump is not yours to schedule: the chart renders a backup.audit CronJob as soon as database.audit carries a Secret of its own, and drops --schema=audit from the clinical job in the same render.
